epithet.en: Illegitimate son turned Count, seeker of meaning
epithet.da: Uægte søn blev greve, søger efter mening

2.modern-en: Pierre is mentioned briefly at Anna Pavlovna's soirée as one of the assembled guests, a large, ungainly young man who attracts little notice among the fashionable crowd.

3.modern-en: Pierre enters the political discussion at Anna Pavlovna's evening, visibly eager to speak his mind about Napoleon but held back by the social conventions of the room.

4.modern-en: Pierre greets Prince Andrei with warm, genuine affection as soon as he arrives at the soirée, and arranges to come to supper with him, glowing with honest pleasure at seeing his friend; he also watches Hélène pass with fascinated, almost frightened admiration.

5.modern-en: Pierre breaks into the drawing room debate about Napoleon, blushing and speaking impulsively before Anna Pavlovna cuts him off, his liberal sympathies already marking him as out of place in the royalist company.

6.modern-en: Leaving the soirée, Pierre awkwardly picks up the wrong hat and fumbles with it, encapsulating his chronic social clumsiness, though his genuine good nature draws forgiveness from Anna Pavlovna.

7.modern-en: At Prince Andrei's home after the party, Pierre and the princess chat warmly, Pierre showing none of his usual awkwardness with her; he is visibly present as a trusted family friend who occupies a peculiar, affectionate place in the Bolkonski household.

8.modern-en: Over supper, Pierre listens intently as Prince Andrei bitterly advises him never to marry; Pierre is moved and struck by the sudden rawness in his friend's face — a side of Andrei he has never seen before.

9.modern-en: After leaving Andrei, Pierre breaks his promise to avoid Kuragin's party, rationalising his weakness to himself; he joins the dissolute evening gathering and is drawn into the chaos of gambling, drinking, and roughhousing with a bear.

10.modern-en: Pierre is not present at the Rostov household gathering; chapter follows Boris, Anna Mikhaylovna, and the Rostov family — Pierre's name is not mentioned.

14.modern-en: Pierre is absent from this chapter, which centers on a private conversation between Countess Rostova and Anna Mikhaylovna, and the young people's romantic tensions in the other rooms.

15.modern-en: Pierre is alluded to indirectly as Count Bezukhov's son and Boris's godfather's relative; Anna Mikhaylovna and Boris visit the dying count's house, where Prince Vasili now holds sway, setting the stage for the inheritance struggle that will engulf Pierre.

16.modern-en: Pierre has been expelled from Petersburg for his part in the bear prank and is now staying in his father's Moscow house; he wanders awkwardly through his rooms, received like a leper by the princesses, and is warned by Prince Vasili to stay away from the dying count.

17.modern-en: Pierre appears only glancingly in this chapter, which is mainly the countess and Anna Mikhaylovna arranging money — Pierre's situation at his ailing father's house forms the backdrop but he is not directly on stage.

18.modern-en: Pierre does not appear in this chapter, which follows the Rostov household's name-day dinner conversation about the coming war.

19.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which covers the patriotic dinner conversation at the Rostovs, but the atmosphere of the coming war and Russia's mobilisation will soon reshape his own path.

20.modern-en: Pierre is absent from this chapter, which covers the Rostov children's evening entertainments and Sonya's heartbreak over Nicholas.

21.modern-en: Word arrives at the Rostov house that Count Bezukhov has had his sixth stroke and is dying; the household falls silent with the weight of this news — the inheritance crisis that will determine Pierre's fate is now fully in motion.

22.modern-en: Pierre is summoned to his dying father's house and brought in through the back entrance by Anna Mikhaylovna; confused and passive, he follows her lead, sensing vaguely that the visit is necessary though he can't quite articulate why.

23.modern-en: Pierre stands in the sickroom beside the dying count for the last rites ceremony, awkward and out of his depth, nearly making the young princess Sophie laugh despite herself as he fumbles with his candle and crosses himself incorrectly.

24.modern-en: In the tense aftermath of the last rites, Pierre trails Anna Mikhaylovna through the house as she manoeuvres against the princesses and Prince Vasili in the race to secure the count's will; Pierre himself is passive, eating nothing, understanding little of the intrigue swirling around him.

25.modern-en: Pierre does not appear in this chapter, which introduces the Bolkonski household at Bald Hills and Princess Mary's life under her demanding father.

50.modern-en: Pierre, having unexpectedly inherited the Bezukhov fortune and title, is swept along by Prince Vasili's social machinery — given a court appointment, invited into his household, and gradually manoeuvred toward a proposal to Hélène, feeling powerless against the current pulling him there.

51.modern-en: Despite privately knowing that marrying Hélène would be a mistake, Pierre is cornered at a name-day dinner by Prince Vasili's orchestrated social pressure; flushing and confused, he proposes to Hélène in a moment of weakness he immediately regrets, sealing his fate.

70.modern-en: Pierre is present at the English Club, dressed in fashionable clothes at his wife's insistence and without his usual spectacles, moving through rooms in a distracted, sad stupor — rich, deferentially treated, and utterly unhappy.

71.modern-en: At the English Club dinner, Pierre sits across from Dolokhov, tormented by an anonymous letter and hints about his wife's infidelity; he is silent and absent, staring into space while an ugly suspicion takes root.

72.modern-en: Unable to contain himself any longer, Pierre challenges Dolokhov to a duel after Dolokhov's toast humiliates him publicly; the confrontation crystallises Pierre's dawning realisation that his marriage to Hélène was a catastrophic mistake.

73.modern-en: Pierre fights Dolokhov in a snow-covered field at dawn; firing first and unexpectedly hitting him, Pierre is overwhelmed not with triumph but with horrified remorse, running toward the wounded man and sobbing.

74.modern-en: Alone in his father's old room the night after the duel, Pierre torments himself with the question of how he came to be here — recognising that marrying Hélène without love was the original lie from which everything bad followed.

78.modern-en: Pierre's duel is smoothed over by the Rostov family's influence; he then confronts Hélène and, furious and humiliated, threatens her with a marble slab before leaving for Petersburg, definitively separating from her and granting her a generous allowance.

85.modern-en: Stranded at the Torzhok post station on his way to Petersburg, Pierre lies inert on a sofa, boots on the table, gripped by an existential paralysis — asking himself unanswerable questions about justice, meaning, and whether anything is worth doing.

86.modern-en: At the post station, an elderly Freemason named Osip Bazdeev strikes up a conversation with Pierre and speaks to him with startling directness about his unhappiness; Pierre, usually guarded, finds himself drawn in and admits his inner emptiness, learning that Bazdeev is a Mason.

87.modern-en: Arriving in Petersburg, Pierre withdraws from society and reads Thomas à Kempis; a week later he is formally invited to join the Masonic Brotherhood, sponsored by Willarski, and after affirming his belief in God he agrees to be initiated.

88.modern-en: Pierre undergoes the Masonic initiation ceremony — blindfolded, his chest bared to swords, led through symbolic trials — with childlike sincerity and genuine emotion, emerging moved and hopeful that he has found a path toward moral renewal.

89.modern-en: The morning after his initiation, Pierre studies Masonic symbolism and daydreams about transforming his estates; Prince Vasili interrupts to pressure him into reconciling with Hélène, and Pierre, unable to resist as always, capitulates and writes the conciliatory letter.

90.modern-en: In Pierre's absence, Petersburg society blames him entirely for the marital rupture and the duel; he is dismissed as half-mad, while Hélène is received with sympathetic deference — Pierre's stock in fashionable society has collapsed.

94.modern-en: Pierre travels to his Kiev estate with ambitious Masonic-inspired reform plans — freeing serfs, building schools and hospitals — but quickly discovers his elaborate instructions are either being ignored or exploited by his stewards, and that his vast wealth has left him personally poorer and more confused than before.

95.modern-en: Pierre visits Prince Andrei at Bogucharovo, glad to see his friend but troubled by Andrei's bleak, shut-down mood; he is struck by how modest the new house is compared to Petersburg, and the two friends begin a long conversation that has clearly been building for years.

96.modern-en: On a carriage ride to Bald Hills, Pierre tries to share his Masonic faith with Prince Andrei, passionately arguing that Freemasonry reveals the true meaning of life — equality, brotherhood, love — while also fearing Andrei's sharp intellect will demolish his convictions.

97.modern-en: Pierre accompanies Prince Andrei to Bald Hills and meets Princess Mary and her wandering pilgrims; he listens respectfully and curiously to the pilgrim woman, treating her devout world with genuine openness rather than the contempt Prince Andrei shows.

98.modern-en: Pierre talks privately with Princess Mary, who speaks of her deep worry for Andrei's spiritual state; Pierre is moved by her concern and her world, and the visit ends warmly when the formidable old Prince Bolkonski interrogates him with sharp, probing questions.

107.modern-en: Pierre is not the focus of this chapter, which describes Prince Andrei's rural life and his encounter with the oak tree — but the chapter notes that Andrei has accomplished the estate reforms Pierre attempted and failed, highlighting the contrast between the two friends.

109.modern-en: Pierre is mentioned briefly as one of the memories flooding Prince Andrei's mind during his regenerative moment by the oak tree — 'Pierre at the ferry' — suggesting how deeply their friendship has shaped Andrei's interior life.

113.modern-en: Now a leading figure in Petersburg Freemasonry, Pierre organises dinners and lodge meetings, supports a poorhouse, and donates heavily — but inwardly grows disillusioned as he sees his brothers as the same petty, self-interested men they are in ordinary life, and feels himself sinking rather than rising.

114.modern-en: In a deep depression after a failed Lodge speech, Pierre lies inert at home; Hélène writes that she is returning, Masonic brothers pressure him to reconcile with her, and he drifts passively toward reunion — recording his anguish and moral struggles in his diary.

115.modern-en: Pierre watches with bewilderment as Hélène, back in Petersburg, has inexplicably become a celebrated hostess of a brilliant salon — her evident stupidity no obstacle whatsoever — while he drifts at the edges of her world, a stranger in his own marriage.

116.modern-en: Pierre's diary entries reveal his daily struggle to live by Masonic principles — fighting laziness, anger, and lust — he records small failures (telling a joke he shouldn't, losing his temper with Boris) and earnest nightly prayers for self-improvement.

117.modern-en: Pierre is a regular visitor at the Rostov household in Petersburg, having been dragged home by old Count Rostov; he is among the steady stream of guests at their suppers, a comfortable, familiar presence in their domestic world.

121.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows Natasha's overwhelmed, ecstatic first arrival at the grand Petersburg ball.

122.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which describes the Emperor's arrival at the ball and Natasha's fear of being left without a dance partner.

123.modern-en: Pierre does not appear in this chapter, which covers Prince Andrei dancing with Natasha at the ball and their growing mutual interest.

126.modern-en: Pierre is called on by Berg, who invites him to a small evening gathering; Pierre cannot bring himself to refuse the earnest, pompous Berg and promises to attend — arriving early, contrary to his usual habit.

127.modern-en: At the Bergs' evening party, Pierre sits at cards and watches with growing fascination as Natasha is transformed before his eyes by Prince Andrei's arrival — something important is happening between them, Pierre feels, and he is both joyful and pained by the knowledge.

128.modern-en: Pierre is not the focus of this chapter, which follows Prince Andrei's daily visits to the Rostovs and Natasha's trembling anticipation of a proposal; Pierre observes from the periphery.

130.modern-en: Pierre is not directly featured in this chapter, which describes the unusual terms of Prince Andrei's engagement to Natasha and the household's gradual adjustment to his presence.

146.modern-en: With Prince Andrei engaged to Natasha and his Masonic mentor dead, Pierre's sense of purpose collapses; he abandons his diary, stops attending the Lodge, drinks heavily, and eventually leaves Petersburg for Moscow to escape his unbearable life.

148.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which centers on the old Prince Bolkonsky's rage during his name-day and his clash with the French doctor Metivier.

149.modern-en: At the Bolkonskys' dinner, Pierre sits comfortably beside Princess Mary after the guests depart, gently warning her about Boris Drubetskoy's likely mercenary intentions toward wealthy heiresses — showing warm, brotherly candor.

153.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows Natasha's aching longing for Prince Andrei as the Rostovs prepare to attend the opera.

154.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which describes Natasha's disorientation at the opera and her first encounter with Anatole Kuragin's gaze.

156.modern-en: Anatole Kuragin arrives in Moscow and moves in with Pierre, who receives him reluctantly at first but gradually gets used to him and occasionally joins his reckless evenings out, even lending him money.

157.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows Natasha's mounting anxiety while waiting for Prince Andrei and her growing confusion after the opera encounter with Anatole.

164.modern-en: Pierre, tormented by feelings for Natasha that go beyond what is proper for a married man toward his friend's fiancée, has been deliberately staying away; returning from Tver, he is summoned by Marya Dmitrievna and learns of the Anatole crisis, arriving to find Natasha pale and transformed.

165.modern-en: Pierre hunts for Anatole across Moscow — the Club, the gypsies', everywhere — seething with protective fury; when he finally finds him at Hélène's drawing room, he confronts him directly and commands him to leave Moscow.

166.modern-en: Pierre covers for Natasha in society, firmly denying rumours of the elopement attempt; he dreads Prince Andrei's return and goes daily to check if he has arrived, and when Andrei comes, Pierre is the first to see him and give him Natasha's letters.

167.modern-en: Pierre delivers Prince Andrei's cold letter to the Rostovs and then, at Natasha's urgent request, meets her face to face; he finds her pale but dignified, and when she begs him to ask Andrei to forgive her, he is overwhelmed with pity rather than reproach.

175.modern-en: Pierre is mentioned as having warned Anatole that Prince Andrei was hunting for him; Andrei pursues Kuragin to Petersburg and Turkey but never catches him, and the chapter follows Andrei's military re-engagement rather than Pierre directly.

178.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows Prince Andrei at the military council near Drissa; Pierre's name is not mentioned.

184.modern-en: Pierre is the one person whose visits bring Natasha comfort during her illness and grief; she looks forward to seeing him above everyone else, though the text focuses on Natasha's inner desolation rather than Pierre's actions.

186.modern-en: Since leaving the Rostovs' with Natasha's grateful smile imprinted on him and gazing at the comet, Pierre has been transformed: the existential paralysis that haunted him dissolves whenever he thinks of her, replacing despair with a quiet joy he keeps entirely secret.

187.modern-en: Pierre arrives at the Rostovs' for a Sunday dinner and discovers Natasha singing again for the first time since her illness; moved and delighted, he reassures her that it is not wrong to sing, and she tells him how much she trusts and values him.

189.modern-en: At the great assembly of Moscow nobility summoned by the Emperor, Pierre sits in a too-tight uniform, excitedly sensing echoes of the French Revolution and the States-General; he is overwhelmed when the Emperor appears and speaks, and weeps openly in the crowd.

190.modern-en: Pierre witnesses the Emperor address the Moscow assembly and is overcome with emotion; he gives a subscription of a thousand serfs and fifty thousand rubles — far more than expected — inflated by his general emotional excitement rather than careful calculation.

207.modern-en: Moscow grows frivolous and festive as the French advance — people dance, give parties, read Rostopchin's comic broadsides — and Pierre, swept along by this current, attends the Club and dinners while struggling privately with the question of whether he should join the army.

208.modern-en: Pierre reads Rostopchin's broadsheets and realises clearly for the first time that the French will enter Moscow; he compulsively lays out a game of patience and interprets its outcome as a sign — it tells him to go to the army, and he resolves to go.

210.modern-en: Pierre, in his green tailcoat and white hat, has ridden out from Mozhaysk to witness the battle of Borodino; he stands on the road watching convoys of wounded pass, begins asking soldiers about the position, and is struck by the gap between the war he imagined and the actual chaotic scene.

211.modern-en: Pierre climbs a knoll to survey the Borodino battlefield and is bewildered by what he sees — he cannot identify formations, positions, or even which side is which, the panorama refusing to resolve into the strategic picture he imagined.

212.modern-en: Pierre at the Borodino position meets Boris Drubetskoy, who offers to show him around; he asks to be taken to Prince Andrei's regiment and is curious to see the left flank, getting drawn into the eve-of-battle preparations.

213.modern-en: Pierre rides the entire Borodino position with Bennigsen's party, trying to understand the battle plan but finding his mind inadequate to the task; he gazes at the redoubt that will become the most memorable spot of the battle to him, unaware of its significance.

214.modern-en: Pierre visits Prince Andrei in his shed the night before Borodino; Andrei is preoccupied with thoughts of death and delivers his famous speech about war — that it is not the noble game soldiers imagine, but murder — while Pierre listens in dismayed silence.

215.modern-en: Pierre spends the evening with Prince Andrei and his officers before the battle; he attempts to talk about military positions and Kutuzov, but Andrei is distant and severe, and Pierre feels the weight of his friend's pre-battle gravity without quite understanding it.

218.modern-en: Pierre is not directly present in this chapter, which is Tolstoy's philosophical essay on historical causation and the battle of Borodino; Pierre has no role in this authorial digression.

220.modern-en: Pierre wakes late in his borrowed corner at Gorki as the battle of Borodino begins; he rushes out and sees the panorama of the battlefield lit by morning sun, then sets off toward the action, unable to stay away.

221.modern-en: Pierre blunders into the actual fighting on the Borodino bridge, smiling in disoriented wonder at the carnage around him while soldiers shout at him to get out of the way; he is drawn toward the Raevsky battery, oblivious to the bullets passing around him.

222.modern-en: Pierre stumbles into the thick of the fighting at the Raevsky Redoubt and instinctively grapples with a French officer, then runs away in terror as the battery is overwhelmed — his first real physical contact with war.

225.modern-en: Pierre is not directly present in this chapter, which focuses on Kutuzov's quiet command style during the battle; Pierre's name does not appear.

236.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows Hélène's scandalous scheme to divorce Pierre and remarry one of two suitors; Pierre himself is absent, merely the inconvenient husband to be disposed of.

237.modern-en: Shaken by the horrors of Borodino, Pierre walks away from the battlefield alone, sits by a roadside in the dark, and is taken in by three common soldiers who share their food without asking who he is — a moment that strikes him as profound and deeply human.

238.modern-en: Unable to sleep in the yard where he has taken shelter after the battle, Pierre lies awake tormented by images of battle and suffering, and begins to feel a desperate wish to shed his identity as a wealthy nobleman and become one of the simple soldiers he has seen.

239.modern-en: Returning to Moscow after Borodino, Pierre is summoned immediately by Count Rostopchin; in the reception room he reads a broadsheet and senses the certainty that Moscow will fall to the French.

240.modern-en: Pierre has a tense interview with Rostopchin, who warns him to break with the Masons and leave Moscow; Pierre pushes back on the accusations against Klyucharev and Vereshchagin, and the meeting ends badly.

246.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows the Rostovs' discovery that the wounded Prince Andrei is among the carriages leaving their yard.

247.modern-en: Paralysed by life's demands and unable to face Hélène's letter, Pierre slips out his back door and hides in Joseph Bazdeev's empty house, where during solitary days he conceives a secret mission: to kill Napoleon.

256.modern-en: Pierre has spent days alone in Bazdeev's house in a near-insane obsessive state, haunted by memories of Borodino's simple soldiers and consumed by his fixed idea — that he is destined to assassinate Napoleon and thereby end the war.

257.modern-en: French troops occupy the house; Pierre watches from behind a corridor door, his curiosity overcoming his intention to hide, and an encounter begins with a French officer who mistakes Gerasim's terror for rudeness.

258.modern-en: Pierre falls into unexpected friendship with the charming French Captain Ramballe, who insists on treating him as a nobleman or fellow Frenchman; Pierre, disarmed by the man's warmth, cannot bring himself to leave and ends up sharing a meal and conversation.

262.modern-en: Pierre wakes with a headache and shame at having spent the evening befriending the enemy; he arms himself with a dagger and slips out into the streets of burning Moscow, his assassination plan still fixed in his mind.

263.modern-en: Pierre rescues a small Armenian girl from the burning streets of Moscow, carrying her through the chaos until he can find her parents; flushed with exertion and purpose, he feels more alive than he has in years, but is then arrested by French soldiers who mistake him for an arsonist.

272.modern-en: Pierre is held in a guardhouse, questioned by French authorities about his identity and purpose, and placed with common Russian prisoners who avoid him because he speaks French; he learns that the prisoners will be tried for arson.

273.modern-en: Pierre is marched with thirteen other prisoners through the burned ruins of Moscow to the Virgin's Field; he stares in stunned recognition at the charred wasteland that was once his city.

274.modern-en: Pierre stands sixth in line at an execution post and watches in silent horror as two pairs of prisoners are shot; the executions destroy something fundamental in him — his faith in the right ordering of the universe.

275.modern-en: After the executions, Pierre is separated from the other prisoners and placed in a ruined shed; he is in a state of spiritual collapse, feeling that all meaning has been destroyed and that he cannot find his way back to faith.

276.modern-en: Pierre meets Platon Karataev in the prisoners' shed — a round, warm, simple peasant soldier who becomes the most vivid and precious figure of his captivity; Karataev's natural goodness and patient contentment begin to quietly heal Pierre.

290.modern-en: After weeks of captivity, Pierre has been physically transformed — bearded, lean, barefoot, wearing peasant clothes — and inwardly transformed too: he has found the peace and inner harmony he had sought his whole life, through deprivation and Karataev's example.

291.modern-en: Pierre reflects on his captivity and recognises that the peace of mind he had spent years seeking through Freemasonry, philanthropy, and love has come to him effortlessly, through hardship and Karataev's simple wisdom; his old anxieties — Napoleon, politics, Hélène, his name — seem laughably remote.

292.modern-en: The French begin evacuating Moscow and the prisoners are ordered to march; Pierre tries to intercede for the sick soldier Sokolov who cannot walk, but the evacuation proceeds regardless, and the prisoners join the retreating French column.

293.modern-en: Pierre marches with the prisoners through the jammed streets of Moscow and across the Crimean Bridge, caught in the enormous chaos of the French retreat — a vast, disordered human flood that carries him along.

309.modern-en: Pierre is not present in this chapter, which follows Denisov, Petya, and the partisan raid on a French convoy.

310.modern-en: Pierre's prisoner column marches westward in the French retreat, the army around him dissolving into disorder — dead horses lining the road, men falling out, wagons abandoned; Pierre endures the hardship with a new equanimity born of his captivity.

311.modern-en: Pierre trudges through mud and rain counting steps, feeling the rain on his face as something simple and vivid rather than a misery; deep inside he is occupied by a comforting insight drawn from Karataev's story the night before, a story about innocent suffering.

312.modern-en: A French marshal passes the prisoner column; Pierre sees Karataev sitting weakened against a birch tree and catches Karataev's eyes — full of tears, wanting to say something — but Pierre, unable to face what he senses, looks away and walks on.

313.modern-en: Lying by a campfire at a village stop, Pierre falls asleep and dreams a vivid philosophical vision — a globe of living drops, each trying to expand and reflect God — with Karataev as the drop that has spread out and disappeared; he wakes to a Frenchman's shout.

329.modern-en: Released from captivity and travelling toward Orel, Pierre collapses with fever and spends three months bedridden; during his recovery, still numb from the ordeal, he gradually processes the news he has absorbed — Petya's death, Prince Andrei's death, Hélène's death — and slowly begins to return to himself.

330.modern-en: Pierre has been fundamentally transformed by captivity: where he once furrowed his brow painfully, he now wears a quiet, ironic, joyful smile; he listens instead of dominating, and people feel genuinely happy in his company — even the princess who had always disliked him grows fond of him.

332.modern-en: Pierre returns to Moscow, warmly received by everyone; visiting Princess Mary, he learns Natasha is also in Moscow, and for the first time in months thinks of her — then goes to see Princess Mary that very evening and finds Natasha there.

333.modern-en: Pierre sits with Princess Mary and Natasha speaking of Prince Andrei's death; he is overcome with emotion and acutely aware that Natasha's judgment of every word he says matters more to him than anyone else's in the world — the beginning of his conscious love for her.

334.modern-en: Pierre dines with Princess Mary and Natasha; the awkwardness of grief gives way to warmth and laughter, and Pierre admits with quiet pride that he considers himself three times richer than before — rich in something more than money.

335.modern-en: Pierre paces his room through the night, unable to sleep after seeing Natasha, turning over a vivid internal argument until he resolves: 'I must do everything so that she and I may become husband and wife' — then wakes the next morning transformed, forgetting his planned trip to Petersburg entirely.

336.modern-en: Pierre walks through the days in a state of private, overwhelming joy, convinced that everything in the world is somehow connected to his happiness; he replays every detail of his meeting with Natasha and needs nothing beyond the hope of being with her.

337.modern-en: Pierre's declaration of his feelings to Princess Mary sets Natasha's long-dormant spirit blazing again — she asks Princess Mary what he said the moment she returns; the chapter shows Pierre's effect on Natasha rather than Pierre himself, but his proposal to Princess Mary is the pivot of everything.

342.modern-en: Pierre and Natasha are married in 1813; their wedding is described briefly as the last joyful event in the old Rostov family before the count's death — Pierre is now a husband and in the background as the Rostov patriarch's end approaches.

346.modern-en: It is December 1820; Pierre has been absent in Petersburg for seven weeks instead of the expected three, and Natasha is irritable and miserable without him — the household awaits his return.

347.modern-en: Natasha has been transformed by marriage and motherhood into a strong, calm, fertile woman; she reads Pierre's letters, cares fiercely for their children, and has largely withdrawn from society — Pierre is the centre of her world.

348.modern-en: Pierre has been in Petersburg longer than expected, attending meetings of a political society; Natasha is increasingly anxious and irritable, dismissing the 'stupid societies' she once respected, because she cannot bear his absence.

349.modern-en: Pierre's return to Bald Hills is a major event for the whole household: servants, children, and young Nicholas Bolkonsky — who worships Pierre as a hero — are all quietly overjoyed; his arrival lifts the entire house.

350.modern-en: Pierre returns with gifts for everyone and reunites with Natasha, who has been miserable in his absence; the old countess receives him warmly but in her usual distracted way, focused on her card game.

351.modern-en: After supper, Pierre sits with the family talking about politics and current affairs; young Nicholas Bolkonsky listens with shining eyes, worshipping Pierre, while Denisov argues sharply about the state of Russia; Pierre speaks with authority about a new political society he is involved in.

352.modern-en: The evening conversation turns to 1812 and war memories — Pierre is 'especially engaging and funny' about the old days; later Countess Mary shows Nicholas her private diary, and the chapter focuses on their marriage.

353.modern-en: Alone at last with Natasha, Pierre talks with her in the rapid, illogical, mutually understood way unique to a husband and wife — they cover everything at once, perfectly comprehending each other; he describes his misery at Petersburg dinners without her, and she presses him with questions about his political work.

epithet.en: Idealistic prince, wounded at Austerlitz and Borodino
epithet.da: Idealistisk fyrste, såret ved Austerlitz og Borodino

1.modern-en: Prince Andrei appears briefly in Anna Pavlovna's salon — a handsome, weary young man who finds the whole gathering tiresome, including his pregnant wife Lise, though he greets his friend Pierre with genuine warmth.

4.modern-en: Andrei arrives at the Scherer evening, his bored contempt for society evident, though he warms immediately when Pierre appears; he has secured a position as aide-de-camp to Kutuzov and is leaving for the Austrian campaign.

5.modern-en: At the salon Andrei expresses sharp, sardonic views on Napoleon and the political situation, cutting through the fashionable chatter with cool intelligence.

6.modern-en: Andrei helps his wife with her cloak in the hallway after the party, detached and cold, while she chatters with Hippolyte — the distance between them painfully visible.

7.modern-en: Back at home, Andrei is irritated by Lise's shallow complaints about his going to war; he opens up to Pierre alone, begging him never to marry and confessing his misery in the marriage.

8.modern-en: Over supper Andrei pours out his disillusionment to Pierre — his wife is fine, but he feels trapped, all his noble potential wasted on drawing-room life; he urges Pierre to avoid marriage while youth still holds promise.

9.modern-en: Andrei is mentioned only as the friend whose warning Pierre ignores when he goes to Anatole's drinking party that night.

25.modern-en: Andrei is expected soon at his father's estate, Bald Hills, where old Prince Bolkonsky maintains his rigid daily routine; the household waits with both anticipation and dread.

26.modern-en: Andrei arrives at Bald Hills with Lise, careful not to disrupt his father's schedule; he greets the old Tikhon warmly and leads his wife to see Princess Mary.

27.modern-en: At dinner Andrei shares a quiet laugh with Mary over their father's eccentricities, but finds himself unable to question the old prince's authority — Princess Mary cannot understand what Andrei finds funny.

28.modern-en: The night before departing for the army, Andrei paces his rooms in serious, tender thought; Princess Mary visits and they speak intimately — she gives him an icon, and he embraces her with rare tenderness before saying goodbye.

30.modern-en: Andrei joins Kutuzov's staff in the field and watches the general diplomatically handle an Austrian representative, learning something about command and strategy.

31.modern-en: As Kutuzov's adjutant, Andrei delivers papers and observes the commander in chief skillfully deflecting Austrian pressure during their meeting; he is beginning to understand the gap between official plans and military reality.

37.modern-en: Andrei is with Kutuzov's retreating army as it crosses the Danube; he is present when Kutuzov receives word of the victory at Krems and must carry the dispatch reporting this first Russian success to the Austrian Emperor in Brünn.

38.modern-en: Andrei arrives in Brünn to deliver the victory dispatch and stays with his friend Bilibin; refreshed by the diplomat's luxurious rooms and company, he listens with amusement and irritation to Bilibin's witty account of Austrian military incompetence.

39.modern-en: Andrei prepares to present himself at Emperor Francis's court; he mixes with Bilibin's diplomatic circle, fascinated by their world of wit and intrigue, though his real passion is for the military glory he still dreams of.

40.modern-en: Andrei has his audience with Emperor Francis, who asks only a few perfunctory questions with no real interest in the answers; the meeting is a disappointment — the emperor seems more nervous than interested.

41.modern-en: Andrei sets off from Brünn to find Kutuzov's army, riding through the chaos of the Russian retreat, haunted by Napoleon's words about destroying the Russian army; he burns with shame and the desire to distinguish himself.

43.modern-en: Andrei reaches Bagration's detachment at Grünth just before the battle of Schöngraben; Bagration gives him freedom to observe and act as he chooses, and Andrei rides out to inspect the position with a staff officer.

44.modern-en: Andrei surveys the Russian position from a forward battery and sketches the terrain, calculating French superiority and the dangers of the ground; he is calm and analytical, looking for his moment.

45.modern-en: When the battle begins, Andrei rides back to Bagration feeling his blood rush — 'It's started! Here it is!' — thinking of his Toulon, his moment for decisive action.

46.modern-en: Andrei accompanies Bagration as the general calmly rides to the front lines under fire; he witnesses Bagration's almost mysterious composure, which steadies the soldiers without a word of command.

48.modern-en: Andrei watches the infantry panic — 'Cut off! We're done for!' — and sees a general desperately trying to stop the rout; he observes the moral crisis of battle at close quarters.

49.modern-en: The battle ends and Andrei watches the aftermath — Tushin's battery withdrawing, wounded men begging for rides, the young hussar cadet Rostov helped onto a gun carriage.

51.modern-en: Andrei is not directly present (chapter follows Pierre and Hélène), but his situation — away at war — shadows the story of his family's life.

52.modern-en: At Bald Hills, a letter arrives from Prince Vasili proposing a visit with his son Anatole, with obvious matchmaking intentions for Princess Mary; Andrei's father receives the news with contemptuous hostility.

53.modern-en: At Bald Hills, Anatole arrives and Princess Mary meets him; Andrei is away at the front.

54.modern-en: After Anatole's visit, the household sleeps uneasily; Princess Mary fears Anatole, the old prince simmers with contempt — Andrei is absent but his family moves without him.

56.modern-en: Andrei is with the army near Olmütz before the Austerlitz review; his presence is implied as part of the headquarters staff.

57.modern-en: The great review before Austerlitz; Andrei is with Kutuzov's staff as the two Emperors inspect the combined allied army of eighty thousand men.

58.modern-en: Boris goes to Kutuzov's headquarters specifically seeking Andrei, wanting to use his connections; Andrei receives Boris politely but efficiently and gives him an appointment with a brief, businesslike interview.

60.modern-en: Andrei attends the council of war before Austerlitz; he listens to Dolgorukov's confident optimism with skepticism, sensing the dangerous overconfidence of the headquarters staff.

61.modern-en: At the Austerlitz council of war Andrei hears Weyrother lay out the complex battle plan while Kutuzov dozes; Andrei comes in to report Bagration's absence and stays, making a mental note of how a real battle plan should look — simpler, with room for the unexpected.

64.modern-en: On the morning of Austerlitz, Andrei rides with Kutuzov through the fog, burning with the conviction that his moment has come; he imagines his Toulon as the army descends into the valley.

65.modern-en: In the confusion of battle, French troops appear suddenly close — Andrei shouts to stop the Apsherons — but panic erupts and he seizes a fallen standard and charges forward into the smoke.

68.modern-en: Andrei lies wounded on the field of Austerlitz with the standard beside him; looking up at the vast sky he feels a profound revelation — how small Napoleon seems against that infinite blue — and dimly hears the Emperor pronounce, 'What a fine death!'

75.modern-en: Two months after Austerlitz, Bald Hills receives Kutuzov's letter saying Andrei fell heroically but his fate is unknown; the old prince, stunned and silent, refuses to show his grief, while Princess Mary prays for her brother.

76.modern-en: At Bald Hills the household waits in grief; Lise's labor begins in the night — Andrei's absence casts its shadow over the birth.

77.modern-en: Andrei returns to Bald Hills unexpectedly in the night of Lise's labor; he arrives too late to help and waits outside the room in anguish as his wife's cries pierce the walls.

92.modern-en: It is 1806-07 and Andrei has settled into a quiet life at Bald Hills and Bogucharovo after Austerlitz; he has lost his wife in childbirth and now raises little Nikolai, managing his estates, reading widely, and writing a military reform proposal — but he seems inwardly dead.

93.modern-en: Andrei receives a long, witty letter from Bilibin at army headquarters describing the disasters of the Prussian campaign; the letter, old by the time it arrives, makes Andrei smile grimly at the military incompetence Bilibin describes.

95.modern-en: Pierre visits Andrei at Bogucharovo and finds him changed — cold, settled into an orderly but joyless existence, convinced life is finished; Pierre is struck by his friend's withdrawal from hope.

96.modern-en: Andrei and Pierre drive to Bald Hills, and Pierre tries to persuade Andrei that Freemasonry and the belief in something higher can redeem life; Andrei listens skeptically but is disturbed by his friend's passionate conviction.

97.modern-en: Andrei brings Pierre to meet Princess Mary and her 'God's folk' — the pilgrims she shelters against their father's wishes; Andrei gently mocks the pilgrims but is fond enough of his sister to indulge her.

98.modern-en: After the pilgrims' visit Andrei leaves Pierre with Princess Mary; she confides her worry about her brother's spiritual state to Pierre — that Andrei keeps everything locked inside and is not recovering from whatever broke him.

107.modern-en: By 1808 Andrei has transformed Bogucharovo — freeing serfs, building schools, reducing rents — and is quietly productive; he has also drafted a major proposal for reforming army regulations, and in spring 1809 he sets out for the Ryazan estate.

108.modern-en: Riding to the Rostov estate at Otradnoe on business, Andrei passes a grove of birches dominated by a gnarled old oak — mirroring his own sense of having finished with life; in the garden he catches a glimpse of the lively, joyful Natasha running and laughing, and feels an unexpected pang.

109.modern-en: Returning from Otradnoe through the same birch forest, Andrei discovers the old oak has burst into full leaf; he is seized by an irrational but powerful feeling that life is not over — that he is thirty-one and everything still lies ahead.

110.modern-en: Andrei arrives in Petersburg in 1809 and is drawn into the orbit of Speransky's reforming circle; he is initially impressed by Speransky's cold, logical mind and begins working on the commission drafting the new legal code.

111.modern-en: Andrei immerses himself in Petersburg society and finds Speransky's committee work absorbing; he is courted by the reforming party as a liberal who has freed serfs, and he begins to believe he has found his purpose.

112.modern-en: Andrei's days fill with social engagements and committee meetings; he is dazzled by Speransky and falls under his spell, seeing in him the perfectly rational, virtuous man he has been seeking.

121.modern-en: At the Bezukhov ball, Andrei notices Natasha Rostova during the polonaise and asks her to dance; she is charming in her excitement and nervousness, and he is quietly captivated.

122.modern-en: Andrei dances with Natasha and finds himself enjoying her freshness, her un-Petersburg quality, and the simplicity of her pleasure; he is more animated than he has been in years.

123.modern-en: During the cotillion Andrei dances with Natasha again, speaking to her about Otradnoe — he remembers her by the window at night — and she blushes delightfully; he is visibly drawn to her.

124.modern-en: The morning after the ball Andrei cannot stop thinking about Natasha — 'There's something fresh, original, un-Petersburg-like about her' — though he tries to dismiss it as a passing impression and return to work.

125.modern-en: Andrei calls on the Rostovs and finds Natasha even more charming at home; he stays for dinner and, when Natasha sings at the clavichord, he feels tears rising in his throat — something he thought impossible.

127.modern-en: Andrei has been calling regularly on the Rostovs; Pierre notices the transformation in Natasha whenever Andrei is in the room — she lights up, becomes herself again — and sees the same new youthfulness on his friend's face.

128.modern-en: Andrei spends the whole day at the Rostovs', clearly trying to be near Natasha; the household senses the seriousness of his intentions, the countess watches with solemn eyes, and Natasha lies awake afterwards trembling with excitement.

129.modern-en: Andrei goes to Bald Hills to ask his father's blessing to marry Natasha; the old prince, angry and contemptuous, agrees only on condition of a year's delay — Andrei complies, seeing through the tactic but feeling he has no choice.

130.modern-en: The engagement is announced privately; Andrei insists it not be made public and gives Natasha complete freedom — if after six months she no longer loves him, she is free to reject him; he calls on the Rostovs every day in the warm, sincere new relationship that has sprung up.

131.modern-en: During the year Andrei is away abroad, the old prince grows more tyrannical toward Princess Mary; Andrei visited Bald Hills in the winter and was more affectionate than usual, though he didn't tell his sister about Natasha.

132.modern-en: From Switzerland Andrei writes to Princess Mary announcing his engagement to Natasha and asking her to give their father his letter; the old prince, unmoved, tells Mary to write that he will set Andrei free soon enough — he will die.

133.modern-en: Andrei is abroad and not directly present in this chapter about Rostov's army life, but his engagement to Natasha remains the distant fact shaping the Rostov family's emotional world.

139.modern-en: Not directly present; Andrei is away in Petersburg and Turkey during this rural autumn hunting chapter.

141.modern-en: Andrei is still abroad; Natasha's longing for him — 'I want him, right now, this minute!' — runs through the chapter like a refrain.

144.modern-en: Andrei is not present; the chapter follows the sleigh ride and Nicholas's declaration to Sonya.

145.modern-en: Not present; this chapter covers the Rostov family's conflict over Nicholas and Sonya's love.

147.modern-en: Andrei is in Turkey, not yet returned; old Prince Bolkonsky has moved to Moscow for the winter with Princess Mary.

148.modern-en: Andrei is still away; at Bald Hills, Princess Mary manages the old prince's worsening moods and the doctor Metivier's visit on the prince's name day.

151.modern-en: Andrei is expected in Moscow imminently; the Rostovs have come to the city partly to finalize trousseau arrangements and to introduce Natasha to old Prince Bolkonsky.

152.modern-en: Andrei has not yet arrived; Natasha and Count Rostov call on old Prince Bolkonsky and are received coldly — Princess Mary, embarrassed and flustered, tries to be kind while the old prince refuses to see them.

154.modern-en: Andrei is not present; Natasha attends the opera for the first time and finds it artificial and absurd — this is the night she first meets Anatole Kuragin.

155.modern-en: Andrei is absent; at the opera Anatole sits beside Natasha in Hélène's box and begins his dangerous courtship, awakening in her a feeling she cannot understand or resist.

157.modern-en: Andrei has still not arrived; Natasha waits for him anxiously, her earlier confidence crumbling as Anatole's image intrudes on her thoughts about her fiancé.

158.modern-en: Andrei absent; Natasha sees Anatole again at Hélène's party and is increasingly disturbed by her feelings for him.

159.modern-en: Andrei is not present; Marya Dmitrievna advises the Rostovs to return to Otradnoe and wait for him there, since old Prince Bolkonsky won't receive them.

160.modern-en: Andrei absent; Sonya discovers Anatole's letter to Natasha proposing an elopement — the crisis of the betrayal begins.

164.modern-en: Andrei has not yet arrived from Turkey; Pierre, dreading his return, tries to help manage the scandal of Anatole's pursuit of Natasha.

166.modern-en: Andrei arrives in Moscow and immediately learns from his father's house that Natasha has broken off the engagement; he receives the letter and goes to Pierre with it — cold, bitter, and proud.

167.modern-en: Andrei has asked Pierre to convey a message to Natasha — he returns her everything and asks her to forget him; when Pierre delivers the message, Natasha begs him to ask Andrei to forgive her.

175.modern-en: Andrei goes to Petersburg pursuing Anatole Kuragin for a duel, then — when Anatole has left — accepts Kutuzov's offer of a posting to the Moldavian army in Turkey; in a new country he finds life easier to bear, though he is inwardly desolate.

176.modern-en: Andrei reports to Barclay de Tolly's headquarters at the Drissa camp in June 1812 and immediately begins assessing the fortified position with a critical military eye; Anatole is not in the army, which relieves him, but the camp strikes Andrei as badly designed.

177.modern-en: Andrei is summoned to present himself to the Emperor; he waits at Bennigsen's quarters and observes the meeting of generals — Pfuel's arrogant certainty, Paulucci's fury — with quiet contempt.

178.modern-en: The Emperor personally receives Andrei and tells him to wait; Andrei then observes the full war council of generals arguing about the Drissa position, each asserting his own theory with confident incompetence.

185.modern-en: Andrei is not directly present in the Moscow chapter about the Rostovs reading the manifesto; he is with the army.

186.modern-en: Not present; Pierre is in Moscow falling deeper in love with Natasha, while Andrei remains far away.

192.modern-en: Andrei has recently visited Bald Hills and quarreled with his father before leaving again; the old prince is ill and bitter in the aftermath of the argument.

194.modern-en: Andrei's regiment is approaching as French forces threaten Bald Hills; Princess Mary, still at the estate, is alerted that she should flee.

195.modern-en: Andrei's regiment marches along the highway past the Bald Hills avenue in the August heat; he turns aside to visit his childhood home and finds it abandoned — his father is dead, the peasants are restless, his sister has already fled.

198.modern-en: After the old prince's death, Princess Mary remains at Bald Hills caring for the household; she learns Andrei's regiment passed nearby but he could not stop long.

199.modern-en: Andrei is not present; background on Bogucharovo's independent-minded peasants, who are now on the verge of rebellion as French forces approach.

200.modern-en: Andrei is not present; Princess Mary, grief-stricken after her father's death, shuts herself in her room at Bogucharovo while the household waits for orders.

203.modern-en: Andrei is not present; Rostov rides into Bogucharovo and helps rescue Princess Mary from the rebellious peasants — without knowing this is his future sister-in-law's estate.

205.modern-en: Andrei reports to Kutuzov at Tsarevo-Zaimishche after Kutuzov has received command of the armies; Kutuzov welcomes him warmly and calls him 'a second son,' then keeps him on his personal staff and consoles him about his father's death.

206.modern-en: Andrei tells Kutuzov about his father's death and what he saw at Bald Hills; Kutuzov is moved and asks Andrei to remain with him, but Andrei requests to go to his regiment instead — he cannot stand inaction.

212.modern-en: On the eve of Borodino, Pierre finds Andrei at his regiment's position and is disturbed by the cold, concentrated anger he sees in his friend's face; Andrei speaks about war with bitter lucidity — it is simply murder.

214.modern-en: The night before Borodino, Andrei lies in his shed thinking about death with a new directness; he reviews his life and feels a cold, clear light strip away all illusions — love, glory, friendship — as the possibility of dying tomorrow becomes real and near.

215.modern-en: Pierre visits Andrei's regiment the evening before Borodino; Andrei receives him with terse, bitter remarks — he no longer believes in strategy, only in the spirit of the soldiers — and the two friends sense this may be their last meeting.

220.modern-en: Andrei's regiment waits in reserve during the Battle of Borodino; he is not directly present in Pierre's account of the battlefield.

226.modern-en: Andrei's regiment stands idle under terrifying artillery fire in the reserve position behind Semenovsk; he orders the men to lie down but stays standing himself, and a shell lands nearby — he is mortally wounded by a fragment in the abdomen.

227.modern-en: Andrei is carried to the field hospital and laid on an operating table; barely conscious, he recognizes on the adjacent table the man he hates — Anatole Kuragin, whose leg is being amputated — and feels a sudden flood of pity and love for his enemy, understanding in that moment what pure love means.

243.modern-en: Andrei is among the wounded men whose carts are moving through Moscow during the evacuation; the Rostovs are preparing to leave.

246.modern-en: Sonya discovers that the wounded prince being transported with the Rostovs' convoy is Andrei himself; she tells the countess, and both women dread telling Natasha.

260.modern-en: Natasha has learned that Andrei is in one of the carts in their convoy and sits in a state of stupor; though Moscow is burning, she can only hear his moans from a nearby house.

261.modern-en: Seven days after Borodino, Andrei has regained consciousness and is being transported with the Rostovs; he asks for tea and speaks with Timokhin — the doctor is surprised he is still alive, having expected him to die.

269.modern-en: Princess Mary has reached Voronezh after her father's death and her flight from Bald Hills; she is anxious about her brother and prays for him, suppressing the new feelings Rostov has awakened.

270.modern-en: Princess Mary hears of Borodino and Moscow's fall and sets out to find Andrei; she encounters Rostov again at a church service.

271.modern-en: Not directly present; Sonya writes to Nicholas releasing him from their engagement — partly driven by the countess's pressure — as the family worry about Andrei's condition.

277.modern-en: Princess Mary travels from Voronezh to Yaroslavl to be with her dying brother, overcoming all difficulties with extraordinary energy and determination.

278.modern-en: Princess Mary enters Andrei's room and is shocked — instead of the suffering she expected, she finds him strangely serene, almost already gone from this world; his gaze is cool and stern.

279.modern-en: Andrei lies dying in Yaroslavl, experiencing a profound spiritual detachment — he has moved beyond fear of death into a state of loving lightness; when Natasha wept at his bedside, he had briefly returned to earthly love, but now he is slipping away toward something larger.

291.modern-en: Andrei has died; Pierre learns of his death at Orel after his own release from captivity — he hears this alongside news of Hélène's death, but in his exhausted state can barely grasp the significance of either.

329.modern-en: Pierre recovers from illness in Orel and is told by Denisov that Prince Andrew died at the Rostovs' house in Yaroslavl; the news barely penetrates Pierre's exhausted consciousness — he feels unable to grasp its meaning.

332.modern-en: Pierre visits Princess Mary in Moscow and learns that Natasha is with her; his thoughts turn to Andrei — he wonders whether his friend died in bitterness or found meaning before the end.

333.modern-en: Pierre, Natasha, and Princess Mary speak together of Prince Andrew; Pierre says what a wonderful boy (young Nikolai Bolkonsky) Andrei left behind, and the conversation becomes the first living contact between Pierre and Natasha since the grief.

334.modern-en: Andrei is gone but his memory fills the room as Pierre dines with Natasha and Princess Mary; his death is the shared grief that has drawn these two women together and now draws Pierre toward them.

335.modern-en: Pierre paces his room all night after seeing Natasha, thinking of Andrei and Natasha's love — feeling guilt about his feelings, then resolving that he must do everything possible to make Natasha his wife.

347.modern-en: By 1820 Andrei is a memory; Natasha mentions him only in conversation with Countess Mary (Princess Mary), never to Pierre, assuming it would pain him — Andrei's death is the wound that shaped her.

351.modern-en: Young Nikolai Bolkonsky — Andrei's son — sits enraptured listening to Pierre and the adults; he is the living continuation of his father, already beginning to feel stirrings of his father's passionate idealism.

353.modern-en: Pierre and Natasha speak of Andrei only obliquely; his shadow is present in their happiness — Natasha is Pierre's wife partly because Andrei's death left her free.

epithet.en: Passionate, impulsive daughter of the Rostov family

11.modern-en: Thirteen-year-old Natasha bursts into the Rostov drawing room mid-run, clutching something in her dress, and stops dead when she realizes how far she has come — her first vivid introduction as a wild, irrepressible child.

13.modern-en: Natasha hides among the flower tubs in the conservatory, waiting impatiently for Boris to follow her, peering out to watch what he does when he thinks he is alone.

14.modern-en: Natasha sits nearby as her mother and Anna Mikhaylovna have a private conversation; Vera is told to leave, making it clear that among the Rostov daughters it is Natasha who holds the warmth of the house.

15.modern-en: Natasha is not present for this chapter's main action, which follows Anna Mikhaylovna and Boris to Prince Bezukhov's mansion — but the chapter shows the family world she belongs to, defined by financial anxiety and social navigation.

18.modern-en: Natasha is among the company assembled in the drawing room awaiting the formidable Marya Dmitrievna, sharing in the family's mixture of fear and amusement at the prospect of her arrival.

19.modern-en: Natasha sits at the women's end of the table during the dinner party while the men debate war with Napoleon; she is part of the festive Rostov household that hums with life even as political storm clouds gather.

20.modern-en: After dinner, Natasha is coaxed by the company to sing with Nicholas, and she performs with the mixture of pride and shyness of a girl who knows she has a gift but is not yet sure how to wear it.

55.modern-en: Natasha is glimpsed in the household background as her father and Anna Mikhaylovna receive Nicholas's letter from the front, the family's relief and tears reflecting how much they have missed him.

62.modern-en: Natasha does not appear directly in this chapter, which focuses on Nicholas's night picket duty, but the memory of home — Moscow, family, and the warmth of the Rostov drawing room — flickers through his half-dreaming thoughts.

69.modern-en: Natasha is waiting at home when Nicholas and Denisov arrive from the front; the moment of reunion is one of the chapter's emotional peaks, as the whole family rushes to meet them.

78.modern-en: Natasha is part of the background of the Rostov household while Nicholas is kept in Moscow by his new duties as adjutant; the chapter's emotional center is the family's daily life continuing around her.

79.modern-en: Natasha is present at the grand farewell dinner for Nicholas and Denisov, and the chapter captures the romantic, holiday atmosphere pervading the Rostov house — a warmth she both embodies and inhabits.

80.modern-en: At Iogel's ball, Natasha dances and is fully in her element — it is the setting where the romantic possibilities gathering around her feel most vivid and where Sonya and Nicholas's attachment deepens beside her.

81.modern-en: Natasha and Sonya are playing at the clavichord when Nicholas returns from Dolokhov's supper, and her presence — pretty, glowing in blue — is part of the tender domestic scene he is about to shatter with his confession.

83.modern-en: When Nicholas returns home after losing his fortune to Dolokhov, Natasha and Sonya are standing at the clavichord in their blue ball dresses, looking pretty and cheerful — a painful contrast to the confession he is about to make.

84.modern-en: Natasha sings a barcarolle while Nicholas listens, moved almost to tears; the beauty of her voice momentarily lifts him before reality crashes back and he must confess his gambling debt to their father.

117.modern-en: The Rostov family has arrived in Petersburg for their last season, and Natasha — now in her mid-teens — is being brought out into society alongside Sonya, the family's financial troubles temporarily set aside.

118.modern-en: Natasha is sixteen and has not seen Boris in four years; she speaks of their childhood kiss and vague promise as something long outgrown, yet in her secret heart the question of what that promise meant still torments her.

119.modern-en: Natasha bursts in on her mother's evening prayers in a dressing gown and curlers, unable to contain her excitement over Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, whom she has just met — she is flushed, breathless, and already half in love.

120.modern-en: Natasha attends the grande's New Year's Eve ball, one of Petersburg's most glittering events, stepping out of the cold carriage into a world of light and music that barely seems real.

121.modern-en: In the cramped, cold carriage on the way to the ball, Natasha imagines what lies ahead with almost unbearable excitement; once inside, she immediately draws attention and is asked to dance by Prince Andrei.

122.modern-en: Prince Andrei singles Natasha out for a dance at the ball, and in that exchange she comes fully alive — sparkling, natural, and entirely herself in a way that captivates him.

123.modern-en: Natasha dances without stopping all evening after Prince Andrei leads her out, so absorbed in her own happiness that she barely notices the Emperor's presence or any of the social dramas unfolding around her.

125.modern-en: Prince Andrei calls at the Rostovs' the next day to see Natasha in her own home; dressed simply and even prettier than at the ball, she and the whole family welcome him with uncalculated warmth.

127.modern-en: Pierre, sitting across from Natasha at cards, notices she has changed since the ball — quieter, less bright, something weighing on her — and wonders at the cause, while Boris sits beside her and she responds to him politely but without feeling.

128.modern-en: Prince Andrei comes daily to the Rostovs and makes no secret of why he is there; the whole house holds its breath around his growing attachment to Natasha, and Natasha herself is enraptured and frightened in equal measure.

129.modern-en: Prince Andrei has gone to his father to ask permission to marry Natasha, and she waits at home in a trembling, exalted state — the happiness she is reaching toward so enormous it barely feels real.

130.modern-en: Prince Andrei is engaged to Natasha, but insists the news not be formally announced and that Natasha be given a year of freedom — she accepts this condition, though it means living with uncertain hope for twelve months.

132.modern-en: Natasha's engagement to Prince Andrei becomes known to Princess Mary through a letter from her brother; the news is tender and joyful on his side, and Natasha exists in the letter as the person who has finally made him understand what life is.

133.modern-en: This chapter is a philosophical interlude on idleness and military life with no direct Natasha scenes; she is off-stage while the narrative rests between the betrothal and what comes next.

135.modern-en: As autumn sets in at Otradnoe, Natasha is part of the country household preparing for the great hunt — young, restless, and in the grip of the year-long wait for Prince Andrei to return.

136.modern-en: Natasha and Petya appear at the porch trying to get Nicholas's attention before the hunt; she is excited and animated, part of the family bustle, and Nicholas hurries past them with no time for her.

138.modern-en: Natasha and Petya have promised to return home soon but the hunt continues past midday; she is part of the scattered hunting party as the chase reaches its high point.

139.modern-en: Natasha spends the evening at 'Uncle's' rural household after the hunt, and here, unexpectedly, she picks up a balalaika and dances with a natural, Russian grace that surprises even herself — it is one of her most fully realized moments.

140.modern-en: Natasha overhears anxious conversations between her parents about the family's worsening finances; the weight of their troubles presses on her even as she moves through the lighter surface of country life.

141.modern-en: During the flat, dull days after Christmas, Natasha grows restless and bored; she finds Nicholas equally at loose ends and the two of them drift together in the sitting room.

142.modern-en: Natasha and Nicholas sit together and she opens up about the strange, inexplicable sadness that sometimes overtakes her — a melancholy that has no cause but feels like grief for something lost or not yet found.

143.modern-en: Natasha joins the mummers at the Melyukovs' Christmas party in disguise, throwing herself into the games with characteristic abandon — a rare evening of pure, unthinking fun.

144.modern-en: On the sleigh ride home from the Melyukovs', Natasha arranges the seating so Nicholas and Sonya are together; she is the quiet matchmaker now, as alert to others' feelings as ever to her own.

145.modern-en: Nicholas tells his mother he intends to marry Sonya, and the countess refuses her blessing; Natasha stands in the background of this family crisis, aware of Sonya's position and the pain being inflicted on both of them.

151.modern-en: Natasha arrives in Moscow with her father and Sonya for the winter, full of anxious anticipation about seeing Prince Andrei's family and ordering the trousseau; the city feels charged with possibility.

152.modern-en: Natasha visits old Prince Bolkonsky with her father, certain she will charm him — but the old man receives them coldly and dismissively, and the encounter is a humiliation that leaves her shaken and confused.

153.modern-en: At the opera, Natasha sits in her box dressed beautifully but low in spirits, missing Prince Andrei and still bruised by the Bolkonsky visit; she is moved against her will by the spectacle and by her own loneliness.

154.modern-en: Sitting in the opera, Natasha begins to let the artificial, glittering world pull her back to life; Hélène invites her into her box, and the world of the Kuragins begins to press in on her.

155.modern-en: Anatole Kuragin is introduced to Natasha in Hélène's opera box, and despite herself she is drawn to him — his boldness, his beauty, and his direct admiration all reach her in a moment when she is vulnerable and lonely.

157.modern-en: Natasha is tormented by the memory of Anatole while waiting for Prince Andrei, who has still not arrived; she feels guilty, confused, and unable to explain to herself what is happening inside her.

158.modern-en: Natasha sees Anatole again at Hélène's drawing room and receives a letter from him; she is being drawn deeper into a situation she does not fully understand, her good sense weakening against the force of his pursuit.

159.modern-en: Marya Dmitrievna tells Natasha bluntly that she must give up Anatole — that he is already married — and Natasha, trapped and ashamed, begins to grasp the depth of the trap she has walked into.

160.modern-en: Sonya finds Anatole's letter in Natasha's room while she sleeps; Natasha, oblivious, had fallen asleep with the letter open on the table, her face calm — a portrait of innocence already compromised.

161.modern-en: The plan for Anatole to abduct Natasha and carry her off in a troika to a defrocked priest has been fully arranged by Dolokhov; Natasha, believing herself in love, has agreed to slip out of the house at ten that night.

163.modern-en: Marya Dmitrievna intercepts the plan, confronts Natasha with the truth, and locks her in her room; Natasha is discovered and protected, but her shame is total — she stares at Marya Dmitrievna with tearless, astonished eyes.

164.modern-en: Pierre comes to the Rostovs on behalf of Prince Andrei and learns the full story of Natasha's near-elopement; he delivers Andrei's release of the engagement and watches Natasha's face as she breaks.

165.modern-en: Pierre hunts through Moscow for Anatole to make him leave the city; Natasha is not present in this chapter but its entire action is driven by what was done to her.

166.modern-en: The night after learning that Anatole is already married, Natasha secretly takes arsenic; the antidote is given in time, but she lies seriously ill, and Pierre learns of it on his return to Marya Dmitrievna's house.

167.modern-en: Natasha insists on seeing Pierre herself; pale and ill, she comes to the drawing room and asks him whether Andrei can ever forgive her — it is a moment of raw, stripped-down honesty, and Pierre tells her she deserves everything good.

179.modern-en: Nicholas hears from his parents about Natasha's illness and broken engagement — they describe it as Natasha having rejected Prince Andrei — and he writes sympathetically but does not seek leave, troubled more by duty than by the private disaster at home.

183.modern-en: The countess arrives in Moscow to be with her; Natasha is so seriously ill that the question of her conduct recedes — she is in physical and moral collapse, her family afraid she will not recover.

184.modern-en: Natasha begins slowly to recover, but the girl who emerges is quieter and graver: she cannot sing without tears, cannot laugh without a catch in her throat, and feels that any joy would be a betrayal of the grief she carries.

185.modern-en: As war news grows alarming and Moscow fills with patriotic anxiety, Natasha is still ill and withdrawn; she hears of the Emperor's appeal and the nation's danger through a kind of fog of her own sorrow.

186.modern-en: Pierre's encounter with the changed, sorrowful Natasha stays with him after he leaves the Rostovs, and her image begins to displace the spiritual emptiness that has haunted him; she is unknowingly transforming him.

187.modern-en: Pierre comes to Sunday dinner at the Rostovs and finds Natasha among the company; she is quieter than before, but something in her presence — her very seriousness — moves him more than her former brightness ever did.

205.modern-en: Natasha is not present in this chapter, which follows Prince Andrei to Kutuzov's headquarters; but she lives in Andrei's consciousness as the love he has lost through his own rigidity.

207.modern-en: While Moscow slowly wakes to the reality of invasion, Natasha is among the Rostov household but still living in the shadow of her own collapse; she is mending but not yet herself.

215.modern-en: Prince Andrei is in this chapter, speaking to Pierre before Borodino, and Natasha is invoked in the emotional weight Andrei carries — the engagement, the betrayal, the wound to his pride that has calcified into hardness.

241.modern-en: The Rostovs prepare to leave Moscow as the French approach; Natasha is part of the panicked household and helps organize the evacuation with practical energy, emerging from her long passivity.

242.modern-en: The Rostov house is in turmoil — furniture being carried out, carts in the yard, servants rushing; Natasha moves through the chaos with the rest of the family as they face the loss of everything.

243.modern-en: As alarming reports of riots and disorder reach the family, the Rostovs rush to finish packing; Natasha is in the middle of it all, the weight of leaving Moscow falling on everyone at once.

244.modern-en: It is Moscow's last Sunday before the French enter, and Natasha shares the strange, muffled atmosphere of a city that has not yet admitted to itself what is about to happen.

245.modern-en: Berg arrives asking Count Rostov for a cart to move furniture; Natasha hears his absurd request and is enraged — she goes to her father and insists the carts carrying their own things be unloaded to make room for the wounded instead.

246.modern-en: As the Rostov carriages finally leave, Sonya discovers that the wounded man in one of the passing carts is Prince Andrei himself; Natasha does not yet know, but the thread that was cut is about to be reconnected.

258.modern-en: This chapter follows Pierre among the French in Moscow; Natasha is traveling with the wounded convoy but is not yet aware that Prince Andrei is among them.

260.modern-en: Natasha sits pale and still in the room at the wayside halt, listening to the moaning of the wounded adjutant in a nearby house; she is numb, as if the exhaustion of the past months has left her unable to respond even to what is happening around her.

261.modern-en: The chapter reveals that Prince Andrei has survived his wound long enough to be moved, and that at one halt he was laid in the same house as the Rostovs; it is the moment when Natasha learns he is there and goes to him.

268.modern-en: Natasha is not directly present in this chapter, which follows Nicholas in Voronezh; she is far away with the convoy, nursing Prince Andrei in the days before his death.

270.modern-en: While Nicholas in Voronezh receives news of Borodino and the fall of Moscow, Natasha is traveling with the convoy containing the dying Prince Andrei — at a distance both from Nicholas and from the world she knew.

271.modern-en: Sonya writes from Troitsa under pressure from the countess, releasing Nicholas from their engagement; Natasha is not present but the letter will ripple back to affect her when she is ready to live again.

277.modern-en: Princess Mary sets out for Yaroslavl to find Prince Andrei, and Natasha is at his bedside — she has been nursing him through his final illness with a devotion that has transformed both of them.

278.modern-en: Princess Mary arrives at Yaroslavl and Natasha leads her into Prince Andrei's room; for the first time she sees the face that has haunted her — not angry, not wounded, but already softened toward death.

279.modern-en: Prince Andrei is dying, and in these last days Natasha is at his side; she witnesses his extraordinary calm and detachment from earthly things, and the experience of watching him die changes her at a level she will not be able to explain.

318.modern-en: After Prince Andrei's death, Natasha and Princess Mary hold each other up; both are crushed, and Natasha is so deep in grief that the world around her barely registers.

319.modern-en: Natasha feels a strange hostility toward her own family — her father, mother, Sonya — as if their ordinary life is an insult to the world of loss she has just lived through.

320.modern-en: For three weeks Natasha stays constantly at her mother's side after Petya's death is reported, sleeping in her room, making her eat, talking endlessly — it is through caring for her mother that she begins, slowly, to return to life.

332.modern-en: Pierre has returned to Moscow and is welcomed everywhere; when he mentions Natasha, Princess Mary tells him she is coming to stay, and something shifts in the air around the name.

333.modern-en: Natasha and Pierre meet again at Princess Mary's, and when he speaks kindly about Petya — 'what a wonderful boy he was' — Natasha's eyes widen and light up; it is the first real spark of feeling she has shown since the deaths.

334.modern-en: Pierre dines with Natasha and Princess Mary; the three of them sit in a tender, awkward silence — the silence of people who have said something true and do not yet know what it means.

335.modern-en: After the evening at Princess Mary's, Pierre cannot sleep: he paces his room, thinking about Prince Andrei, about Natasha, about love — and by morning he knows something decisive about himself and about her.

337.modern-en: From the evening Pierre returned, something in Natasha awoke that she cannot name — a force of life and hope she thought had died; she begins to emerge from grief not all at once but irresistibly.

342.modern-en: Natasha marries Pierre in 1813, and the novel marks it as the last happy event of the old Rostov family before illness and loss scatter what remains; in her marriage she finds not a new chapter but the beginning of a different kind of life.

345.modern-en: Natasha is present at Bald Hills as part of the extended Rostov-Bolkonsky household; her marriage and family life have settled into a new rhythm, still shaped by the love she and Pierre share.

346.modern-en: It is St. Nicholas Day eve, 1820, and Natasha, Pierre, and their children are staying with Nicholas; Pierre is expected back from Petersburg any day, and the household waits for him with varying degrees of patience.

347.modern-en: By 1820 Natasha has grown heavier and quieter, the restless girl unrecognizable in this robust, devoted mother of four; she has narrowed her world deliberately around her husband and children, finding wholeness in that constriction.

348.modern-en: Natasha reads Pierre's political letter and insists he go to Petersburg, attributing absolute importance to his work in the world; her confidence in him, and her willingness to let him go, is its own kind of love.

349.modern-en: Pierre's return is the joy of the whole household in its different registers; for Natasha it is simply Pierre — the arrival of the person around whom her domestic world turns.

350.modern-en: Natasha and Pierre enter the drawing room together; he distributes presents, and she watches him with the ease and attentiveness of a wife who knows her husband deeply and loves what she knows.

351.modern-en: Young Nikolai Bolkonsky asks to stay up and listen while Pierre talks; Natasha gives permission with the naturalness of a woman comfortable in the role of generous household center.

352.modern-en: The evening conversation turns to memories of 1812, and Natasha is part of the family circle listening to Pierre's animated, funny recollections — a moment of warmth and history shared among people who lived through it.

353.modern-en: Alone with Pierre after the others have gone to bed, Natasha talks with him in the private, fast, illogical language that belongs only to the two of them — understanding each other's thoughts before the words are finished.

epithet.en: Natasha's brother, hussar officer, honest and brave
epithet.da: Natasjas bror, husarofficer, ærlig og modig

11.modern-en: Nikolai bursts into the Rostov drawing room as a young university student, brimming with energy, and soon gets into a spirited argument about the war with the visiting colonel, declaring passionately that Russians must either die or conquer — embarrassing himself with his exaggerated heat.

12.modern-en: Nikolai announces to the family that he intends to join the hussars rather than take a comfortable post in the Archives, insisting the army is his true calling, and flirts with both Sonya and the young visitor as he defends his choice against his father's gentle protests.

13.modern-en: Nikolai slips into the conservatory and, believing himself unseen, tenderly kisses Sonya and reassures her that she is everything to him, unaware that the hidden Natasha watches the whole scene with delighted curiosity.

14.modern-en: Nikolai sits with Sonya at the window copying out verses he has written for her, their quiet happiness observed and disrupted by the disapproving Vera, who threatens to tell their mother about the relationship.

15.modern-en: Nikolai accompanies Anna Mikhaylovna and Boris to the Bezukhov mansion, where they try to gain entry to the dying Count Bezukhov's presence; he watches as his mother navigates the aristocratic intrigues with practiced skill.

16.modern-en: Nikolai is introduced to Pierre during the visit to the Bezukhov house and observes the awkward, idealistic young man, forming a first impression of this unusual figure who will become central to his life.
