18.modern-en: At the Rostov name-day dinner, Nikolai listens to the patriotic debate between the German colonel and Shinshin, then declares hotly that Russians must die or conquer, drawing both praise and a telling blush from Sonya.

19.modern-en: Nikolai engages passionately in the men's war conversation at dinner, siding with the German colonel's patriotism, then catches himself noting how his words came out more theatrical than he intended.

20.modern-en: Nikolai sings with the family at the clavichord after dinner and then slips away to find Sonya crying on her chest — moved to tears by the knowledge that he is leaving for the army and by the verses he wrote her.

25.modern-en: Nikolai is absent from this chapter, which focuses on Bald Hills; his departure for the army has already disrupted the Rostov household and is felt in the family's changed mood.

28.modern-en: Nikolai is referenced as the companion who has encouraged Boris to leave the university and join the army; Prince Andrei is shown leaving while Nikolai is already serving — the two trajectories diverging.

32.modern-en: Nikolai returns from a foraging expedition as a hussar cadet, happily greeting the German landlord and his horse, before finding Denisov still asleep after an all-night card session — a vivid picture of his easy, fraternal life in the regiment.

33.modern-en: Nikolai gets into a fierce quarrel with his regimental colonel, accusing an officer of theft, and is pressured by the staff captain and Denisov to apologize; he refuses on principle, insisting his honor requires it, though he eventually backs down.

36.modern-en: Nikolai's hussar squadron covers the retreat across a bridge under French cannon fire, and he watches the enemy appear on the heights for the first time, feeling the strange exhilaration and terror of being within sight of death.

47.modern-en: Nikolai's regiment on the left flank is caught unprepared when the French attack during the Schon Grabern engagement; after the German colonel and the infantry commander fall into a bitter dispute, Nikolai's squadron is nearly overrun.

49.modern-en: Wounded and in pain from a sprained arm, Nikolai is helped onto Tushin's gun carriage and carried from the field; he is frightened, pale, and ashamed — his first real taste of battle has stripped away all his romantic illusions of glory.

55.modern-en: A letter arrives at the Rostov house saying Nikolai has been wounded and promoted to officer; his father weeps with relief and pride, while Anna Mikhaylovna carefully manages the countess's reaction so the news doesn't overwhelm her.

56.modern-en: Nikolai rides to Boris's Guards camp to borrow money, arriving in his worn cadet coat and feeling shabby beside the polished guardsmen; he is struck by Boris's social polish and the different world of the Guards.

57.modern-en: At the great review before the two Emperors, Nikolai is overwhelmed by the spectacle and falls into a kind of rapturous worship of Emperor Alexander, convinced he would gladly die for him at that moment.

59.modern-en: Nikolai spends the eve of Austerlitz frustrated in reserve, watching others win glory while his squadron does nothing; on picket duty that night, he drifts between drowsiness and fantasies of impressing the Emperor.

62.modern-en: Nikolai stands on the night picket line before Austerlitz, half-dreaming of the Emperor noticing him and giving him an order, and imagines killing a treacherous German to prove his loyalty — a young soldier's sentimental fantasy on the edge of battle.

66.modern-en: On the morning of Austerlitz, Nikolai is sent by Bagration as a messenger to find Kutuzov and the Emperor, setting off in high spirits on what feels to him like the most glorious day of his life.

67.modern-en: Nikolai rides through the chaos of the Austerlitz defeat, unable to find Kutuzov or the Emperor; when he hears that Alexander was seen weeping alone, his idealized image of the Tsar shatters and he is left with a sense of spiritual desolation.

69.modern-en: Nikolai returns home on leave and bursts into the Rostov house in Moscow with Denisov, overcome with joy at seeing his family again after the campaign.

70.modern-en: Back in Moscow, Nikolai is celebrated as a hussar officer and war hero; he enjoys his new status, keeps fashionable company, and begins drifting from Sonya, telling himself there are plenty of other girls and plenty of time for love.

71.modern-en: At the English Club dinner in honor of Bagration, Nikolai socializes with Dolokhov, who has recently been reinstated, and begins to fall under his fascinating, dangerous influence.

72.modern-en: Nikolai sits across from Pierre and Dolokhov at the Bagration dinner; he senses Pierre's dark mood and witnesses the charged atmosphere between Pierre and Dolokhov, though he doesn't yet understand its cause.

73.modern-en: Nikolai acts as one of the seconds in the duel between Dolokhov and Pierre; he watches in horror and amazement as Pierre, expected to be helpless, shoots Dolokhov and wounds him badly.

78.modern-en: Nikolai is kept in Moscow as adjutant and grows very close to Dolokhov during his recovery; he listens to Dolokhov's confessions about his secret tenderness and his cynical views on women.

79.modern-en: Nikolai returns home from various Christmas visits to find Sonya and Dolokhov in a strange mood; Natasha whispers that Dolokhov has proposed to Sonya and been refused, and something breaks in Nikolai's heart — he cannot say whether from relief or regret.

80.modern-en: At Iogel's dance, Nikolai watches his sisters and the other young people, then dances with Sonya; by the end of the evening he has made up his mind about her, telling Natasha he intends to commit to Sonya once and for all.

81.modern-en: Nikolai arrives at Dolokhov's farewell supper and is pressured into a card game; though he has resolved not to play, he finds he cannot resist when Dolokhov challenges him directly.

82.modern-en: Nikolai loses 43,000 rubles to Dolokhov in a single sitting — a catastrophic sum — torturing himself as each card turns against him, feeling trapped and unable to stop.

83.modern-en: Nikolai comes home to find the household in its usual festive mood, Denisov singing to Natasha, and cannot bring himself to break the scene; he sits with his mother, struggling with shame and dread before confessing everything to his father.

84.modern-en: Nikolai confesses his gambling debt to his father and asks for the money; the old count quietly agrees to pay, and Nikolai is overwhelmed with shame and tenderness. That same evening, Denisov proposes to Natasha, who tells her mother with excitement.

92.modern-en: Nikolai is briefly referenced as still serving in the regiment during the renewed campaign, while his father's role in the Moscow militia is described; his absence from home increases his parents' anxiety.

98.modern-en: Nikolai is mentioned in passing: his father, the count, has failed to send his full quota of recruits to the militia, drawing the old Prince Bolkonsky's sharp criticism.

99.modern-en: Returning to his regiment after leave, Nikolai feels the profound relief of being back in the ordered, simple world of military life — away from Moscow's entanglements, Sonya, debt, and family anxiety.

100.modern-en: Nikolai lives contentedly in his dugout with Denisov in the spring of 1807, lying on his bed one morning while Denisov fumes at the quartermaster; he is called out when Denisov's forage mission turns into a confrontation with the commissariat.

101.modern-en: After Friedland and the armistice, Nikolai takes leave to visit Denisov in hospital, anxious about his wound and the legal trouble stemming from Denisov's seizure of the bread convoy.

102.modern-en: Nikolai finds Denisov in hospital, weak, swollen-faced, and obsessively rereading his petition against the commissariat; he sees the hospital's filth and despair and recognizes in Denisov a man transformed by confinement.

103.modern-en: Nikolai rides to Tilsit disguised in civilian clothes, carrying Denisov's petition to deliver to the Emperor; he arrives and accepts Boris's hospitality, feeling increasingly uncomfortable with Boris's social calculations.

104.modern-en: Nikolai wanders Tilsit on the day the peace is signed, brooding over how to deliver Denisov's petition; he decides to confront the Emperor directly and walks to the royal quarters, resolved not to miss his chance.

105.modern-en: Nikolai sees Napoleon and Alexander together at the ceremony and is shocked to find that Napoleon seems perfectly at ease with the Tsar as an equal; his idol worship of Alexander cracks further, and Denisov's petition is never delivered.

108.modern-en: Nikolai's regiment is stationed near the Rostov estate; Prince Andrei glimpses Natasha running outside and is moved without knowing why, while Nikolai's presence at home is implied through his family's ongoing debts.

117.modern-en: Nikolai's continued service in the regiment, modest spending, and infrequent letters home are described; the family's finances have deteriorated further, and his mother hopes to arrange a rich match for him.

119.modern-en: Natasha speaks to her mother late at night about Boris and about love; Nikolai is peripheral but his situation with Sonya and the family's hopes for a wealthy match form the subtext of the conversation.

130.modern-en: Nikolai does not appear directly in this chapter about Natasha's engagement to Andrei, but the chapter notes that his sister's coming marriage and his own regiment life are both pulling him in different directions.

131.modern-en: Nikolai is in his regiment abroad during 1810 and receives letters from home; the chapter establishes his deliberate avoidance of returning to deal with family problems and his quiet guilt about Sonya.

132.modern-en: Nikolai receives letters about Natasha's engagement and is annoyed — partly at losing his sister to the household, partly at Bolkonsky's presumption — but defers his return as usual.

133.modern-en: Nikolai finally returns home in 1810 after his mother's increasingly urgent letters; his regiment life has been a blessed respite from family complications, but he arrives knowing he must deal with the estate's ruin and his promise to Sonya.

134.modern-en: Nikolai tries to sort out the estate accounts and, finding them hopelessly corrupt, drags the steward Mitenka out and kicks him off the property in a rage; it accomplishes little but gives him a brief sense of control.

135.modern-en: Nikolai throws himself into his greatest pleasure — the autumn hunt — and the whole household is mobilized; he leads the expedition with practiced authority, this outdoor life showing him at his most confident and happiest.

136.modern-en: Nikolai leads the great hunt through the fields and woods near Otradnoe, coordinating with his neighbor Uncle and managing the enormous pack of dogs and huntsmen; he and Natasha ride together, both fully alive.

137.modern-en: Nikolai waits breathlessly at his post as the wolf approaches, prays silently for luck, and is rewarded when the great gray wolf runs directly toward him; he releases the borzois and experiences a moment of pure, timeless joy.

138.modern-en: During the afternoon fox hunt, Nikolai gets into a dispute with one of the Ilagin huntsmen over a fox that both packs chased; he handles the confrontation and then meets the neighboring landowner Ilagin graciously.

139.modern-en: The hunting party ends at Uncle's small house, where Nikolai sits at ease in the bachelor's simple household; he watches Natasha dance to the balalaika, moved by her joy and by the Russian country air of the whole evening.

140.modern-en: Nikolai is told by his mother that Julie Karagina — now a rich heiress — would be a suitable match; he is resistant, knowing it would mean abandoning Sonya, and the growing financial ruin of the estate presses on him.

141.modern-en: During the dull Christmas holiday at Otradnoe, Nikolai falls into a melancholy conversation with Natasha about sadness and the strange passing of happy times — a rare moment of quiet introspection between brother and sister.

142.modern-en: Nikolai and Natasha sit together and slip into warm reminiscence about their shared childhood, the mysterious man they half-remember from the old house, and the stories of their earliest years — Sonya joins in but can only partly keep pace.

143.modern-en: Nikolai goes mumming with the family at the Melyukovs', dressed as a lady hussar; disguised and laughing, he dances and plays games, and by the end of the evening he finds himself looking at Sonya in a new, transformed way.

144.modern-en: Driving home in the sleigh after the Melyukovs', Nikolai gazes at the disguised Sonya and makes up his mind: he calls out to Natasha that he has decided about Sonya, and she is radiant with approval.

145.modern-en: Nikolai tells his mother of his firm resolve to marry Sonya; the countess is cold and refuses her blessing, his father is helpless and ashamed, and Nikolai storms at his mother before the conflict ends in silence and tears.

147.modern-en: Nikolai is with his regiment but his family — especially his mother's desperate match-making schemes and the estate's ruin — is the offstage pressure on this chapter's action in Moscow.

148.modern-en: Nikolai is peripheral; the chapter is set in Moscow with Princess Mary and the old prince.

151.modern-en: Count Rostov brings Natasha and Sonya to Moscow to stay with Marya Dmitrievna; Nikolai is not present but his family's financial struggles and his regiment are the background to the visit.

152.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; his family visits Princess Mary and the old Prince Bolkonsky, who refuses to receive them.

153.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; Natasha and Sonya go to the opera and Natasha's encounter with Anatole Kuragin begins.

157.modern-en: Nikolai is absent from Moscow; his family is in crisis but he is with his regiment.

158.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; the chapter follows Natasha and Anatole at Helene's soiree.

160.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; Sonya finds Anatole's letter to Natasha and the crisis over Natasha's near-elopement begins.

175.modern-en: Nikolai is not in this chapter; it follows Prince Andrei after Natasha's betrayal.

179.modern-en: At the start of the 1812 campaign, Nikolai receives a letter about Natasha's illness and the broken engagement; he replies to his parents that honor keeps him from leaving, and writes Sonya a passionate letter promising to return and marry her as soon as the war is over.

180.modern-en: On campaign in Poland before battle, Nikolai and his fellow officers crowd around Mary Hendrikhovna in the tavern, flirting and joking in the warmth while rain pours outside — a moment of lighthearted camaraderie before the coming fighting.

181.modern-en: Nikolai leads his squadron out at dawn toward Ostrovna, riding at ease on his fine Don horse, feeling no fear — a transformation he notes with satisfaction in himself since his first terrified battle.

182.modern-en: Nikolai spots the French dragoons chasing the Russian Uhlans and, acting on pure instinct without orders, leads his squadron in a charge that saves them; he singles out a French officer on a gray horse, cuts him down — and is left shaken when he sees the small, frightened man he has wounded.

184.modern-en: Nikolai is absent from Moscow during Natasha's long recovery; he is still with his regiment.

186.modern-en: Nikolai is briefly referenced as still in the army; the chapter is mainly about Pierre and Natasha.

188.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; the chapter follows Petya's attempt to see the Emperor in Moscow.

189.modern-en: Count Rostov and the nobles of Moscow gather to pledge men and money to the Tsar; Nikolai is with his regiment but his family's contribution is made in his name.

190.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; the chapter follows Pierre and the Emperor's appeal to the Moscow nobility.

192.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; the chapter is at Bald Hills with Princess Mary and the old prince.

197.modern-en: Lavrushka — Denisov's former serf and now Rostov's orderly — is captured by the French and interviewed by Napoleon himself; Lavrushka's insolent jokes and the anecdote illustrate the Russian soldier's contempt for the invader.

203.modern-en: Nikolai rides with Ilyin to Bogucharovo to secure provisions before the French arrive, not knowing it is Bolkonsky's estate; he encounters the rebellious peasants who are preventing Princess Mary from leaving.

204.modern-en: Nikolai takes charge of the Bogucharovo peasant uprising with brisk, instinctive authority; he strides into the crowd with fierce energy and the peasants back down — he then meets Princess Mary and escorts her safely away, feeling an unfamiliar emotion.

207.modern-en: Nikolai is with his regiment in the army retreating toward Moscow; this chapter describes Moscow's surprisingly frivolous mood as the French advance, which the army beyond the city does not share.

241.modern-en: The countess's terror for both her sons — Nikolai in the army and Petya newly enlisted — is the emotional center of this chapter; Nikolai is away near Voronezh buying horses and his letter does not ease her mind.

251.modern-en: A young officer — revealed to be a relative of the Rostovs — stops at the abandoned Rostov house in Moscow; through Mavra Kuzminichna's kindness he receives money, illustrating the Rostov spirit even in the deserted city. Nikolai is absent.

259.modern-en: The Rostov family refugees camp at Mytishchi and watch the glow of Moscow burning in the distance; Nikolai is not present — he is still with the army — but the burning city and Petya's death will soon break the family.

267.modern-en: Nikolai is back with the army during the French occupation of Moscow, serving without heroic self-consciousness; the chapter describes how ordinary soldiers like him simply did their duty, and were more useful for it than those consumed by patriotic posturing.

268.modern-en: Nikolai is in Voronezh buying remount horses, attending a ball and flirting with a blonde lady; the governor's wife introduces him to Princess Mary's aunt Malvintseva and drops hints about Princess Mary.

269.modern-en: Nikolai meets Princess Mary properly in Voronezh society; both are embarrassed and deeply moved, and the governor's wife and Malvintseva maneuver them toward each other with cheerful matchmaking energy.

270.modern-en: With the news of Borodino and Moscow's fall, Nikolai grows restless and ashamed of being in comfortable Voronezh; he sees Princess Mary at church, goes to her, and offers comfort about her brother — their mutual feeling deepens without words.

271.modern-en: Sonya's letter from Troitsa reaches Nikolai — she releases him from his promise, guided partly by necessity and partly by Natasha's intervention — though Nikolai does not yet know its full significance.

275.modern-en: Nikolai is not present in this chapter, which follows Pierre in captivity.

277.modern-en: Princess Mary travels from Voronezh to Yaroslavl to see Prince Andrei; Nikolai is back with his regiment but the chapter establishes that Princess Mary now knows she loves him and is loved in return.

278.modern-en: Nikolai is absent; the chapter is Princess Mary and Natasha's visit to the dying Prince Andrei.

302.modern-en: Nikolai briefly appears in the partisan operations context as the chapter opens with Denisov's guerrilla unit; the chapter is primarily Denisov's story but Nikolai's regiment and the broader campaign frame it.

333.modern-en: Nikolai is referred to only through the death of young Petya — Pierre learns that the Rostovs have lost their youngest son and that the family is in grief. Nikolai is still with the army.

342.modern-en: After the war, Nikolai learns of his father's death and returns to Moscow; he accepts the enormous debts rather than repudiate his father's memory, dedicating himself to paying them off through years of austere farming.

343.modern-en: Princess Mary comes to Moscow and calls on the Rostovs; Nikolai receives her with cold formality, his pride wounded by circumstance, but he cannot suppress his real feeling for her — and after her visit he is irritable and confused.

344.modern-en: In the winter of 1813, Nikolai marries Princess Mary and moves to Bald Hills; over the next seven years he pays off all his debts, buys back land, and becomes an expert, humane estate manager — fulfilled in work and love.

345.modern-en: Nikolai's quick temper leads him to beat a serf one summer; when Princess Mary shows her silent distress, he is overcome with shame and promises never to do it again, the broken ring on his finger becoming a permanent reminder.

346.modern-en: On the eve of his name day, Nikolai manages his estate business and sits down to dinner with his large household; brief friction with Princess Mary during the meal is quickly resolved by mutual tenderness.

348.modern-en: Nikolai is one of the people most relieved by Pierre's return, partly because Pierre's presence makes him more cheerful and good-humored, and partly because it ends Natasha's anxious suffering.

349.modern-en: The household at Bald Hills is described in its different overlapping worlds; Nikolai presides over the estate and family with quiet authority, and his closeness to Pierre and Natasha is evident in the warm reunion scene.

350.modern-en: Nikolai joins the family gathering after Pierre's return, sitting by his borzoi bitch, asking Pierre about Petersburg and the current political affairs with serious interest.

351.modern-en: At the evening gathering, Nikolai listens to the political conversation and asks Pierre careful questions; he takes the affairs of government very seriously, viewing them as weighty duties rather than intellectual games.

352.modern-en: Nikolai goes to his study after supper, then finds Princess Mary writing in her diary; he reads her entries about the children with growing admiration and tenderness, understanding for the first time the depth of her quiet moral effort.

353.modern-en: Nikolai is asleep while Pierre and Natasha talk, and while young Nikolai Bolkonsky lies awake in the dark in a fever of youthful idealism about Pierre — the next generation already stirring in the shadows.

epithet.en: Andrei's devout sister, marries Nikolai Rostov
epithet.da: Andrejs fromme søster, gifter sig med Nikolaj Rostov

1.modern-en: Princess Marya is discussed by Anna Pavlovna and Prince Vasili as a potential match for Anatole Kuragin—described as unhappy and living under her eccentric, exiling father. She is not yet present in the narrative.

2.modern-en: Marya is absent from the chapter, though the little Princess Bolkonskaya (Lise), Andrei's pregnant wife, attends Anna Pavlovna's soiree and charms the gathering with her lively chatter.

10.modern-en: Not appearing directly, Marya is referenced as the reason Prince Vasili's party visits Anna Pavlovna—he is pondering the arranged marriage between Anatole and the 'unhappy' princess at Bald Hills.

18.modern-en: Marya is not at the Rostov name-day celebration; she exists only as a name floated among Petersburg matchmakers thinking of Anatole's future.

19.modern-en: Marya does not appear in this chapter.

20.modern-en: Marya does not appear in this chapter.

25.modern-en: At Bald Hills, Princess Mary enters her father's study each morning for their geometry lesson—a ritual of fear and failed comprehension. After a rough session she retreats to her room and reads a letter from her friend Julie Karagina, revealing her deep loneliness and her quietly devout, self-sacrificing nature.

26.modern-en: Princess Mary is practicing the clavichord when her brother Andrei and his pregnant wife Lise arrive unexpectedly; she and Lise embrace in tears of joy, and Mary is visibly moved by the brief reunion, already anxious about her brother's imminent departure for the war.

27.modern-en: At dinner, Princess Mary defends her father's eccentric brilliance with genuine reverence while Andrei mocks it gently—she cannot fathom his irony. She later reassures the frightened little princess by calling the old man 'so kind.'

28.modern-en: Princess Mary slips away from the household the evening before Andrei's departure to speak with him privately, calling him by the childhood name 'Andrusha.' She pleads with him to be kind to the pregnant Lise, offering compassionate counsel that reveals her tender, forgiving heart.

52.modern-en: Prince Vasili and Anatole arrive at Bald Hills as suitors. Princess Mary braces herself with prayer, acutely aware of the social and spiritual weight of a potential marriage she has resolved to accept as God's will—whatever form it takes.

53.modern-en: When Princess Mary enters the drawing room, she is overwhelmed by Anatole's physical beauty and cannot quite look at him directly. She senses immediately that he is not thinking of her at all but is entirely self-absorbed, while she struggles to behave naturally in front of the guests.

54.modern-en: Alone at night after the visit, Princess Mary is tormented by fear—Anatole's blank handsomeness frightens her more than plain rejection would. Her old prince, meanwhile, rages privately because he suspects Anatole's real interest lies with Mademoiselle Bourienne, not his daughter.

75.modern-en: After news arrives that Andrei may have been killed at Austerlitz, Princess Mary goes to her father, who shouts 'Killed!'—and in that instant something transcendent lights up her face: grief mingled with a strange, selfless joy beyond sorrow. The old prince breaks down; she endures his pain alongside her own.

76.modern-en: As the little princess goes into labor at Bald Hills, Princess Mary runs frantically to fetch the midwife, then spends agonized hours waiting alone, praying desperately but finding prayer impossible, listening to sounds from her sister-in-law's room.

77.modern-en: Princess Mary waits outside the bedroom through the screams of labor. When the newborn cries and Lise is found dead, the terrible event falls on her as both loss and new responsibility—she will become the mother figure for the infant Nikolai.

92.modern-en: In the years after Austerlitz, Princess Mary dedicates herself to raising her nephew Nikolai and caring for pilgrims who visit Bald Hills. Her father is consumed by his new military duties; she quietly bears the household alone, finding solace in her nephew and her faith.

93.modern-en: Princess Mary is not the focus of this chapter, which is dominated by Bilibin's humorous letters to Andrei about the military campaigns. She appears only in the background of the narrative.

95.modern-en: Marya does not directly appear in this chapter, which centers on Pierre visiting Andrei at Bogucharovo.

97.modern-en: When Andrei brings Pierre to Bald Hills, Princess Mary is caught entertaining her beloved 'God's folk'—pilgrims and wanderers—and blushes with embarrassment at her brother's amused disapproval, though she defends her guests with quiet dignity.

98.modern-en: Princess Mary speaks privately with Pierre about her anxiety for Andrei's spiritual and physical health, asking him to persuade her brother to seek treatment abroad—revealing how deeply she watches and worries for the people she loves.

109.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear in this chapter about Andrei's spring journey and his renewed hope after seeing the reborn oak.

121.modern-en: Marya does not appear in this chapter, which is the Rostovs' first great ball in Petersburg.

131.modern-en: As her father grows more tyrannical and mocking—targeting her devotion to little Nikolai and to religion—Princess Mary endures his cruelty through her Christian law of love. She writes to Julie Karagina in mourning, keeping silence about Andrei's engagement to Natasha.

132.modern-en: Princess Mary receives Andrei's letter from Switzerland announcing his engagement to Natasha and begging her to give their father the enclosed letter. She does so, and the old prince's anguished, bitter response—'Write and tell him to wait until I'm dead'—lands on her with the full weight of his pain.

147.modern-en: In Moscow for the winter, Princess Mary is even more isolated than at Bald Hills—excluded from society by her father, living only for little Nikolai's education. The private life behind the grand facade is exhausting and joyless.

148.modern-en: On the old prince's name day, Princess Mary manages the household's formal dinner while quietly absorbing her father's rages—first against the French doctor Metivier, then against his guests, bracing herself through the day as she always does.

149.modern-en: After the dinner guests leave, Princess Mary stays with Pierre, distracted by anxiety about her father's hostile mood. Pierre gently warns her that Boris Drubetskoy courts her only for her fortune, but she can barely take it in.

150.modern-en: Princess Mary is the subject of Boris's matrimonial calculations, though she is largely absent from his thoughts; her awkward manner at their previous meeting has made him prefer the more welcoming Julie.

151.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear in this chapter, which concerns the Rostovs' arrival in Moscow.

152.modern-en: When Natasha and Count Rostov visit the Bolkonsky house, Princess Mary enters flushed and agitated. She takes an instant dislike to Natasha—finding her too fashionable, too cheerful, and too vain—a reaction rooted in her own insecurity before having formed any real impression.

153.modern-en: Princess Mary is not directly featured in this chapter about the Rostovs at the opera.

157.modern-en: Princess Mary remains in the background as the Rostovs wait for Andrei and worry about the old prince's hostility; she is not a direct actor in these events.

159.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear directly—the chapter focuses on Marya Dmitrievna's advice to the Rostovs to return to Otradnoe.

160.modern-en: Princess Mary is not present in this chapter about Sonya discovering Anatole's letter.

163.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear in this chapter concerning Marya Dmitrievna's handling of the elopement crisis.

164.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear directly; the chapter concerns Pierre's investigation and discovery of the Kuragin situation.

166.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear directly, but it is revealed that Mademoiselle Bourienne has stolen Natasha's letter breaking off the engagement and given it to the old prince, who shares it with Andrei—a betrayal that will shape his cold reception of Natasha's break.

167.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear in this chapter about Natasha meeting Pierre.

175.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear; the chapter follows Andrei's departure to find Anatole and then join the army in Turkey.

192.modern-en: After Andrei leaves again for the army, the old prince turns his fury entirely on Princess Mary—blaming her for the quarrel with his son—and refuses to see her for a week. She submits with patient love, spending her days with little Nikolai and her pilgrims.

193.modern-en: Princess Mary does not appear directly in this chapter, which shows the old prince giving Alpatych his long list of errands for Smolensk.

194.modern-en: As war approaches Bald Hills, Dessalles urges Princess Mary to write to the governor in Smolensk for news of their danger—advice she follows, sending a letter while her father remains oblivious to the threat.

198.modern-en: As French forces near Bald Hills, the old prince orders Princess Mary to leave while he prepares to defend the estate. She refuses—for the first time in her life disobeying him openly—and endures the storm of his fury, knowing in her heart that he is secretly glad she has stayed.

200.modern-en: After her father's death, Princess Mary locks herself in her room, prostrated by grief and tormented by guilt—she wonders if there was spiritual corruption in her own heart during his final illness. She lies on the sofa staring at the wall, unable even to pray.

201.modern-en: With French forces approaching Bogucharovo, Princess Mary goes out alone to address the rebellious peasants who refuse to help her leave—an act of moral courage that leaves her shaking but resolute, determined to fulfill what she believes her brother would do.

202.modern-en: In the still night after the peasant confrontation, Princess Mary sits by her window reliving vivid memories of her father's last days—his helplessness, his whispered nighttime words, his final stroke—and slowly begins to grieve him without horror.

203.modern-en: The chapter introduces Rostov arriving at Bogucharovo; Princess Mary has not yet been rescued. Her situation—trapped with rebellious peasants and approaching French forces—is the context for his arrival.

204.modern-en: Rostov intervenes on Princess Mary's behalf, intimidating the rebellious Bogucharovo peasants into compliance. Princess Mary receives him with grateful, luminous eyes, and he is struck—against all expectation—by her beauty in that moment of distress.

207.modern-en: Princess Mary is not featured in this chapter about Moscow's frivolous mood during the French approach.

236.modern-en: Princess Mary is not featured in this chapter about Helene Bezukhova's remarriage schemes.

241.modern-en: Princess Mary is referenced indirectly; Nicholas's encounter with her at Bogucharovo has stirred the Rostov family's matchmaking instincts, troubling the countess.

268.modern-en: At a social event in Voronezh, Nicholas Rostov is told that Princess Mary's aunt Malvintseva is there and wants to meet him—the man who rescued her niece. Nicholas flushes at the mention of Princess Mary's name.

269.modern-en: Princess Mary is in Voronezh at her aunt Malvintseva's house, outwardly at peace but inwardly quietly suppressing the feelings that her encounter with Rostov had stirred. When the governor's wife mentions Rostov to her, her mental peace is disturbed again—desires and self-reproach revive.

270.modern-en: On hearing of the fall of Moscow and Andrei's wound at Borodino, Princess Mary immediately resolves to go find her brother. At a church service she and Rostov see each other; he is struck by the transcendent expression of sorrow and prayer on her face—quite different from the woman he met before.

271.modern-en: Princess Mary is discussed by the Rostov family as the obvious match for Nicholas, causing the countess to pressure Sonya into releasing him from their engagement—a chain of events triggered by the depth of Nicholas's admiration for the princess.

277.modern-en: Princess Mary sets out from Voronezh to find her dying brother, traveling difficult roads with remarkable energy. Her love for Rostov has settled quietly into her soul—no longer tormenting but now simply a part of her—as she focuses entirely on reaching Andrei.

278.modern-en: Princess Mary enters the room where the dying Andrei lies and immediately feels her sobs dry up. His cold, detached gaze silences her—he seems already half gone, looking not outward but inward. She kisses him and sits beside Natasha, sharing a vigil of love and helplessness.

279.modern-en: Princess Mary is present as Andrei moves deeper into the spiritual realm—the novel's extended meditation on his dying. She and Natasha attend him in silence, witnessing the extinction of a brother she has loved all her life.

318.modern-en: In the days after Andrei's death, Princess Mary and Natasha are bound together in grief—speaking little, guarding each other from painful intrusions, living in a hushed world where ordinary life feels like an insult to the sacred mystery they have witnessed.

320.modern-en: Princess Mary postpones her departure to stay with the devastated Rostov family after Petya's death. For three weeks she watches over Natasha, who nurses the shattered Countess—and in their shared mourning, the bond between the two women deepens into something like sisterhood.

332.modern-en: Pierre visits Princess Mary in Moscow shortly after the French withdrawal. She talks to him about Andrei's final days, moved to tears, while sensing that something new and hopeful is forming between him and Natasha.

333.modern-en: Princess Mary, with Natasha, receives Pierre for a long evening conversation. She gently draws Pierre into telling stories of his captivity, watches the play of Natasha's feeling for him, and feels both joy and a tender grief at what she sees unfolding.

334.modern-en: Princess Mary hosts a dinner for Pierre and Natasha and quietly manages the mood of the gathering with warmth. She sees Pierre struggling with his feelings for Natasha—and understands, without reproach, that love and life are reasserting themselves.

335.modern-en: Princess Mary is not directly present in this chapter, which is Pierre's sleepless night deciding to pursue Natasha.

337.modern-en: After Pierre's late-night conversation with Princess Mary, Natasha meets her at the door—glowing with the certainty that Pierre has spoken—and Princess Mary confirms it with tender, slightly sad eyes. She feels the weight of her brother's memory alongside her joy for Natasha.

343.modern-en: Princess Mary comes to Moscow, steels herself, and visits the Rostovs. Nicholas receives her with cold formality—trapped between guilt over Sonya and the crushing family debt—and she leaves hurt and confused. But his behavior afterward reveals to himself how much she means to him.

epithet.en: Andrei's stern, eccentric father

1.modern-en: Old Prince Bolkonsky does not appear in this chapter, though he is discussed: Anna Pavlovna describes him to Prince Vasili as a brilliant but eccentric man who was exiled by the previous emperor and still lives at Bald Hills with his daughter Princess Mary.

4.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear directly, but the contrast between Andrei's manner and his father is implied—Andrei's cold social mastery and barely concealed boredom carry the father's stamp.

25.modern-en: The old prince runs Bald Hills with iron regularity—mathematics lessons, lathe work, gardening—and greets Marya's morning visit with a rigorous geometry drill that humiliates and terrifies her, followed by an unexpected tenderness when he tucks a religious book into her hands with a pat on the back.

26.modern-en: When Andrei arrives with the pregnant Lise, the old prince maintains his routine without interruption, only greeting his son during the allotted dressing hour—yet in that brief scene his pride and gruff affection for Andrei are unmistakable beneath the theatrics.

27.modern-en: At dinner the prince holds court—directing conversation at Mikhail Ivanovich to demonstrate his egalitarian principles, dismissing the current generals as children who couldn't hold a candle to Suvorov, and arguing with sharpness and wit that Bonaparte succeeds only because there are no real commanders left to stop him.

28.modern-en: The old prince retires as usual after dinner, but earlier gave his son farewell during the dressing hour—his characteristic blend of pride, military commentary, and barely expressed love as Andrei prepares to leave for the war.

38.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear in this chapter, which takes place at Bilibin's quarters in Brünn.

39.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear in this chapter.

40.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear in this chapter.

41.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear in this chapter.

52.modern-en: The old prince receives the news of Prince Vasili's visit with contemptuous hostility—he has always despised Vasili, and suspects the visit is a marriage scheme for Anatole. He stalks the estate in his foulest mood, snapping at the steward over the swept path and working himself into barely suppressed fury before the guests arrive.

53.modern-en: During the visit, the old prince is prickly and deliberate—making clear his low opinion of Prince Vasili while testing Anatole with a sharp question about his military knowledge. He watches everything, misses nothing, and forms his verdict quickly.

54.modern-en: Alone after the guests retire, the old prince rages to himself through the night—enraged that Anatole barely looked at Princess Mary and showed every sign of preferring Mademoiselle Bourienne. He decides to protect his daughter by pointing this out, and begins calculating how to engineer the situation to keep Mary with him.

68.modern-en: After the battle of Austerlitz, Andrei is left for dead on the field—the shadow of the old prince's demanding love hanging over the scene as his son has done exactly what his father raised him to do: fight courageously, lead by example, and fall with a standard in his hand.

75.modern-en: Word comes to Bald Hills that Andrei has fallen at Austerlitz—possibly dead. The old prince tells Princess Mary the news by crying 'Killed!' and then breaking down—a rare, devastating crack in his iron composure, revealing the depth of his love beneath the severity.

76.modern-en: As Lise goes into labor, the old prince cannot sleep—pacing his study, tormenting himself. He is excluded from the birth chamber but his invisible presence fills the house.

92.modern-en: After Austerlitz, old Prince Bolkonsky is appointed military commander for three provinces and throws himself into the work with renewed energy—he travels constantly, is meticulous and tyrannical with subordinates, and clearly uses the duty as a bulwark against grief over Andrei's wound and Lise's death.

97.modern-en: The old prince receives Pierre warmly when he arrives with Andrei at Bald Hills—'Very glad! Give me a kiss!'—and engages him in a fierce, jovial debate about war and human nature before supper, his intellectual energy as fierce as ever.

98.modern-en: At supper, the old prince cheerfully challenges Pierre's optimism about the end of wars—'Drain the blood from men's veins and fill them with water, and then there'll be no more war!'—and then debates Napoleon's campaigns with relentless combative intelligence.

110.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear directly in this chapter about Andrei's time in Petersburg with Speransky.

111.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear directly in this chapter.

112.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear directly in this chapter.

131.modern-en: Now more tyrannical and senile than before, the old prince targets Princess Mary's two greatest sources of comfort—her devotion to little Nikolai and her religious faith—mocking both with deliberate cruelty. Yet Mary's love for him never wavers.

147.modern-en: Moved to Moscow for the winter, the old prince has aged visibly—dozing off in company, forgetting recent events, yet arriving for tea each evening in his old-fashioned coat and powdered wig to deliver biting judgments. He is the center of Moscow's anti-government salon, unaware that his mental powers are failing.

148.modern-en: On his own name day, the old prince explodes at the French doctor Metivier—accusing him of being a spy and throwing him out. He is in one of his worst raging moods, and Princess Mary must manage the consequences.

149.modern-en: At dinner, the old prince is in full performance mode—directing cutting remarks at Boris Drubetskoy and holding court with the authority that still commands the room, even as his behavior grows less predictable.

151.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear directly in this chapter about the Rostovs' arrival in Moscow.

152.modern-en: When Count Rostov and Natasha arrive to call, the old prince refuses to receive them and forces Princess Mary to handle the visit—a deliberate insult to the Rostovs and a hostile signal about the engagement.

157.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky's hostility toward the Rostov visit lingers—Marya Dmitrievna reports that she confronted him and he shouted at her, and the practical advice is to simply remove the Rostovs from Moscow rather than try to change his mind.

166.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky receives Natasha's letter breaking off the engagement—stolen from Princess Mary by Mademoiselle Bourienne—and passes it to Andrei on his return, apparently in better spirits at the engagement's collapse.

175.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear directly in this chapter.

192.modern-en: After Andrei's departure for the army, the old prince falls into a week-long illness, then re-emerges to throw himself into building projects and to cut off Mademoiselle Bourienne completely—his way of showing Princess Mary he blames her for nothing, while blaming her for everything.

198.modern-en: As French forces approach, the old prince makes a dramatic decision to stay and defend Bald Hills—ordering his household to leave while he remains. When Princess Mary refuses to go, he erupts in a storm of recrimination, then clearly feels secret relief at her refusal to abandon him.

199.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky prepares to visit the local commander in full dress uniform—his energy wildly feverish, his preparations grandiose. He reviews his armed peasants like a commanding general, though his mental state is clearly deteriorating.

205.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky does not appear in this chapter, which concerns Andrei's meeting with Kutuzov.

332.modern-en: Old Bolkonsky has been dead for many months by this chapter—his story concluded with his stroke and death as the French approached Bald Hills.

epithet.en: Pierre's beautiful, corrupt first wife

2.modern-en: Hélène arrives at Anna Pavlovna's soirée to collect her father Prince Vasili, already in her ball gown, wearing her lady-in-waiting badge — her beauty commands the room without any effort on her part.

3.modern-en: At Anna Pavlovna's reception, the younger guests arrange themselves around Hélène as naturally as planets around a sun; she is the social center of the gathering, her radiance requiring nothing so crude as conversation.

4.modern-en: Hélène is present in the background of the drawing room as Prince Andrei arrives; she is part of the glittering company her husband finds so tiresome, though she is not yet singled out beyond her usual conspicuous beauty.

50.modern-en: Prince Vasili, always managing affairs without quite admitting to himself that he is, begins maneuvering Pierre toward Hélène — engineering proximity, allowing the young man's infatuation to do the work for him.

51.modern-en: Hélène receives Pierre's awkward, love-struck visits at her father's house with perfect, practiced composure; she is the object of his embarrassed adoration, and the proposal Prince Vasili is engineering is nearly inevitable.

74.modern-en: After the duel, Pierre lies awake reliving the discovery of Hélène's affair with Dolokhov — swinging between memories of her beauty in their early marriage and the cold realization that the whole thing was arranged, that she never loved him.

89.modern-en: Prince Vasili arrives at Pierre's to arrange a reconciliation with Hélène; he bullies and weeps and manipulates until Pierre, unable to hold out against the pressure, agrees to see her again.

90.modern-en: Society blames Pierre, not Hélène, for the failure of the marriage; she emerges from the duel scandal with her reputation intact, even enhanced — the wronged, beautiful wife — while Pierre is condemned.

91.modern-en: Hélène is at Anna Pavlovna's salon and the chapter's social comedy turns on Hippolyte's nonsensical joke; she is part of the assembled company, her presence always decorative and her opinions never solicited.

115.modern-en: Hélène has established herself as a brilliant figure in Petersburg society, her salon drawing the Francophile aristocracy and even Napoleonic dignitaries she met at Erfurt; she has become a genuine political and social force.

118.modern-en: Hélène is not the focus of this chapter but is part of the Petersburg world in which Boris now moves; she has drawn him into her orbit and is the reason he has avoided the Rostovs, whose provincial warmth makes him uncomfortable.

121.modern-en: Hélène is at the New Year's Eve ball, magnificent as always; Natasha catches her eye, and Hélène's attention to the young girl is the first step in the chain that will lead to disaster for Natasha.

122.modern-en: At the New Year's ball Hélène is in full command of her social position, splendid and self-possessed; she facilitates Natasha's encounter with Prince Andrei by being part of the setting that makes it possible.

146.modern-en: Pierre feels the emptiness of his life most sharply through the contrast with Hélène: she is now the intimate of a very important personage at court, and their marriage is a hollow arrangement that neither acknowledges as such.

153.modern-en: Hélène has invited Natasha to join her in her opera box; this is the evening that opens the catastrophic chapter of Natasha's Moscow visit, and Hélène is its facilitator — the glamorous, smiling door through which danger enters.

154.modern-en: At the opera, Hélène draws Natasha into her box with warm, worldly attentiveness; her interest is not quite innocent — she has a plan that involves her brother Anatole, and Natasha's engagement to Prince Andrei does not trouble her.

155.modern-en: Hélène introduces Anatole to Natasha in her opera box with a flicker of unease in her eyes; she is the instrument of the seduction, knowing what her brother is doing and choosing to enable it.

157.modern-en: Hélène's influence on Natasha continues through letters and visits in the days after the opera; she is the channel through which Anatole's pursuit reaches Natasha, keeping her distracted from the reality of her engagement.

158.modern-en: Hélène hosts the evening at which Anatole and Natasha meet again; Count Rostov is uncomfortable with the company she keeps, but Hélène's authority as hostess holds the room and she manages Anatole's access to Natasha with smooth efficiency.

170.modern-en: Hélène is at Vilna with the court during the weeks before the French invasion; she is part of the glittering social world surrounding the Emperor, her presence as fixed and decorative as ever even as war approaches.

196.modern-en: Five years of war and political upheaval have not altered Hélène's salon in Petersburg by a single chair; it continues on its original principles while Anna Pavlovna's runs on opposite ones — the two together mapping the impossible contradictions of Russian society.

235.modern-en: Hélène has returned to Petersburg with two simultaneous suitors — an elderly Russian magnate and a young foreign prince — and rather than hide the situation she resolves it with breathtaking audacity by persuading each man she should marry him.

236.modern-en: Hélène maneuvers to obtain a Catholic divorce from Pierre on the grounds that she was never properly married, converting to Catholicism in the process; her absolute self-assurance, which reads as innocence, makes even her confessor believe in the simplicity of her case.

265.modern-en: Hélène dies during this chapter's period — suddenly, under the official explanation of angina, though gossip connects her death to an overdose taken to end an unwanted pregnancy from one of her liaisons; her disappearance is almost as offhand as her existence, society moving on without pause.

epithet.en: Scheming courtier, father of Hélène and Anatole
epithet.da: Rænkefuld hofmand, far til Hélène og Anatole

1.modern-en: Prince Vasili arrives first at Anna Pavlovna's soirée, playing his usual role of charming, languid courtier — he works the room with effortless manipulation and seizes the opportunity to float the idea of marrying his wayward son Anatole to the wealthy Princess Mary Bolkonskaya.

2.modern-en: Prince Vasili departs Anna Pavlovna's party with his daughter Hélène, pausing only to fend off Princess Drubetskaya's impassioned plea on behalf of her son Boris — ultimately promising, with reluctant generosity, to use his influence to have Boris transferred to the Guards.

4.modern-en: Prince Vasili makes a smooth exit from the soirée with Hélène, grasping Pierre's hand in passing and cheerfully palming off the socially awkward young man onto Anna Pavlovna, clearly not yet seeing Pierre as anything more than a nuisance to be managed.

8.modern-en: Pierre lives in Vasili's household and has fallen in with the dissolute lifestyle of Vasili's son Anatole — a fact Prince Andrei warns Pierre against, noting the corrupting influence of the Kuragin circle.

9.modern-en: Anatole's late-night gathering — which Pierre cannot resist attending despite his promise — takes place in Prince Vasili's son's apartments, where the reckless company organizes Dolokhov's famous window stunt; Vasili himself is absent but his household is the stage.

10.modern-en: Prince Vasili is reported to have kept his promise regarding Boris, securing his Guards transfer, and has arrived in Moscow — ostensibly on official inspection, but in truth to position himself at Count Bezukhov's bedside as the dying old man's fortune hangs in the balance.

14.modern-en: Anna Mikhaylovna tells Countess Rostova that it was Prince Vasili who secured Boris's transfer — 'He agreed to everything right away' — speaking of him with warmth, while the count recalls him as someone they once performed theatricals with.

15.modern-en: At the dying Count Bezukhov's house, Prince Vasili emerges from the count's apartments wearing a look of weary authority; he receives Anna Mikhaylovna with cold wariness and barely acknowledges Boris, suspicious of any rival claimants to the enormous inheritance.

16.modern-en: Prince Vasili installs himself in control of access to the dying count's household, summoning Pierre and warning him bluntly to behave — 'if you act here as you did in Petersburg, you'll come to a very bad end' — treating Pierre as an inconvenient presence while positioning himself over the will.

21.modern-en: Prince Vasili moves with anxious urgency through the dying count's house on the night of the last rites — pale, twitching, exhausted — and slips away to the eldest princess's room where he schemes urgently about finding and suppressing the will that would leave everything to Pierre.

22.modern-en: As the last rites unfold, Pierre catches a glimpse through a doorway of Prince Vasili and the eldest princess in furtive, urgent conversation — and later Vasili enters the reception room looking majestic but tense, grips Pierre's hand and tells him curtly that the count has asked to see him.

23.modern-en: Prince Vasili participates in the count's last rites with a carefully performed expression of pious submission, but slips away with the eldest princess to the back rooms — almost certainly searching for the will in the inlaid portfolio — before returning to his place before the service ends.

24.modern-en: The battle over the will comes to a head: Prince Vasili and the eldest princess struggle with Anna Mikhaylovna over the portfolio, Vasili urging the princess to surrender it; after the count dies, Vasili collapses on the sofa beside Pierre, weeping and murmuring about sin and death in an uncharacteristically genuine display of emotion.

25.modern-en: Julie's letter to Princess Mary mentions Prince Vasili as having 'played a thoroughly contemptible role' in the Bezukhov inheritance affair, returning to Petersburg 'completely humiliated' after Pierre is recognized as legitimate heir and inherits everything.

39.modern-en: Hippolyte Kuragin — Prince Vasili's son — appears among the diplomatic set at Bilíbin's quarters, where he is affectionately mocked as a hopeless social poseur, his absurd political pronouncements greeted with laughter rather than deference.

50.modern-en: Prince Vasili orchestrates Pierre's Petersburg life with masterful, instinctive manipulation — arranging his appointment as Gentleman of the Bedchamber, keeping him in his household, and steering the unsuspecting Pierre steadily toward a marriage with Hélène, all while appearing to act purely out of friendly concern.

51.modern-en: Prince Vasili decides the time has come to settle the question of Pierre and Hélène at Hélène's name-day supper, hosting and circling the table in high spirits while engineering the atmosphere that will force Pierre's hand; he later embraces Pierre with tearful triumph when the engagement is effectively secured.

52.modern-en: Prince Vasili writes to old Prince Bolkonsky announcing his forthcoming visit with Anatole — framing it as a courtesy inspection — and arrives at Bald Hills to propose a match between Anatole and Princess Mary, whom he needs married to a wealthy heiress to solve his son's chronic financial ruin.

53.modern-en: Prince Vasili plays the gracious, worldly guest at Bald Hills, deflecting the old prince's sharp questioning about Anatole with bland assurances of his son's honest character, while the visit proceeds as an exercise in gentle social pressure aimed at securing Princess Mary's hand.

54.modern-en: Prince Vasili sits before the old prince with theatrical sentimentality — a real tear in his eye — as Princess Mary is asked to give her answer; he accepts her refusal with surface grace and departs, his matrimonial scheme for Anatole having failed entirely.

84.modern-en: Prince Vasili does not appear directly in this chapter, which focuses on Nicholas Rostov confessing his gambling debt to his father.

89.modern-en: Prince Vasili calls on Pierre after the duel with Dolokhov, breezily insisting that Hélène is innocent and pressing Pierre to reconcile with his wife — but Pierre, newly fortified by Masonic resolve, dismisses him from the house with unexpected firmness, leaving Vasili visibly shaken.

90.modern-en: Prince Vasili publicly distances himself from Pierre after the duel scandal, shrugging whenever Pierre is mentioned and tapping his forehead to suggest Pierre is mentally unbalanced — while Hélène, who has returned to Petersburg, is received with sympathetic deference as a wronged wife.

102.modern-en: Prince Vasili does not appear in this chapter; it focuses on Rostov visiting Tushin and Denisov in the military hospital.

150.modern-en: Prince Vasili sends Anatole to Moscow on the pretext of a posting, with the real purpose of finding him a wealthy wife — either Julie Karagina or Princess Mary; Anna Mikhaylovna reports this intelligence to Boris, which finally spurs him to propose to Julie before Anatole can.

154.modern-en: At the opera, Anatole arrives in the Rostovs' box area — his entrance noted by the whole house — and sits beside Dolokhov in the stalls, gazing at Natasha with open admiration, while the count and Shinshin remark on how alike he and Hélène look.

155.modern-en: Prince Vasili's daughter Hélène introduces Anatole to Natasha during the intermission, providing the encounter that leaves Natasha dangerously enchanted and confused about her feelings for her absent fiancé.

156.modern-en: Prince Vasili is revealed to have exiled Anatole from Petersburg for excessive debts and arranged his Moscow posting as adjutant to the commander in chief — hoping a wealthy marriage would solve the twenty-thousand-ruble annual problem; it also emerges that Anatole is secretly married, a fact Vasili has concealed.

160.modern-en: Prince Vasili does not appear directly; Sonya discovers Anatole's letter to Natasha and confronts her friend about the dangerous infatuation that threatens to destroy the Bolkonsky engagement.

161.modern-en: Prince Vasili is not present in this chapter depicting Dolokhov and Anatole's final preparations for the elopement scheme.

165.modern-en: Prince Vasili does not appear directly; Pierre searches Moscow for Anatole after learning of the elopement attempt and finally confronts him at Hélène's drawing room.

166.modern-en: Prince Vasili is implicated indirectly in the aftermath of the scandal — the old Prince Bolkonsky has learned of the elopement attempt through Mademoiselle Bourienne, and the broken engagement becomes known in their circle.

175.modern-en: Anatole has already fled Petersburg ahead of Prince Andrew, who sought him to avenge the Natasha affair; Prince Vasili is not directly present but his son's dishonorable conduct casts a long shadow over the chapter.

176.modern-en: Prince Vasili does not appear in this chapter; it surveys the factional politics swirling around army headquarters at Drissa.

196.modern-en: Prince Vasili shuttles restlessly between Anna Pavlovna's patriotic salon and Hélène's pro-French circle, frequently confusing his talking points between the two camps — a comic figure of salon opportunism who adjusts his opinions to whichever room he occupies.

264.modern-en: Prince Vasili performs the reading of the Bishop's patriotic letter at Anna Pavlovna's soirée with his practiced, singsong delivery, tears in his voice at the theatrical moments — his performance the social centerpiece of an evening designed to stir patriotic sentiment.

265.modern-en: Prince Vasili's opportunism reaches a pitch: having previously disparaged Kutuzov as 'blind' and 'depraved,' he now claims Kutuzov as his protégé and celebrates the appointment with proprietary pride — but when Hélène suddenly dies, he is left grieving and disgraced, attacking Kutuzov again when Moscow falls.

279.modern-en: Prince Vasili does not appear in this chapter, which depicts Prince Andrew's final days and peaceful death in Natasha's presence.

epithet.en: Dissolute son of Vasili, tries to elope with Natasha
epithet.da: Udsvævende søn af Vasilij, forsøger at flygte med Natasja

1.modern-en: Anatole Kuragin is mentioned in passing at Anna Pavlovna's soirée — his father Prince Vasili describes him as an 'active fool' whose restlessness and misbehavior require managing, framing the upcoming proposal to marry him off to a wealthy heiress.

8.modern-en: Pierre has moved into the Kuragin household and fallen under Anatole's dissolute influence — Prince Andrei warns Pierre that Anatole's circle of reckless pleasures is corrupting, but Pierre is helplessly drawn to the warmth and energy of the company.

9.modern-en: Anatole hosts the late-night gathering at which Dolokhov performs his famous window-ledge drinking stunt — the event is a riotous expression of Anatole's world: bravado, excess, and total disregard for consequence.

10.modern-en: Anatole is implicated in the bear-and-policeman escapade that finally exhausts his father's tolerance; Prince Vasili resolves to exile him from Petersburg by arranging a posting and, more importantly, a marriage to solve his chronic financial ruin.

39.modern-en: Anatole does not appear directly in this chapter; his brother Hippolyte is among the Vienna diplomatic set at Bilíbin's, where he is affectionately mocked as a social poseur — the Kuragin family's reputation for charming futility precedes Anatole wherever he is absent.

50.modern-en: Anatole is living his customary dissipated Petersburg life while Pierre returns to the city — Pierre, newly changed by Freemasonry, observes with different eyes the same reckless circle he once found so irresistible.

52.modern-en: Anatole arrives at Bald Hills with his father to be assessed as a marriage prospect for Princess Mary — he is handsome, confident, and utterly bored, his attention immediately caught not by the awkward princess but by the flirtatious Mademoiselle Bourienne.

53.modern-en: At Bald Hills, Anatole makes no real effort to win Princess Mary; he passes the time exchanging significant glances and whispers with Mlle Bourienne in the conservatory, indifferent to the matrimonial scheme his father is working so hard to execute.

54.modern-en: Princess Mary refuses the match, and Anatole departs Bald Hills without visible regret — he has spent the visit in a pleasant flirtation with Mlle Bourienne and exits gracefully, leaving his father to absorb the failure alone.

121.modern-en: At a grand Petersburg ball, Anatole is pointed out to Natasha as a figure of note — she notices him across the room but they do not yet meet, his presence registering only as one glamorous element of the dazzling social world she is entering.

150.modern-en: Anatole arrives in Moscow on his father's orders, ostensibly posted as adjutant to the commander in chief but in reality sent to find a wealthy wife — his arrival immediately changes the social calculus, prompting Boris to finally propose to Julie before Anatole can sweep in.

153.modern-en: At the opera, Anatole arrives in the Hélène's box area and sits in the stalls, his gaze fixed on Natasha with undisguised admiration — the whole house notices his entrance, and Natasha feels herself looked at in a way she has never quite experienced before.

154.modern-en: Anatole is introduced to Natasha in Hélène's box during the intermission — he speaks with easy intimacy, holds her gaze, and takes her hand, leaving her flushed and confused, the memory of Prince Andrew suddenly seeming distant.

155.modern-en: Hélène engineers a second encounter, and Anatole presses his advantage with the same bold, uncomplicated charm — he gazes at Natasha as if she is the only person in the world, and she finds herself unable to resist the pleasure of being so admired.

156.modern-en: The full picture of Anatole's situation is revealed: his father exiled him from Petersburg for mounting debts; he is secretly already married to a Polish woman, a fact Prince Vasili has carefully concealed while searching Moscow for a rich heiress.

157.modern-en: Hélène visits the Rostov household under the pretext of friendship, smoothing the path for Anatole to continue his pursuit of Natasha — he has enlisted his sister as an accomplice in a seduction campaign whose real stakes Natasha cannot yet see.

158.modern-en: At the theatrical performance at Hélène's house, Anatole dances with Natasha, steals a moment alone, and kisses her — she is intoxicated by his boldness, pulled between guilt over her absent fiancé and the overwhelming force of his physical presence.

159.modern-en: Natasha receives a letter — eloquently phrased by Dolokhov but signed by Anatole — professing passionate love and urging elopement; she reads it again and again, torn between her promises to Prince Andrew and the vivid reality of what Anatole makes her feel.

160.modern-en: Anatole does not appear directly but his letter to Natasha is discovered by Sonya, who confronts her friend — the paper trail of his scheme begins to unravel even as Natasha has already written breaking off the Bolkonsky engagement.

161.modern-en: Anatole and Dolokhov make their final preparations for the elopement — Balaga the troika driver is summoned, the route planned, the timing set; Anatole is exhilarated, treating the whole adventure as a lark, wholly unconcerned with what it will cost Natasha.

162.modern-en: Anatole departs in the troika to carry out the elopement, arriving at the appointed window — but Sonya and Marya Dmitrievna have been warned, the household is on guard, and he is turned away; the scheme collapses without him ever comprehending the damage he has done.

164.modern-en: Pierre learns from Marya Dmitrievna that Anatole has already been married in Poland — the hidden fact that makes the entire Moscow adventure a cynical fraud — and sets out to find him and force him to face what he has done.

165.modern-en: Pierre confronts Anatole at Hélène's drawing room, demanding he return Natasha's letters and leave Moscow immediately; Anatole, initially defiant, is cowed by Pierre's unexpected fury and surrenders the letters, agreeing to go — he departs without apology or evident remorse.

166.modern-en: Anatole has already left for Petersburg; in his wake, Natasha lies gravely ill after a poisoning attempt, and the full consequences of his charming, careless campaign begin to settle on the Rostov household — he is absent, unaccountable, already moving on.

175.modern-en: Anatole has fled Petersburg ahead of Prince Andrew, who arrived seeking him to force a duel over Natasha; he is untraceable, and Prince Andrew is left with nowhere to direct his cold fury — Anatole escapes consequence once more through sheer mobility.

176.modern-en: Anatole is not found at army headquarters at Drissa; his whereabouts remain unknown as the war with Napoleon resumes its full urgency and the personal drama around Natasha recedes before larger events.

185.modern-en: Anatole does not appear directly — but at a Moscow church, Natasha prays for those she loves and for her enemies, and Anatole's name rises in her thoughts; he remains a presence in her interior life even as she tries to move past what happened.

227.modern-en: At the field dressing station after Borodino, Prince Andrew — lying with a mortal wound — sees Anatole on the next table, his leg just amputated, weeping like a child; something breaks open in Prince Andrew, and he feels a sudden, unexpected wave of compassion and love for his enemy.

238.modern-en: Pierre, wandering in a dazed state, dreams of the dissolute Petersburg world and Anatole figures in that dream-memory — an emblem of the empty, pleasure-seeking life Pierre has left behind and is still working to understand the meaning of.

279.modern-en: Anatole does not appear in this chapter, which depicts Prince Andrew's final days and peaceful death attended by Natasha and Princess Mary.

epithet.en: Generous patriarch, financially reckless

10.modern-en: The count hosts a lively name-day celebration at the Povarskaya house, entertaining dozens of guests in his study with his Turkish pipe collection and bustling between rooms with cheerful, slightly guilty energy—the picture of an affectionate, extravagant father.

11.modern-en: When Natasha bursts into the drawing room, the count leaps up laughing and catches her in his arms—his open, tender love for his children is the emotional center of his household. He tolerates the countess's mild scolding with a rueful grin.

12.modern-en: The count chats warmly with the visitor and shows gentle pride in Nicholas, who is about to join the army—acknowledging with a sigh that he would rather see his son stay, but that the boy insists on following Boris into service.

15.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter, which follows Anna Mikhaylovna and Boris's visit to dying Count Bezukhov.

16.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter.

17.modern-en: The countess sends for the count after seeing off Anna Mikhaylovna; he comes waddling in with a guilty, cheerful expression and, with practiced good nature, agrees to provide five hundred rubles—though visibly pained by the expense.

18.modern-en: Count Rostov holds court in his tobacco-filled study while waiting for the formidable Marya Dmitrievna, entertaining his male guests and stirring debate about the war—the genial, slightly pompous host enjoying himself thoroughly.

19.modern-en: At dinner the count plays the amiable host, setting guests against each other in animated political argument while staying carefully noncommittal himself—enjoying the spectacle of debate more than any particular outcome.

20.modern-en: After dinner, the count struggles to stay awake over his cards, laughing at everything, his card-fan spread wide—the picture of contented domesticity, utterly indulgent toward the young people gathered around the clavichord.

21.modern-en: The count does not appear in this chapter about the dying Count Bezukhov.
