55.modern-en: When Nicholas's letter arrives announcing his promotion and wound at Schöngraben, the count retreats to his study to weep and laugh simultaneously—his relief and pride overwhelming him. Anna Mikhaylovna helps him plan how to break the news gently to the countess.

62.modern-en: The count does not appear in this chapter.

67.modern-en: The count does not appear in this chapter.

69.modern-en: The count is not featured in this chapter about Nicholas's return to Moscow.

70.modern-en: The count is glad to have Nicholas home and proud to show him off, keeping up his extravagant hospitality and enjoying his son's new social success—oblivious to the mounting financial ruin this good cheer is costing.

71.modern-en: At the English Club, the count moves among members with his characteristic warmth and generosity, playing the beloved host of Moscow society while Nicholas basks in his reflected glow—neither man aware of the looming financial catastrophe.

84.modern-en: When Nicholas comes home and admits gambling away forty-three thousand rubles to Dolokhov, the count turns red, spreads his arms, and then—in the depths of his goodness—agrees to pay the debt rather than shame the family. The weight of his own financial recklessness hangs over the scene.

94.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter about Pierre's visit to his Kiev estates.

108.modern-en: Count Rostov receives Prince Andrei at Otradnoe in his capacity as district marshal—warm, hospitable, and oblivious to the depth of Andrei's growing interest in Natasha.

117.modern-en: In Petersburg, the count's financial troubles are mounting—debts from years of extravagant living. He has come to the capital to find a government post, but their circle is uncertain; he entertains as lavishly as ever, unable to change his ways.

119.modern-en: The count is not directly featured in this intimate nighttime scene between Natasha and the countess.

120.modern-en: The count joins the family in last-minute preparations for the great New Year's ball, fussing over carriages and tickets—his generous good humor as infectious as always, though the family's straitened finances cast a quiet shadow.

130.modern-en: After Andrei's formal proposal, the count warmly welcomes his future son-in-law and adapts willingly to the new rhythm of the house—proud, affectionate, slightly bewildered by the formal terms of the engagement but trusting in his daughter's happiness.

134.modern-en: Back at Otradnoe after years of military service, Nicholas confronts the estate manager Mitenka about financial chaos; the count has handed the business entirely to his son and watches Nicholas's explosive intervention with something between relief and shame.

136.modern-en: The count rides out eagerly to join the great autumn hunt, delegating management of the proceedings to Nicholas—his joy in hunting and the outdoor life as pure as ever, untouched by his many financial cares.

137.modern-en: At the hunt, the count waits at his designated spot, part of the cheerful spectacle of the Rostov household's seasonal pleasures—the established world that Tolstoy treats with affectionate nostalgia.

138.modern-en: After the wolf is killed, the count heads back to Otradnoe contentedly, leaving the younger generation to continue with the day's sport.

140.modern-en: The count's resignation as Provincial Marshal has not eased the family's finances. He maintains the old extravagant household routine—twenty people for dinner daily—even as he and the countess exchange worried whispers about selling the Moscow house.

141.modern-en: During the dull midwinter Christmas week, the count naps comfortably in his study as the household around him hums with restless young energy—his elderly contentment a gentle contrast to Natasha's burning impatience.

142.modern-en: The count is in the background as Nicholas and Natasha share a late-night philosophical conversation; he represents the older world of habit and acceptance that both children are unconsciously growing beyond.

145.modern-en: When Nicholas announces his love for Sonya, the count listens to the countess's tearful rejection and then, acutely aware of his own financial failings toward his son, half-heartedly lectures Nicholas before falling silent—unable to press a demand he knows is tainted by his own guilt.

151.modern-en: The count brings Natasha and Sonya to Moscow in winter, staying at Marya Dmitrievna's because the family house is too cold. His main concerns are practical—the trousseau, the estate sale, presenting Natasha to old Bolkonsky.

152.modern-en: Count Rostov takes a nervous Natasha to call on old Prince Bolkonsky, his old anxiety about the difficult man visible in his timidity at the door. His gentleness in the awkward visit stands in contrast to the old prince's hostility.

153.modern-en: The count takes Natasha and Sonya to the opera at Marya Dmitrievna's invitation—pleased to give the girls a pleasure, somewhat distracted by the grand social atmosphere.

154.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter about Natasha at the opera.

157.modern-en: The count is quietly managed by Marya Dmitrievna in conversations kept from Natasha; he delegates authority in this crisis with his customary deference to stronger personalities.

158.modern-en: Count Rostov takes the girls to Hélène Bezukhova's salon—uneasy about the company, but unable to refuse—and watches with growing discomfort as Anatole attaches himself to Natasha.

159.modern-en: At breakfast with Marya Dmitrievna, Count Rostov listens to her blunt account of confronting old Prince Bolkonsky and agrees with her advice to return to Otradnoe—relieved to have a practical course of action.

160.modern-en: The count is not directly featured in this chapter about the Kuragin letter.

163.modern-en: The count is not directly featured in the chapter dealing with Marya Dmitrievna's confrontation with Natasha over the elopement.

164.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter.

183.modern-en: When the countess falls ill from the shock of Natasha's scandal, the count brings the whole family back to Moscow and settles into the family house. He is helpless before his daughter's illness and the family's grief, delegating to others as always.

187.modern-en: On a Sunday at home with close friends including Pierre, the count sits contentedly in his usual social role—warm, hospitable, unaware how fundamentally his household is about to change as war approaches.

188.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter about Petya's determination to go to the Emperor.

189.modern-en: At the great assembly of the Moscow nobility, Count Rostov appears among the patriotic crowd—moved by the Emperor's speech, he weeps and shouts 'Hurrah!' like the others, his sincere love for Russia as uncomplicated and generous as his love for everything.

207.modern-en: The count is briefly mentioned as part of the Moscow establishment living in the odd, festive mood of denial as the French approach—his household continuing its customary rhythms even as everything changes.

233.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter at Kutuzov's council of war.

239.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter about Pierre visiting Rostopchin.

241.modern-en: As the French near Moscow, the count gets Petya transferred to Bezukhov's training regiment near the city, managing the family crisis in his characteristic way—finding a compromise that soothes the countess while Petya chafes under the restraint.

242.modern-en: On the eve of Moscow's fall, the count is away from the house all morning while the packing chaos mounts—characteristically absent from the detail work, his authority yielding to Natasha's urgent energy.

243.modern-en: As the count tries to take charge of departure preparations, his contradictory orders create more confusion than they resolve—his good intentions undermined by his inability to organize in a crisis. Petya and Sonya are overwhelmed by his instructions.

244.modern-en: On Moscow's last Sunday, the count appears among the departing Muscovites—managing the leave-taking with emotional generosity, signing over carts to the wounded without calculation.

245.modern-en: When Berg arrives requesting furniture from the household in the middle of the evacuation, the count is irritated but too soft-hearted to refuse outright—finally agreeing to let him take a small chest.

246.modern-en: As the family's carriages prepare to leave, the count discovers that the mortally wounded Prince Andrei is among the wounded being transported in their train—a fact the countess will not tell Natasha. He navigates the crisis with gentle anxiety.

251.modern-en: The count does not appear directly—the Moscow house has been left behind, and he is traveling with the family.

259.modern-en: The count does not appear directly as the family rests at Mytishchi—he is present but in the background as Natasha's grief over Andrei dominates.

260.modern-en: The count comes out in his dressing gown to look at the burning Moscow. He witnesses the glow of the fire and tries to explain the situation to his household—an old man watching the destruction of the world he has always known.

265.modern-en: The count does not appear in this chapter.

277.modern-en: The count does not appear directly in this chapter.

285.modern-en: The count does not appear in this chapter.

320.modern-en: In the weeks after Petya's death, Count Rostov is broken—he weeps helplessly, unable to absorb the loss of his youngest son, while Natasha holds the household together by tending to the shattered countess.

330.modern-en: The count does not appear in this chapter.

342.modern-en: Count Ilya Rostov dies in 1813 following Natasha's wedding—the accumulated blows of the past years, from the burning of Moscow to Petya's death, have left him without the will to live. He dies quietly, the last of the old world of the Rostov household.

epithet.en: Mother of the Rostov family

10.modern-en: The countess receives name-day visitors in the drawing room with practiced, warm hospitality, gently managing the social traffic and mildly reproving her husband for spoiling Natasha—the loving, slightly harried mother at the center of an enormous household.

11.modern-en: As Natasha bursts in and the count catches her, the countess issues a fond, ineffectual scolding—her affectionate authority over her exuberant children both genuine and cheerfully ignored.

12.modern-en: The countess chats with the visitors while keeping a watchful eye on her brood—she is the social lubricant of the household, smoothing over the gaps left by the count's cheerful distraction.

14.modern-en: The countess does not appear in this chapter.

15.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter.

17.modern-en: The countess sends for the count to ask for five hundred rubles to help Anna Mikhaylovna, pressing her handkerchief to her eyes with sympathetic distress—her generosity and her tendency to weep in company are both on full display.

18.modern-en: The countess presides over the crowded drawing room awaiting the terrifying Marya Dmitrievna—her deference to that formidable woman revealing the social hierarchy beneath the Rostovs' easy warmth.

19.modern-en: The countess sits at the women's end of the dinner table, politely maintaining the social atmosphere while the men argue politics—her role as gracious hostess never resting.

20.modern-en: After dinner, the countess suggests the young people gather around the clavichord—she engineers the evening's pleasures with practiced maternal intelligence.

55.modern-en: Anna Mikhaylovna and the count conspire carefully to break the news of Nicholas's wound to the countess—an indication of how deeply her maternal anxiety is expected to run and how fragile the household considers her composure under such strain.

74.modern-en: The countess is not directly featured in this chapter about Pierre's night of self-examination after the duel.

84.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter about Nicholas gambling away forty-three thousand rubles.

91.modern-en: The countess does not appear in this chapter.

116.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter about Pierre's diary.

118.modern-en: When Boris visits the Rostovs in Petersburg after years' absence, the countess notes wistfully that 'old friends are forgotten these days'—her quiet resentment of his coldness toward Natasha hinting at the maternal watchfulness she exercises over all her children's feelings.

119.modern-en: The countess prays on her knees in her nightcap before Natasha interrupts her, and then spends a long, warm intimate session in bed listening to her daughter's excited chatter about Prince Andrei—her patient tenderness and quiet wisdom shining through.

120.modern-en: The countess anxiously supervises the family's preparation for the great New Year's ball, fretting over dress details and the girls' excitement—her maternal concern mixed with genuine pleasure at the occasion.

121.modern-en: The countess stands near Natasha at the ball, watching her daughter's first dance with nervous maternal pride—and is close to tears of joy when the Emperor dances with Natasha.

122.modern-en: The countess watches from the sidelines as Natasha is singled out by the Emperor for the polonaise—her maternal happiness at her daughter's social success is pure and uncomplicated.

126.modern-en: The countess is mentioned briefly as too superior to associate with the Bergs—her social pride a mild contrast to the count's broader, more democratic warmth.

128.modern-en: As Prince Andrei's attentions to Natasha become unmistakable, the countess watches with 'sad, solemnly serious eyes'—sensing both the joy and the weight of what is unfolding for her daughter.

129.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter.

130.modern-en: The countess welcomes the awkward terms of the engagement—a year's delay, no formal announcement—with anxious goodwill, trusting that Natasha's happiness and God's will align.

134.modern-en: The countess summons Nicholas home from the army to deal with the estate's mounting financial crisis—her letter framing the practical emergency in terms of duty to aging parents.

140.modern-en: The countess continues her customary extravagant household management even as the finances worsen, exchanging worried private whispers with the count about selling properties while the dining table stays full.

141.modern-en: The countess plays solitaire on a slow Christmas afternoon—a quiet domestic image of a woman who has organized her world around the needs of others for so long that her own stillness seems unfamiliar.

142.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in the intimate sibling conversation between Nicholas and Natasha.

145.modern-en: When Nicholas declares his love for Sonya, the countess breaks into tears of frustration rather than sorrow—she cannot bear to see the family's last financial hope compromised by a match with a portionless niece, and her objection, though felt as love, is also strategy.

151.modern-en: The countess stays in Moscow, still unwell—the chapter notes her absence from the trip to Moscow as significant. Her worsening health becomes a fact of the household's daily anxiety.

165.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter.

166.modern-en: On hearing of the poisoning attempt, the countess is summoned to Moscow from the country—her arrival is awaited as a stabilizing presence for Natasha's crisis.

183.modern-en: The countess falls ill from the shock of Natasha's near-elopement, and the entire household returns to the Moscow house to care for both mother and daughter. Her fragility in crisis is the domestic counterweight to Natasha's dramatic recoveries.

184.modern-en: The countess is in the background of the household's slow recovery from scandal—her illness and Natasha's grief running in parallel, two different kinds of collapse.

187.modern-en: The countess is part of the Sunday family gathering with Pierre—her warm, established role as center of the household unchanged, even as financial and emotional pressures mount.

239.modern-en: As the French approach Moscow, the countess is consumed by terror for her sons—both now at war—and cannot sleep, dreaming of them dead. The count's arrangement to transfer Petya to a safer regiment near Moscow is her fragile consolation.

241.modern-en: The countess's anxiety over Petya and Nicholas reaches its peak—she has tried every means to bring them home and failed, and the knowledge that both might die torments her daily.

242.modern-en: The countess lies in the new sitting room with a headache on the day of packing—overwhelmed by the chaos, she withdraws into her own fragility while Natasha takes command.

243.modern-en: The countess is barely functional during the final evacuation preparations—unable to absorb the scale of what is happening. The servants and Natasha work around her.

244.modern-en: The countess carries out the leave-taking with the wounded with quiet grace—quietly agreeing when Natasha insists on giving carts to the soldiers.

245.modern-en: The countess is ill and resting while the evacuation crisis swirls around her—Berg's visit to request furniture from the household during the general flight strikes her as incomprehensible.

246.modern-en: The countess is told in secret that the mortally wounded Andrei is traveling with them—and she must keep it from Natasha. She bears this terrible burden with anguished protective love.

260.modern-en: The countess remains indoors at Mytishchi, physically and emotionally shattered, while others go out to see Moscow burning—her suffering is internal and quiet.

261.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter about Andrei's slow recovery.

264.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter.

270.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter.

271.modern-en: The countess summons Sonya and tearfully begs her to sacrifice herself by releasing Nicholas from their engagement—framing it as repayment for the Rostov family's generosity, while the real motive is securing a wealthier match for her son.

277.modern-en: The countess does not appear directly in this chapter about Princess Mary's journey.

319.modern-en: When the news of Petya's death arrives, the countess's cries of anguish echo through the house—a wild, animal grief that breaks Natasha out of her own mourning and drives her to her mother's side.

320.modern-en: Petya's death has transformed the countess: in one month she ages from a vigorous woman of fifty into a listless old woman. Only Natasha's constant presence at her side—talking, feeding her, sitting with her through the nights—keeps her from giving in entirely to despair.

342.modern-en: After the count's death in 1813, the countess becomes entirely dependent on Natasha and Nicholas for her existence—she is the survivor of the old world, carried forward by the new generation's love.

343.modern-en: The countess praises Princess Mary enthusiastically to Nicholas in private while growing ill-humored whenever she actually starts talking about her—a contradiction that reveals her own complicated hope for a match she cannot quite bring herself to engineer openly.

349.modern-en: In the epilogue household at Bald Hills, the countess lives out her last years as a cherished dependent—playing patience, dispensing mild complaints, grateful for Pierre's presents but most glad that the family is intact around her.

350.modern-en: The countess receives Pierre's gifts with practiced grace—not deeply moved but fond, and still holding her position as the emotional anchor of the household, however diminished her capacities have become.

epithet.en: Youngest Rostov son, dies in battle

55.modern-en: Petya is mentioned only in passing—he is part of the Rostov household when Nicholas's letter about his wound arrives, one of the younger children in the background of the emotional family drama.

69.modern-en: Petya is part of the excited household welcoming Nicholas home on leave from the army—his particular role in the homecoming is not singled out, but the joyful chaos of the reception is the atmosphere he inhabits.

94.modern-en: Petya does not appear directly in this chapter about Pierre's reforms on his Kiev estates.

107.modern-en: Petya does not appear directly in this chapter about Prince Andrei's country life.

133.modern-en: Petya is part of the Rostov family at Otradnoe, mentioned in letters home as one of the domestic life Nicholas is coming back to manage—the youngest of the Rostov sons, still a boy.

135.modern-en: On the eve of the great hunt, Petya runs up to Nicholas with Natasha, trying to tell him something about the preparations—a small eager presence at the edges of the adults' activity.

136.modern-en: Petya rides out for the great autumn hunt—still a boy young enough to be associated with Natasha's reckless energy rather than the serious huntsmen, present as a cheerful, dashing figure.

138.modern-en: After the wolf hunt, Petya goes with Natasha and Nicholas to 'Uncle's' house for the evening, his presence adding to the family's holiday mood as they all pile into the old hunter's cramped, warm rooms.

139.modern-en: At Uncle's house, Petya joins the impromptu dancing and music with the family—a boy fully caught up in the joy of the moment, belonging to the world of uncomplicated Rostov happiness that the chapter celebrates.

141.modern-en: During the midwinter Christmas dullness, Petya is among the restless young household members—his absence at a tutor's creates one of the empty spaces that frustrates Natasha's craving for amusement.

142.modern-en: Petya is present at the edges of Nicholas and Natasha's late-night philosophical conversation—the youngest sibling, still too much a child to fully participate in the mood they share.

178.modern-en: Petya does not appear in this chapter about Prince Andrei at the military strategy meetings.

184.modern-en: Petya does not appear directly in this chapter about Natasha's recovery from illness.

187.modern-en: At the Rostov Sunday dinner, Petya is present as part of the lively household—his soldier's ambitions are already forming, though war still seems distant.

188.modern-en: Petya announces his determination to join the army and is refused—his mother is terrified, his father dismissive. He locks himself in his room and weeps bitterly, then the next morning slips out of the house in his best dress to go see the Emperor.

189.modern-en: Petya fights his way through a massive crowd at the Sloboda Palace to catch a glimpse of the Emperor—he is swept up and nearly crushed, but manages to tear off a piece of biscuit that the Tsar has tossed to the crowd, which he carries home as a sacred trophy. He comes home resolved more than ever to serve.

218.modern-en: Petya does not appear directly in this chapter—the narrative essay on the nature of historical causation at Borodino does not feature individual characters.

237.modern-en: Petya does not appear directly in this chapter about Pierre after Borodino.

241.modern-en: The countess's terror over Petya at war drives the count to get him transferred to a training regiment near Moscow—Petya, far away with Obolensky's Cossacks, is the axis around which his mother's maternal anxiety revolves.

242.modern-en: On the eve of the family's evacuation from Moscow, Petya is absent—he has gone to see a friend about getting himself transferred back to active service, revealing his restless eagerness to be where the fighting is.

243.modern-en: Petya takes charge of the yard during the chaotic packing and evacuation preparations—energetic, practical, and proud to be useful in a crisis larger than anything he has faced before.

245.modern-en: Petya is not directly featured in Berg's furniture-requesting visit.

246.modern-en: Petya has not yet been told about the mortally wounded Andrei traveling with the family—the chapter focuses on the adults managing this secret from Natasha.

302.modern-en: Petya rides with Denisov's guerrilla detachment through autumn rain—he has been assigned as orderly to a general but has talked his way into joining this more adventurous unit. He is introduced as a boy burning with the desire to prove himself, in a permanent state of 'blissful excitement at being grown up.'

303.modern-en: Crouching with Denisov at the forest's edge to observe the French camp, Petya's heart pounds with excitement—he absorbs every detail of the enemy position with the alertness of a boy who has never truly faced danger and cannot wait to.

304.modern-en: Back at the watchman's hut, Petya bonds with the captured French drummer boy—a child like himself—and impulsively asks Denisov to spare him. His compassion is as impetuous as his courage.

305.modern-en: Having resolved to stay with Denisov's detachment despite orders to return, Petya spends the evening before the attack in a state of feverish joy—eating, chatting with Dolokhov and the soldiers, feeling fully alive for the first time.

306.modern-en: Petya is dazzled by Dolokhov and can barely take his eyes off him—hero worship of the famous fighter mixing with his own need to prove himself worthy of such company. He sharpens his saber and cleans his pistol with anxious care.

307.modern-en: Petya rides out in the dark with Dolokhov to reconnoiter the French camp, speaking French with a pounding heart at the enemy sentries. It is a moment of pure thrilling terror—and he carries it off. He returns to the hut intoxicated by his own daring.

308.modern-en: Before the attack, Petya cannot sleep and goes outside into the dark—an extraordinary nocturnal passage in which he hears music in everything: the horses, the wind, the soldiers' voices, the universe itself seems to be singing to him. He is in a state of ecstatic, premonitory joy.

309.modern-en: The attack begins at dawn. Petya gallops headlong into the French camp, shouting 'Hurrah!' with everything he has—and is shot and killed almost immediately, falling from his horse before the battle is even properly joined. His death is sudden, absolute, and devastating.

348.modern-en: Petya is dead—he has been dead for years. His absence is the permanent wound in the family: the bright-eyed, snub-nosed boy who went away and never came back. The epilogue household at Bald Hills carries that grief beneath its surface.

epithet.en: Orphaned cousin of the Rostovs, devoted to Nikolai
epithet.da: Forældreløs kusine til Rostov-familien, hengiven til Nikolaj

12.modern-en: Sonya is introduced as a slender, dark-haired niece of the Rostovs, her girlish adoration for Nicholas visible through every polite smile she forces — she is already 'the kitten that promises to become a beautiful cat,' watching the cousin she loves with undisguised devotion.

13.modern-en: Natasha spies from hiding as Sonya runs into the conservatory in tears after seeing Nicholas; Nicholas follows, takes her hand, and kisses her — their secret love confirmed in this tender, overheard scene.

14.modern-en: Sonya sits at the window copying out Nicholas's verses while he dips his pen; Vera reproaches them all for their schoolroom secrets and threatens to tell their mother — Sonya absorbs the humiliation quietly, as she will do throughout the novel.

18.modern-en: Sonya trembles with emotion at the dinner table when Nicholas speaks too passionately about dying for the Emperor; her love and fear for him are on full display even in this crowd.

19.modern-en: Sonya trembles again when Nicholas makes his overwrought speech about dying for Russia at the table; she is one of those who sees his theatrical excess for what it is but loves him no less.

20.modern-en: Sonya is found weeping on the chest in the hallway — the traditional mourning spot in the Rostov house — because Nicholas's army papers have arrived and he is leaving; she wails that she can't help loving him though all obstacles stand in the way, and Natasha comforts her.

55.modern-en: Sonya is a quiet presence in the Rostov household when Nicholas's letter about his wounding arrives; she shares in the family's anxiety but the chapter focuses on the countess and Anna Mikhaylovna.

69.modern-en: Sonya is at home with the family when Nicholas returns on leave, part of the warm household greeting, and the prospect of his love and her own loyalty to him fills the air around the reunion.

70.modern-en: Sonya is mentioned as Nicholas grows subtly more distant during his Moscow leave — he finds her pretty and sweet but tells himself there will be time enough for love later, and she senses this cooling without being able to change it.

78.modern-en: Sonya is a background presence in the Rostov house as Nicholas grows close to the recovering Dolokhov during the Moscow leave; the household's romantic atmosphere thickens around her and Natasha.

79.modern-en: Sonya refused Dolokhov's proposal — a socially advantageous match for a penniless orphan — in order to remain faithful to Nicholas; when Natasha tells Nicholas, he feels 'something break inside him' before rallying to see it as her courage.

80.modern-en: At Iogel's ball, Sonya is radiant — she danced home in her pink ribbons, proud of her refusal of Dolokhov and of her conversation with Nicholas — and she dances in white muslin with such happiness that she seems transformed.

81.modern-en: Sonya is present at Dolokhov's farewell supper as the catastrophic card game unfolds, witness to Nicholas's losses without being able to stop them.

83.modern-en: Sonya is at the clavichord when Nicholas comes home crushed by the gambling debt; she plays the prelude to Denisov's barcarolle in the warm household scene that breaks apart the moment Nicholas confesses to his father what he has lost.

108.modern-en: Sonya is one of the girls Prince Andrei glimpses running across the path in the Otradnoe avenue — the dark-haired one in the yellow dress who vanishes laughing — though he notices Natasha first; Sonya is present but peripheral in his memory.

118.modern-en: Sonya is mentioned as the person Natasha speaks to freely about Boris, as though it were all long forgotten — the surface contrast of Natasha's easy forgetting and Sonya's patient constancy is implied.

120.modern-en: Sonya is dressed and ready in white gauze for the grand New Year's Eve ball, helping Natasha with her hair; the two cousins go as a pair, Sonya poised and dignified alongside the vibrant, more volatile Natasha.

122.modern-en: Sonya stands at the ball beside Natasha and the countess, sharing the agonized wait to be asked to dance; she is part of the small, anxious Rostov group before Prince Andrew rescues Natasha for the mazurka.

130.modern-en: Sonya is part of the household during Natasha's engagement to Prince Andrei; she participates in the poetic, quiet household life that surrounds the betrothed couple, working on her needlework and listening to conversations about the future.

133.modern-en: Nicholas mentions Sonya in his letters from the regiment, holding his promise to her — and the countess reads them with growing anxiety about the family's finances and the obstacle Sonya represents to a profitable marriage.

140.modern-en: The countess, watching the family's financial ruin, identifies Sonya as the chief obstacle to Nicholas's making a rich match; she has begun writing to propose a match between Nicholas and Julie Karagina, treating Sonya as a problem to be solved.

141.modern-en: Sonya sits in the drawing room copying an embroidery pattern during the dull Christmas week, the very picture of patient, contained domesticity, while Natasha wanders restlessly looking for Nicholas.

142.modern-en: Sonya participates in the siblings' nostalgic reminiscence of childhood memories — she tries to keep pace but admits she doesn't quite remember everything; she only truly engages when they recall the memory of her own arrival in the family.

143.modern-en: Sonya goes to the mummers' party at the Melyukovs' in a Circassian costume that suits her so well that the hostess singles her out admiringly; she joins the group of disguised young people and is genuinely merry.

144.modern-en: On the sleigh ride home from the Melyukovs', Nicholas stares at Sonya by starlight and resolves he will never be parted from her; he announces his decision to Natasha and then tells the costumed Sonya — 'that Circassian was Sonya, and that Sonya was certainly his future happy and loving wife.'

145.modern-en: Nicholas tells his mother he intends to marry Sonya; the countess refuses her blessing with cold severity and, a few days later, reproaches Sonya directly for trying to 'catch' Nicholas, an accusation Sonya receives in silence and grief — she cannot bring herself to stop loving Nicholas even as she knows she may have to sacrifice this love.

151.modern-en: Sonya travels to Moscow with the count and Natasha to prepare for the engagement; she is a quiet, indispensable presence in the household, helping to manage the practical arrangements.

152.modern-en: Sonya accompanies the Rostovs to visit old Prince Bolkonsky; Princess Mary does not take to Natasha, and the chapter focuses on the painful meeting, but Sonya is in the household party.

153.modern-en: Sonya goes to the opera with Natasha and is ready on time while Natasha dawdles; at the theater she watches Natasha's slow re-enchantment with the world and whispers a reminder about Natasha's hair — small caretaking gestures that mark her character.

160.modern-en: Sonya returns late one evening to find Natasha asleep on the sofa with Anatole's letter on the table; she reads it, goes pale with fright, and sits weeping — torn between loyalty to Natasha and the knowledge that what is happening will destroy everyone she loves.

163.modern-en: Marya Dmitrievna finds Sonya weeping in the corridor and makes her confess everything about Natasha's planned elopement with Anatole; Sonya's disclosure — unavoidable, however painful — is what enables Marya Dmitrievna to intervene in time.

164.modern-en: Sonya is part of the distressed household after the Anatole crisis; she is present when Pierre comes to Marya Dmitrievna's and glimpsed around the edges of the scene of Natasha's shame.

166.modern-en: Sonya is in the Rostov house as Natasha recovers from her attempted poisoning after learning Anatole is already married; she is one of those who woke Natasha's plea for help in the night.

167.modern-en: Sonya brings Pierre the news that Natasha wishes to see him; she is the quiet intermediary between the shattered household and the outside world, performing small acts of service without being seen.

179.modern-en: Nicholas writes separately to Sonya when he writes to his parents at the start of the 1812 campaign — an ardent letter promising marriage when the war ends; Sonya is the imagined domestic happiness he holds in his mind.

183.modern-en: Sonya is in the Moscow household as Natasha recovers from her illness; she tends to her cousin loyally while the family turns inward around Natasha's suffering.

187.modern-en: Sonya is present in the Rostov house on the Sunday Pierre visits; the chapter centers on Natasha's re-engagement with life and Pierre's feeling for her, and Sonya is a quiet background figure.

241.modern-en: Sonya is in the Moscow household as the Rostovs prepare to flee the city before Napoleon's arrival; the countess finds Sonya's presence less comforting than Petya's return but she is part of the close circle keeping the family together.

242.modern-en: Sonya is overseeing the packing of the china and glassware in the ballroom when the evacuation begins — she is doing the practical work Natasha is too distracted to manage.

243.modern-en: Sonya tries to restrain Natasha's impulsive packing decisions during the evacuation — 'Don't, Natasha! Leave it — we'll manage!' — but Natasha's force of will overwhelms her caution.

245.modern-en: Sonya is part of the Rostov household scrambling to load carriages on the day of departure from Moscow; Berg arrives and Sonya is among those he greets.

246.modern-en: Sonya is the first to notice that the carriage carrying the wounded officer is Prince Andrei; she runs to tell the countess, knowing the news will shatter Natasha — and her disclosure, motivated by complicated love for Nicholas and pity for everyone, triggers the novel's most painful reunion.

260.modern-en: Sonya, to the surprise and anger of the countess, tells Natasha that Prince Andrei is wounded and traveling with them; the countess thinks it was unnecessary and cruel, but Sonya did it because she genuinely felt Natasha had the right to know; now she tends to Natasha as she sinks into numb grief.

268.modern-en: Sonya is not present in Voronezh but is on Nicholas's mind; the governor's wife and his dawning attraction to Princess Mary exist in the shadow of his old promise to Sonya.

269.modern-en: Sonya is still the obstacle the countess wants removed; the matchmaking scheme for Nicholas and Princess Mary is gathering momentum in Voronezh.

270.modern-en: Sonya's letter to Nicholas from Troitsa — the letter releasing him from his engagement — is being prepared in the background of this chapter, her act of supreme self-sacrifice precipitated by the countess's pressure.

271.modern-en: The full story of Sonya's letter is told: the countess tearfully begged her to sacrifice her love for Nicholas so he could marry Princess Mary; Sonya, after initial resistance, decided she would wait and bind him more firmly — but ultimately wrote the release letter, driven by her habit of self-sacrifice and the recognition that the family's welfare required it; she is the novel's supreme example of love as renunciation.

277.modern-en: Sonya is in the household traveling toward Yaroslavl; she is part of the family group attending to Prince Andrei in his dying days, present but eclipsed by Natasha's and Princess Mary's grief.

279.modern-en: Sonya is sitting by Prince Andrei's bedside in the chapter where he dies; when Natasha comes in and silently takes Sonya's place, it is the final displacement — Sonya steps back so Natasha can be where she is needed.

319.modern-en: Sonya is in the Rostov household when the news of Petya's death arrives; the countess is wild with grief and Natasha must hold her — Sonya is present but peripheral, overtaken by the violence of the family's loss.

342.modern-en: Sonya is living in the Rostov household in the epilogue — the old countess's charity case now that the family's fortunes have collapsed; she is part of the quiet household Nicholas maintains, accepted but not quite integrated.

343.modern-en: Sonya is present when Princess Mary makes her first formal visit to the Rostovs in Moscow; Nicholas says disparagingly that he 'can't stand these ladies' in front of Sonya, and her barely hidden delight that he nonetheless went to visit the princess shows how complicated her love has become.

345.modern-en: Sonya is living quietly in Nicholas and Mary's household; she witnesses Nicholas's occasional outbursts of temper and is part of the domestic order that Princess Mary gently moderates.

346.modern-en: Sonya is at the table for the family dinner on the eve of St. Nicholas Day; she is one of the permanent members of the household, her place settled and modest, loved but without a future of her own.

347.modern-en: Sonya continues as a fixture in the Rostov-Bolkonsky household; the epilogue implies her permanent position as the gentle, self-effacing cousin who sacrificed everything for a love that was redirected elsewhere — 'an empty flower' is the phrase Tolstoy uses of her, without cruelty.

epithet.en: Eldest Rostov daughter, cold and proper

12.modern-en: Vera is present in the drawing room as the eldest daughter — older than Natasha by four years and already behaving like an adult — though it is Sonya and Natasha who draw the narrative's warm attention while Vera remains at the room's cooler edge.

14.modern-en: When the countess and Anna Mikhaylovna want to speak privately, they ask Vera to leave — an exchange that reveals her uncomfortable position in the family as the eldest but least beloved daughter, treated as an obstacle rather than a confidante.

18.modern-en: Vera is among the daughters seated in the drawing room as the household waits for the formidable Marya Dmitrievna; she is part of the family tableau but never the center of it, maintaining the composed surface that sets her apart.

20.modern-en: After dinner, the young people gather around the clavichord and Vera is among them; while Natasha and Nicholas are urged to sing, Vera watches from the dignified distance she always seems to keep from the family's warmer impulses.

55.modern-en: Vera is part of the household background when Nicholas's letter arrives from the front; the family's tearful, joyful commotion plays out around her with the usual implication that she participates without quite belonging to it.

69.modern-en: Vera is present in the Rostov house when Nicholas and Denisov arrive on leave; the reunion scene belongs to the others, and she is part of the family gathering without drawing any particular thread of the narrative toward herself.

83.modern-en: Vera is standing at the clavichord in her blue theater dress when Nicholas comes home after the gambling disaster; she is pretty and composed, part of the romantic scene Nicholas walks into — but this is one of the few chapters where the narrative notes her alongside Natasha rather than subordinating her.

117.modern-en: Soon after the Rostovs arrive in Petersburg for what the count calls the girls' last season, Berg proposes to Vera and is accepted; the engagement is noted briskly and without sentiment, exactly in keeping with her place in the family.

126.modern-en: Berg invites Pierre and Natasha to a small party at his and Vera's new apartment — Vera is the occasion for the gathering, the new wife whose establishment Berg is proudly showing off, though she barely appears beyond this function.

127.modern-en: Vera is at Berg's evening party, seated near Natasha at the tea table; she is a hostess now, Berg's wife, and the domestic competence she has always displayed in the Rostov house has found its natural outlet in her own household.

207.modern-en: Berg and Vera are mentioned as a couple whose marriage and domestic arrangements represent one of the comic threads running through Moscow society as the city slowly faces the reality of French invasion.

245.modern-en: Berg arrives at the Rostov house with a request to borrow a cart to move furniture; Vera is at home with the family during the desperate evacuation of Moscow, part of the household being packed up and abandoned, her husband's absurd request a dark joke beside the weight of what is happening.

epithet.en: Reckless officer and gambler, duels Pierre
epithet.da: Hensynsløs officer og spiller, duellerer med Pierre

9.modern-en: Dolokhov is the cold, precise center of Anatole's wild household — it is at his instigation that the window-ledge drinking stunt takes place, with him holding a bottle of rum while perched on a third-floor window sill without holding on, winning his bet with an Englishman and displaying the combination of nerve and self-mastery that defines his character.

10.modern-en: Dolokhov is mentioned as one of the three young men who tied a policeman to a bear and threw them both into the Moika Canal — a prank that earns him demotion to the ranks while his well-connected companions escape more lightly.

29.modern-en: Demoted to the ranks, Dolokhov stands out from the regiment in his blue broadcloth coat — he stares down the furious regimental commander with cool, insolent blue eyes and refuses to be humiliated, telling him flatly that he is not required to endure insults.

30.modern-en: When Kutuzov inspects the regiment, Dolokhov steps forward from the ranks and makes a direct appeal for the opportunity to redeem himself and prove his devotion to the Emperor — Kutuzov receives the speech with a tired half-smile, recognizing it for what it is, but walks away without refusing.

43.modern-en: Dolokhov is with his company near the French picket lines at Schöngraben and is drawn into a heated argument in French with a French grenadier — asserting with rough soldier confidence that the Russians have not retreated and will drive the French back, before shouldering his musket and walking away.

48.modern-en: At Schöngraben, Dolokhov fights alongside Timokhin's company in the surprise counter-attack that stops the Russian rout — he is the first to seize a surrendering French officer by the collar, and afterward presents himself to the regimental commander with blood matted in his hair from a bayonet wound, demanding in his precise, ringing voice that his bravery and his prisoner be recorded.

49.modern-en: At the post-battle review at Bagration's headquarters, the general who saw him in action mentions Dolokhov's exceptional courage — and this public acknowledgment, combined with Prince Andrew's defense of Captain Tushin, helps shape the account of the day's fighting.

67.modern-en: Dolokhov does not appear directly in this chapter, which focuses on Rostov's ordeal after Austerlitz as he searches for the Emperor on a field of dead and wounded — but he remains among the forces that have retreated, his fate as yet unknown.

70.modern-en: Moscow has heard that Dolokhov compromised Hélène — Pierre's wife — during his time as a guest in Pierre's household, and Anna Mikhaylovna reports this gossip to the Rostovs; the scandal is already circulating as the city prepares the banquet for Bagration.

71.modern-en: Dolokhov attends the English Club banquet for Bagration in the company of Rostov, whom he has recently befriended — now reinstated to officer rank, he is pointedly treated as a respected younger figure by the older men around the table.

72.modern-en: At the banquet, Dolokhov goads Pierre with a toast 'to beautiful women and their lovers,' knowing Pierre suspects him of an affair with Hélène — when Pierre snatches back the poem and issues a challenge, Dolokhov accepts with cold amusement, and the next morning's duel is agreed at Sokolniki.

73.modern-en: The duel in the Sokolniki woods: Dolokhov advances without raising his pistol, calm and deliberate, then is struck by Pierre's shot and falls in the snow — but from the ground he steadies himself and fires, missing Pierre, before collapsing; he is carried away by Rostov in the sleigh, and in the carriage reveals an utterly unexpected tenderness, weeping over what the news of his wounding will do to his beloved mother.

74.modern-en: The aftermath of the duel is recounted from Pierre's perspective — Pierre processes his discovery that Hélène is guilty and that Dolokhov was his intimate friend who betrayed him, with the full weight of his own self-deception about the marriage becoming clear.

78.modern-en: During his convalescence at his mother's house, Dolokhov confides to Rostov his personal code: he loves fiercely the few people he cares about and is indifferent or ruthless to everyone else — he describes his search for a pure, devoted woman with a sincerity that surprises Rostov; he also begins visiting the Rostov household and falls visibly in love with Sonya.

79.modern-en: Dolokhov has proposed to Sonya and been flatly refused — news that disturbs Rostov more than he expects; he is clearly angry and cold toward Sonya in the days that follow, and his farewell supper is being arranged at the English Hotel that evening.

81.modern-en: Dolokhov hosts a farewell card party at the English Hotel before his departure, and as Rostov sits down to play, Dolokhov methodically destroys him — 'killing' ten cards in a row and watching Rostov spiral into a losing session with a cold, strategic patience, almost as if exacting personal revenge for the Sonya refusal.

82.modern-en: The card session ends with Rostov owing Dolokhov the carefully chosen sum of forty-three thousand rubles — a number Dolokhov selected because it combines their ages — and Dolokhov collects the debt with the same precise, merciless efficiency he brings to everything.

83.modern-en: Rostov goes home carrying the weight of forty-three thousand rubles in debt that will devastate his family — while in the next room Natasha sings, and the beauty of her voice dissolves his despair temporarily; Dolokhov is not present but his shadow falls over the entire scene.

99.modern-en: Dolokhov is mentioned as the gambling debt Rostov is still paying off, the loss that has reshaped his entire relationship with money and family obligation — the wound he left behind defines Rostov's regimental stint as a kind of penance.

116.modern-en: In Pierre's diary, Dolokhov appears twice as the object of a fantasized revenge confrontation — Pierre catches himself imagining bitter, cutting replies to Dolokhov's taunting remark after the duel scandal, recognizes his anger, and reproaches himself for failing to master the passion.

153.modern-en: Dolokhov appears at the opera in a flamboyant Persian outfit, his hair brushed into a dramatic shock, standing in the stalls in full view of the audience with the effortless self-assurance of a man who knows everyone is watching him — Moscow ladies are said to be captivated by his exotic reputation as 'Dolokhov the Persian.'

154.modern-en: Dolokhov sits beside Anatole in the stalls during the opera intermission as Anatole watches Natasha with open admiration — Dolokhov is the cooler, more calculating presence beside his impulsive companion.

156.modern-en: Dolokhov has reconnected with Anatole in Moscow after returning from exile and Persian adventures, and is making deliberate use of him — he uses Anatole's name and connections to draw wealthy young men into his gambling circle, while Anatole, genuinely fond of him, has no idea he is being exploited; after the opera, Dolokhov listens to Anatole describe Natasha and warns him that she is 'not for us,' though he does not refuse to help.

161.modern-en: Dolokhov has organized the elopement down to the last ruble and the last witness — he counts the money, assigns Khvostikov and Makarin their roles, and tries one more time to talk Anatole out of the scheme, telling him bluntly it is dangerous and stupid; when Anatole refuses to back down, Dolokhov prepares the troika and the arrangements with his characteristic cold efficiency.

162.modern-en: Dolokhov drives in the troika with Anatole and Balaga to Marya Dmitrievna's house for the elopement — when the scheme is exposed and Gabriel the footman blocks Anatole, it is Dolokhov who shoves the yard porter aside, pulls Anatole out through the gate, and gets them both safely away in the waiting sleigh.

165.modern-en: Anatole dines with Dolokhov that day while Pierre searches Moscow for him — and Dolokhov is at Hélène's drawing room when Pierre arrives to confront Anatole; he witnesses Pierre's fury but is not named as the target, serving as the background presence who organized the whole scheme.

212.modern-en: Before the Battle of Borodino, Dolokhov appears at Kutuzov's position, working to regain a favorable position — he has crawled into the enemy's picket lines the night before and is proposing some scheme to the commander; when Pierre encounters him afterward, Dolokhov takes his hand publicly and asks for forgiveness for their past enmity, with what appears to be genuine emotion in his eyes.

226.modern-en: Dolokhov does not appear in this chapter, which depicts Prince Andrew's regiment enduring artillery fire at Borodino until Andrew is struck by a shell fragment.

238.modern-en: In Pierre's dream after Borodino, Anatole and Dolokhov appear together as representatives of the old dissolute world — the category of 'those people' — contrasted with the simple soldiers who are 'they'; Dolokhov also flashes into Pierre's waking memory as the occasion of the duel, a turning point Pierre now sees as the moment he could have escaped his old life.

301.modern-en: Denisov's partisan band is operating near Shamshevo in coordination with Dolokhov's band — the two commanders plan a joint attack on a large French convoy carrying fifteen hundred men and Russian prisoners; Dolokhov is operating from the opposite side of the road to verify French dispositions before the combined assault.

302.modern-en: Denisov waits anxiously for news from Dolokhov, who has not yet confirmed his arrival at the watchman's hut rendezvous — the reconnaissance and timing of the ambush depend on Dolokhov's intelligence about the French column.

304.modern-en: Dolokhov arrives at the forest watchman's hut looking like a clean-shaven Guards officer rather than a guerrilla — he immediately demands precise intelligence about the French column, refuses to accept Denisov's estimates, and volunteers to ride into the French camp himself wearing a French uniform to count their numbers firsthand.

306.modern-en: Dolokhov argues coldly with Denisov about what to do with French prisoners, dismissing Denisov's moral qualms as 'sweet talk' — he agrees to take Petya with him on the reconnaissance, and the scene establishes the ruthless pragmatism with which he approaches partisan warfare.

307.modern-en: Dolokhov leads Petya into the French camp in French uniform at night — with icy nerve he bluffs past the sentinel, sits by the campfire with French officers, lights his pipe, and extracts the information he needs about troop numbers before riding out; he kisses the ecstatic Petya goodbye at the edge of camp and rides off with the agreed signal for tomorrow's assault.

309.modern-en: In the dawn attack on the French convoy, Dolokhov commands his men with precise authority — when Petya gallops recklessly into the courtyard and is shot dead, Dolokhov walks over to the body, says simply 'Done for' with a grim frown, and immediately turns to ensure no prisoners are taken from his portion of the attack, his personal ruthlessness unchanged even in the face of Petya's death.

313.modern-en: Dolokhov stands at the gate of the ruined house after the convoy is captured, watching the disarmed French file past — he taps his boots with his whip and counts the prisoners with a chalk line on the gate, his cold glassy eyes causing the French to fall silent as they pass him, the same merciless authority he has always projected unchanged by the chaos of the campaign.

epithet.en: Hussar officer, Nikolai's friend, has a lisp
epithet.da: Husarofficer, Nikolajs ven, har en talelidelse

32.modern-en: Denisov, the squadron commander and Nikolai's billet-mate, is introduced: he has been up all night gambling and hasn't come home when Rostov returns from foraging, establishing the colorful, boisterous atmosphere of their shared quarters.

33.modern-en: Denisov listens gloomily as the staff captain pressures Rostov to apologize to the colonel; though he shakes his head in disapproval at Rostov's stubbornness, he does not actively intervene, caught between comradeship and protocol.

35.modern-en: Denisov's squadron is one of the last units covering the retreat across the bridge over the Enns, holding position while the infantry and baggage cross under enemy observation.

36.modern-en: Denisov's hussar squadron holds the far side of the bridge as the last unit facing the French; under cannon fire, he keeps his men steady, and when the signal comes he leads the charge to destroy the bridge, coolly commanding through the danger.

57.modern-en: Denisov rides with his squadron at the great Olmutz review, and Nikolai observes him from the ranks as part of the magnificent military spectacle before the two Emperors.

59.modern-en: Denisov sits by the road with a flask and food during the day at Wischau, inviting Rostov to drink and drown their frustration at being left in reserve while others get the glory.

62.modern-en: Denisov is on the night picket line near Rostov's post before Austerlitz; the chapter notes his proximity as part of the squadron's vigil in the foggy darkness.

69.modern-en: Denisov travels to Moscow with Nikolai on leave, drunk and asleep in the sleigh the whole way, and is bundled into the Rostov house where he is welcomed as a beloved regular visitor.

70.modern-en: Denisov is staying at the Rostov house in Moscow during Nikolai's leave and is mentioned as one of Nikolai's regular companions at drinking bouts and horse racing.

71.modern-en: At the English Club dinner, Denisov moves among the members with the easy air of a man comfortable in any military company, part of the younger set that includes Rostov and Dolokhov.

72.modern-en: Denisov sits at the Bagration dinner and acts as a counterweight to the charged atmosphere between Pierre and Dolokhov, part of the lively young officers' group.

73.modern-en: Denisov acts as one of the seconds in the Dolokhov-Pierre duel, announcing the rules in his clipped, emphatic manner, and watches the outcome with evident astonishment when Pierre wounds Dolokhov.

78.modern-en: Denisov recovers from his wound after the duel and his friendship with Nikolai deepens; he is mentioned as one of Nikolai's closest companions during his Moscow leave.

79.modern-en: On the evening before the Iogel ball, Denisov has dinner with the Rostovs and declares himself ready to dance the pas de châle at Natasha's command, playfully adopting the role of her devoted knight.

80.modern-en: At Iogel's ball, Denisov dances with Natasha and is enchanted by her; he watches her with an admiring tenderness that is more than a soldier's appreciation of a pretty girl.

81.modern-en: Denisov attends Dolokhov's farewell card supper and witnesses Nikolai's catastrophic losing streak, powerless to stop it.

83.modern-en: Denisov is at the Rostov house that evening, sitting at the clavichord composing a barcarolle and singing it passionately to Natasha, lost in his admiration for her — until Nikolai's confession about the gambling debt shatters the household's Christmas peace.

84.modern-en: Denisov proposes to Natasha that same evening — the countess is stunned by his seriousness — and is gently but firmly refused; he leaves Moscow the next day to rejoin the regiment, the episode treated with tender comedy.

99.modern-en: Denisov has already returned to the regiment before Nikolai; when Rostov arrives, Denisov rushes out of the mud hut to embrace him, and Nikolai is struck by how completely the regiment feels like home.

100.modern-en: Denisov and Nikolai share a dugout in the spring campaign of 1807; Denisov fumes at the quartermaster about soldiers eating bad food and rides out with his squadron on a bread requisition — the action that will ruin him.

101.modern-en: Denisov is in a Prussian military hospital after being wounded and getting into legal trouble over his seizure of a bread convoy meant for the infantry; Nikolai rides from the army on leave to visit him.

102.modern-en: In the hospital, Denisov is found lying in bed, pale and swollen, consumed by his petition against the commissariat officers; he barely registers Nikolai's news from the regiment, obsessively rereading his grievances to anyone who will listen.

103.modern-en: Denisov gives Nikolai his petition to carry to the Emperor in Tilsit, hoping to clear his name over the bread convoy affair; his case becomes the occasion for Nikolai's uncomfortable visit to Boris and his frustrated attempt to approach Alexander.

104.modern-en: Denisov's case goes unresolved — Nikolai cannot deliver the petition — and the chapter ends with the humiliating understanding that justice is inaccessible even to a deserving officer in wartime.

105.modern-en: Denisov's petition is still in Nikolai's pocket when the latter watches Napoleon and Alexander meet at Tilsit; the contrast between the ceremonial exchange of honors and Denisov's ignored grievance is implied though not stated.

133.modern-en: Denisov is referenced as the officer who handed command of the Pavlograd squadron to Nikolai; his earlier trouble with the commissariat is the reason Nikolai took over.

205.modern-en: Denisov, now a lieutenant colonel commanding a partisan detachment, meets Prince Andrei at headquarters while both wait for Kutuzov; he introduces himself warmly, aware of Andrei's connection to Natasha, and the two men share a brief, poignant conversation.

285.modern-en: Denisov is part of the larger guerrilla operations near Tarutino; his detachment is mentioned as one of the groups watching a major French convoy, and he coordinates with other partisan commanders about the coming attack.

286.modern-en: The Battle of Tarutino is described from above; Denisov and his partisans are part of the action, though the chapter focuses on Kutuzov's deliberate restraint of the larger operation.

301.modern-en: Denisov leads his partisan band in the forests during the French retreat, one of hundreds of guerrilla commanders who are destroying the Grande Armée piece by piece; he has kept his men together with steady leadership since early autumn.

302.modern-en: Denisov rides through driving autumn rain to scout a large French convoy, foul-tempered with hunger and impatience, debating whether to attack before Dolokhov's band arrives; his character — energetic, irritable, morally precise — is on full display.

303.modern-en: Denisov observes the French positions from the forest edge with Petya and the esaul, interrogates the captured French drummer boy, and begins planning the convoy attack — insisting on waiting for Dolokhov despite his eagerness to strike.

304.modern-en: Denisov returns to camp, reviews Tikhon's reckless solo expedition against the French with a mixture of exasperation and admiration, then settles in to wait for Dolokhov with barely suppressed impatience.

305.modern-en: Denisov manages the arrival of young Petya Rostov in his camp and tries — unsuccessfully — to keep him from taking part in the planned attack, recognizing a boy's recklessness but too fond of him to enforce the order firmly.

306.modern-en: Denisov welcomes Dolokhov and they discuss the convoy attack; Denisov refuses to let Petya go on the reconnaissance but is overruled; the two leaders reveal their different characters — Denisov morally scrupulous about prisoners, Dolokhov coldly practical.

307.modern-en: Denisov waits anxiously at camp while Dolokhov and Petya ride into the French camp in disguise; he paces the hut, regretting having let Petya go.

308.modern-en: Denisov is greatly relieved when Petya returns safely from the French camp; he tries to make Petya sleep but the boy is too wound up, and Denisov soon falls asleep himself while Petya goes outside.

309.modern-en: Denisov leads the dawn attack on the French convoy; he gives final orders calmly, then charges down into the ravine at the signal shot — only to see Petya gallop ahead recklessly and be shot dead in the first moments. Denisov rushes to the boy and weeps over his body.

329.modern-en: Denisov tells Pierre, during his recovery at Orel, about Prince Andrei's death at the Rostovs' house — one of the painful pieces of news Pierre receives after his liberation.

346.modern-en: Denisov is visiting the Rostovs at Bald Hills on the eve of St. Nicholas Day, now a retired general; he breaks the dinnertime awkwardness between Nicholas and Princess Mary with his lively, opinionated conversation.

348.modern-en: Denisov has been at the Rostovs' for a fortnight during Pierre's extended absence; he watches Natasha's anxiety and dejection with sad surprise, remembering the radiant girl he once loved and proposed to.

350.modern-en: Denisov sits with the family at tea after Pierre's return, his curly hair now half-gray, still sharp-tongued and dissatisfied with the government's direction.

351.modern-en: At the evening gathering, Denisov gets up with Nicholas to smoke and listen to Pierre, then launches into biting political commentary — bitter about the state of affairs in Russia and resentful of his career disappointments.

352.modern-en: Denisov kicks off the after-supper conversation about memories of 1812, and Pierre joins in warmly; their reminiscences bring the family together before they separate for the night.

epithet.en: Ambitious young officer, childhood friend of Natasha
epithet.da: Ambitiøs ung officer, barndomsven af Natasja

4.modern-en: Boris appears peripherally at Anna Pavlovna's soiree, where his mother Anna Mikhaylovna maneuvers on his behalf; he is a polished, composed young man being positioned by a calculating parent.

10.modern-en: Boris transfers from the infantry to a coveted Guards cornetcy, the result of Anna Mikhaylovna's tireless lobbying of Prince Vasili; his career advancement is secured entirely through social pressure rather than merit.

11.modern-en: Boris is present at the Rostov name-day party as a newly minted Guards officer, his manner already more polished and deliberate than the boisterous Nikolai's — the first sign of the careful self-fashioning that will define him.

12.modern-en: Boris leaves university to join the army alongside Nikolai, the two friends heading off to the war together, though their paths and ambitions are already diverging.

13.modern-en: Natasha leads Boris to the conservatory and, on a childish dare, asks him to kiss her; he kisses only her hand with measured reserve and solemn courtesy, establishing himself as someone who keeps his feelings under careful control.

14.modern-en: Boris sits at the window with Natasha and gently defends her propriety to the arch Vera, earning the label 'such a diplomat' — a description he will live up to for the rest of the novel.

15.modern-en: Boris reluctantly accompanies his mother to the dying old Count Bezukhov's house, uncomfortable with the begging and scheming but obedient to Anna Mikhaylovna's imperatives.

16.modern-en: Boris visits Pierre and asks for money; his calculating, polished manner — the careful framing of the request as a matter of soldierly honor — contrasts starkly with Pierre's chaotic generosity.

18.modern-en: Boris travels with Berg to join the army, the two young officers neatly paired as social climbers with very different personalities — Berg open and earnest about his ambitions, Boris more quietly strategic.

20.modern-en: Boris is called upon by Natasha to participate in the musical evening at the Rostovs, present at the gathering as part of the family circle before departure for the campaign.

55.modern-en: Boris is absent from this chapter, which focuses on the Rostov family's receipt of Nikolai's wounded-officer letter, but Anna Mikhaylovna — his mother — is central to the scene.

56.modern-en: Boris, lodged with Berg near Olmutz before the great review, receives Nikolai's visit; he has already attached himself to Prince Andrei and secured an introduction through Pierre, and his Guards quarters — neat, comfortable, socially correct — contrast pointedly with Nikolai's worn hussar jacket.

58.modern-en: Boris rides to Kutuzov's headquarters in Olmutz to exploit his connection with Prince Andrei, navigating the layers of staff hierarchy with practiced patience; his determination to enter the elite world of headquarters adjutants is put on full display.

66.modern-en: Boris is at the Tilsit meeting peripherally, part of the glittering suite that surrounds the two Emperors; he is already moving in circles well above his original station.

69.modern-en: Boris is bundled into the Rostov house in Moscow, drunk and asleep in the sleigh alongside Nikolai, welcomed as a familiar and beloved visitor despite his growing distance from his old friends.

70.modern-en: Boris is mentioned as one of Nikolai's regular companions during the Moscow leave, though his ambitions are pulling him toward a more calculated social life than the carefree Rostov circle offers.

90.modern-en: Boris appears at Anna Pavlovna's soiree in Petersburg, already comfortably established in the highest social circles; he is navigating the political salons with practiced ease as the war with Napoleon approaches.

91.modern-en: Boris moves between Anna Pavlovna and Helene at the soiree, his response to Prince Hippolyte's joke carefully calibrated to be taken as either ironic or appreciative — the perfect social lubricant; Helene summons him pointedly for Tuesday.

103.modern-en: Boris secures a place in the suite at the Tilsit meeting through his connection to a senior personage; at the historic encounter of the two Emperors he watches and records everything — noting the meeting lasted one hour and fifty-three minutes — as a young man building a résumé of historical proximity.

104.modern-en: Boris receives Nikolai in Tilsit with polite embarrassment; he cannot help with Denisov's petition and his reluctance reveals how completely his loyalty now runs to career rather than old friendship — Nikolai leaves the next morning, their friendship effectively over.

105.modern-en: Boris is present at Tilsit among the higher ranks while Nikolai watches Napoleon award the Legion of Honor; Boris's smooth ascent through military society is contrasted with Rostov's frustrated attempt to reach the Emperor.

115.modern-en: Boris is now firmly established in Petersburg high society, moving in Helene's brilliant circle; he has become one of those polished young men who cultivate exactly the right connections and are welcomed everywhere.

116.modern-en: Pierre records in his diary that Boris visited him, irritated him from the start, and that Pierre lost his temper with him — a moment of honest self-criticism that reveals Boris's effect on those who see through his calculated charm.

118.modern-en: Boris calls on the Rostovs in Petersburg with the deliberate intention of signaling that their childhood bond is not binding; he is stunned by how beautiful Natasha has become but keeps his composure, and she reads his manner with sharp accuracy.

119.modern-en: Natasha confides to her mother that night that Boris's visit unsettled her; the countess confirms Boris is turning her head and warns against the attachment, recognizing Boris's calculations even if Natasha does not.

126.modern-en: Boris is at Berg's soiree as one of the guests, his presence part of the social texture of Moscow's mid-tier military society — he is observed by Pierre as being present wherever wealthy heiresses are to be found.

127.modern-en: Boris sits beside Natasha at Berg's party and she barely notices him; she is entirely occupied by Prince Andrei's arrival, and Boris's attentions are rendered invisible by her absorption in the man she truly loves.

148.modern-en: Boris is visiting Bald Hills for the third time, courting Princess Mary as part of his calculated search for a wealthy match; Pierre quietly identifies to Mary that Boris is simultaneously pursuing Julie Karagina.

149.modern-en: Pierre tells Princess Mary plainly that Boris visits wherever there is a wealthy heiress and is hesitating between her and Julie; Princess Mary absorbs this with a mixture of sadness and self-awareness.

150.modern-en: Boris's cold-blooded courtship of both Princess Mary and Julie Karagina is laid out at length: he finds Princess Mary more attractive but Julie more available; he cultivates Julie's fashionable melancholy and eventually proposes, calculating that her fortune outweighs his feelings.

153.modern-en: Boris is at the opera in Petersburg's social world, part of the glittering background against which Natasha's re-enchantment with public life begins; he is present but peripheral as Anatole Kuragin enters and occupies everyone's attention.

154.modern-en: Boris is visible in the social scene at the opera as Anatole makes his bold play for Natasha; Boris's own interest in her belongs to an already-concluded chapter.

170.modern-en: Boris is at Bennigsen's ball in Vilna on the eve of Napoleon's crossing of the Niemen, wealthy and self-sufficient now, dancing the mazurka with Helene and speaking to her with the easy familiarity of old acquaintances who share a complicated history.

212.modern-en: Boris encounters Pierre on the field at Borodino and smoothly offers to show him around the position, angling Pierre toward Bennigsen's sector rather than Kutuzov's; he has attached himself to Bennigsen's faction and is working both sides with practiced tact, careful never to commit too openly to either commander.

epithet.en: Petersburg hostess, opens the novel

1.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna opens the novel and her soirée simultaneously, greeting Prince Vasili with a volley of anti-Bonapartist indignation delivered in French — she is the mistress of form, deploying social conversation as though arranging troops.

2.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna's drawing room fills with Petersburg's highest society; she circulates among her guests with the efficiency of a spinning-wheel hostess, managing the evening's tone and keeping its various conversations synchronized.

3.modern-en: The reception is in full swing, and Anna Pavlovna positions herself at the center of one of the three conversational groups, holding Mortemart to herself like a rare delicacy she will share with guests in careful portions.

4.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna receives Prince Andrei with a graciousness that cannot quite conceal her sense of entitlement to everyone's good behavior in her drawing room; she is the standard against which all social conduct is measured here.

5.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna leads the political conversation with her characteristic mix of genuine alarm about Napoleon and aristocratic wit, setting the tone for the kind of society talk that mistakes clever indignation for thought.

6.modern-en: As the guests leave, Anna Pavlovna bids each farewell with calibrated warmth; she sends Pierre off with the polite condescension of a woman who has forgiven his social blundering as a matter of Christian duty.

7.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna is not present in this chapter set at Prince Andrei's house, but she is invoked by the little princess as the model of Petersburg social virtue — the woman who, according to Liza, should have been married long ago.

8.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna is not present in this chapter but her party is what Prince Andrei and Pierre discuss afterward — the evening she hosted stands as the exemplar of the gilded, empty world Andrei is desperate to escape.

10.modern-en: Prince Vasili has fulfilled his promise to Princess Drubetskaya, made at Anna Pavlovna's soirée, and Boris is transferred to the Guards; her party is thus revealed as a venue where real favors are exchanged beneath the polished surface.

15.modern-en: This chapter follows Boris and Anna Mikhaylovna to old Count Bezukhov's mansion; Anna Pavlovna appears only as the place where the promise was made that now bears fruit.

50.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna appears in the background of Prince Vasili's Petersburg world; she is one of the social forces whose approval he navigates as he maneuvers his children and Pierre into advantageous positions.

51.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna's salon is briefly invoked as part of the ongoing Petersburg world in which Prince Vasili manages his affairs; she remains the fixed social star around which these machinations orbit.

53.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna is not present in this chapter set at Bald Hills, but her world — the Petersburg world of form — stands in implicit contrast to the earnest, provincial awkwardness of Princess Mary's life.

90.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna is part of the societal chorus that judges Pierre harshly after the duel and his separation from Hélène; her salon's verdict — that Pierre is to blame — exemplifies the way this world shapes and enforces reputation.

91.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna hosts Boris and others at her soirée, managing the conversation and gently rescuing it from Hippolyte's unintelligible joke; she narrates the story of Bonaparte stealing Frederick the Great's sword with practiced dramatic flair.

196.modern-en: Seven years on, Anna Pavlovna's salon continues to run on exactly the same principles as in 1805 — unchanged by peace, war, or any shift in political reality — and this chapter treats its unchanging character as both absurd and somehow reassuring.

264.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna is at the center of a soirée as Moscow burns and Russia faces catastrophe; in her drawing room the disaster is present only as a topic to be handled with appropriate feeling, kept at the safe distance that form always provides.

265.modern-en: Anna Pavlovna's premonition about the battle of Borodino is fulfilled: Kutuzov's dispatch announces a victory, and her salon immediately fills with patriotic celebration — she is the first to confirm the good news, her drawing room a barometer of official sentiment.

epithet.en: Emperor of France, the war's driving force

1.modern-en: At Anna Pavlovna Scherer's salon in July 1805, Napoleon is the charged topic of conversation — Anna Pavlovna calls him an Antichrist and urges Prince Vasili to stop defending him, setting the political anxieties of Petersburg society squarely on the French emperor's ambitions.

3.modern-en: The salon continues to debate Napoleon's coronation in Milan and the murder of the Duc d'Enghien — the Vicomte Mortemart argues that Bonaparte has destroyed French society through intrigue and executions, while Anna Pavlovna expresses hope that Europe's sovereigns will unite against the usurper.

5.modern-en: Napoleon's coronation in Milan causes outrage at the salon: Anna Pavlovna cites his self-crowning words as the last straw, and the Vicomte laments that sovereigns are sending ambassadors to congratulate a murderous usurper rather than challenging him.

8.modern-en: Prince Andrei uses Napoleon as the measure of an unconstrained, purposeful life — he tells Pierre that Napoleon could advance step by step toward his goals only because he was free of domestic entanglements, contrasting the emperor's freedom with Andrei's own sense of being shackled by marriage.

12.modern-en: War with Napoleon is discussed at the Rostov household as Nicholas prepares to join the hussars — the count and his guests speak of it as a possibility that has been rumored for years but may finally arrive.

16.modern-en: Napoleon is barely mentioned directly, but his wars form the backdrop for Pierre's return to Moscow after his Petersburg disgrace, and the larger political climate he represents shapes the anxious conversations among the old prince's household.

26.modern-en: Napoleon's campaign against Austria and Russia is the unseen force driving Prince Andrei's departure for the war — his visit to Bald Hills before joining the army takes place against the backdrop of the approaching conflict with Bonaparte.

27.modern-en: Old Prince Bolkonski dismisses the military threat from Napoleon and expresses contempt for the way the campaign is being managed, suggesting Bonaparte's success is due more to others' incompetence than to any genuine genius on his part.

30.modern-en: Bonaparte's army of one hundred thousand, with Napoleon himself in command, is pursing the Russian force of thirty-five thousand under Kutuzov down the Danube — the strategic situation is described as desperate, with the Russians retreating under constant pressure from the superior French force.

37.modern-en: The chapter opens with Napoleon's army of a hundred thousand men pursuing Kutuzov's exhausted Russians, who have already fought rearguard actions at Lambach, Amstetten, and Melk — Napoleon's relentless advance has stripped Austria of allies and left Kutuzov's army in a nearly impossible position.
