38.modern-en: At Brünn, Bilibin tells Prince Andrei the bitter joke of Prussian generals proudly surrendering their arms to the French and the King of Prussia writing servile letters to Napoleon, illustrating how swiftly Bonaparte has humiliated the continental powers.

40.modern-en: Napoleon's crossing of the Vienna bridge by a ruse is recounted with incredulous laughter among the diplomats at Brünn — the Frenchman has outwitted Murat's own credulity, and Prince Andrei hears how the army intends to try the same trick on Bonaparte in reverse at Hollabrünn.

42.modern-en: Napoleon's army of a hundred and fifty thousand has crossed the Vienna bridge and threatens to cut off Kutuzov entirely — the strategic crisis forces Kutuzov to send Bagration's four thousand to Hollabrünn to delay the French and buy time for the retreat.

43.modern-en: Napoleon's aide-de-camp has not yet reached Murat with orders when Prince Andrei arrives at Bagration's position — the truce negotiations and the possibility of battle revolve around whether Bonaparte's intentions are genuine or another stratagem.

58.modern-en: Napoleon is glimpsed only at a distance — Boris Drubetskoy corrects himself from calling him 'Buonaparte' to 'Emperor Napoleon,' learning that at headquarters such precision now matters, while the diplomatic machinery around both emperors fills the town of Olmütz.

60.modern-en: Napoleon sends his aide Savary to propose a personal meeting with Alexander, which is refused; instead Prince Dolgorukov is sent to meet Napoleon and returns convinced the emperor is frightened and weak — a fatally mistaken impression that will shape the disastrous Allied plan at Austerlitz.

62.modern-en: On the eve of Austerlitz, Rostov on skirmish duty daydreams about catching Napoleon's eye and being rewarded by the emperor — Napoleon appears only in his imagination, yet the young hussar's fantasy captures the almost mythic hold the French emperor has over soldiers' minds.

63.modern-en: The Allied columns begin their fateful advance at Austerlitz under cover of thick fog, following the plan urged against Kutuzov's objections — Napoleon's trap is already sprung, though none of the marching men yet know it.

68.modern-en: Napoleon rides across the Austerlitz battlefield after the victory and pauses over the wounded Prince Andrei — he praises the dying man's courage, orders him carried to a dressing station, and rides on, appearing to Andrei at that moment as a tiny, insignificant creature against the vast sky above.

78.modern-en: Napoleon is not directly present but his wars form the background of Moscow society life in 1806 — the period of French victory at Jena and Auerstadt is noted, and the social consequences of the ongoing conflict begin reshaping the characters' worlds.

90.modern-en: At year's end 1806, Napoleon's destruction of the Prussian army at Jena and Auerstadt is the talk of Petersburg salons, and a second war with Napoleon is beginning — Anna Pavlovna's circle regards him with moral horror while Helene's pro-French salon speaks of the 'great man' with admiration.

92.modern-en: The renewed war with Napoleon and his advance through Prussia is the event that reshapes the Bolkonski household — old Prince Bolkonski takes command of a provincial recruitment district while Prince Andrei, disillusioned after Austerlitz, avoids active duty.

93.modern-en: In Bilibin's long sardonic letter, Napoleon demolishes the Prussians in two strokes, settles into the Potsdam palace, and receives groveling letters from the Prussian king — the 'enemy of the human race' has made Europe into a kind of dark farce, and Bilibin's ironic dispatch conveys both the scale of the disaster and the incompetence of Russia's leadership.

103.modern-en: Napoleon meets Alexander on a raft on the Niemen at Tilsit — Boris Drubetskoy observes everything carefully, notes that Napoleon stepped forward quickly to greet Alexander and extended his hand, and records that their meeting lasted one hour and fifty-three minutes, now treating Napoleon as a figure of historical record rather than a monster.

105.modern-en: Napoleon rides up to join Alexander at the ceremony presenting the Legion of Honor to a Russian soldier — Rostov sees him at close range in his small hat and blue uniform, notes that he sits poorly in the saddle, and is disturbed to see Alexander treating Bonaparte as a complete equal, perfectly at ease in the tsar's presence.

106.modern-en: By 1809, Napoleon and Alexander are spoken of as the world's two arbiters, their intimacy so close that a Russian corps has crossed into Austria to fight alongside its former enemy; the possibility of Napoleon marrying one of Alexander's sisters is even discussed at court.

111.modern-en: Napoleon and the reform era are woven together in Petersburg political life — the French alliance shapes the reformist circle around Speransky, and Prince Andrei navigates a world where Napoleon's influence reaches into the very vocabulary of Russian politics.

115.modern-en: Helene's salon is openly aligned with Napoleon's France — she attended the Erfurt meetings, Napoleon himself noticed her in the theater and praised her, and her drawing room has become a gathering place for pro-French diplomats who regard the war as a temporary inconvenience to be resolved by peace.

131.modern-en: Napoleon's wars are the distant backdrop to the increasingly bitter domestic misery at Bald Hills — Prince Andrei has gone to the army, old Prince Bolkonski's temper worsens, and Princess Mary's letters describe a world where national catastrophe and private grief have become inseparable.

146.modern-en: Napoleon is the unseen cause reshaping Pierre's Moscow retreat — his wars have created the crisis that will soon demand something from everyone, and Pierre's restless purposelessness takes on a new edge as broadsheets about the French emperor and apocalyptic prophecies begin to fill his mind.

148.modern-en: Napoleon's influence appears grotesquely in old Prince Bolkonski's paranoia — he ejects his fashionable French doctor Metivier, calling him a spy and Bonaparte's lackey, an episode that reveals how the threat of Napoleon has poisoned even private domestic life.

168.modern-en: Tolstoy opens the 1812 campaign with a philosophical meditation on Napoleon as cause and effect — the chapter argues that attributing the invasion to Napoleon's personal ambition is as absurd as attributing the Saint Bartholomew massacre to a king's upset stomach, insisting the real causes lie in the collective movement of millions.

169.modern-en: Napoleon leaves Dresden with his court of kings and emperors, writes a letter to Alexander calling him 'mon frere' while simultaneously ordering his armies east, crosses the Niemen into Russia in a Polish uniform, and watches from a hill as his troops pour across the three bridges — he is at the height of his power and apparently his confidence.

170.modern-en: Napoleon's crossing of the Niemen is the immediate backdrop to Alexander's ball at Bennigsen's estate — the French emperor's advance into Russia begins on the very night the Russian emperor dances at a party, the two scenes framing the enormous gap between the reality of war and the life of courts.

171.modern-en: Napoleon's vanguard crosses into Russia and pushes aside the Cossack outposts — Balashev, carrying Alexander's letter to Napoleon, encounters the French army and is made to feel the raw insolence of an invading power, waiting hours before officers of decreasing importance deign to receive him.

172.modern-en: Balashev is kept waiting by Davout, who treats him with deliberate rudeness as a demonstration of France's contempt for Russian diplomacy — the comparison to Arakcheev underlines how both powers produce the same kind of brutal enforcer, each in the service of his sovereign's will.

173.modern-en: Napoleon receives Balashev in Vilna, walking in with his bouncing step and plump self-satisfied figure — he delivers a lengthy monologue about being forced into war while clearly relishing the power, hardly looking at Balashev as he speaks, entirely absorbed in his own theatrical self-presentation.

174.modern-en: Napoleon hosts Balashev at dinner and questions him about Moscow with the breezy curiosity of a man certain he will soon see it for himself — he makes a dismissive remark about Russian churches as a sign of backwardness and fails to notice Balashev's pointed reminder that Spain, too, has many churches and has resisted France.

176.modern-en: Napoleon's invasion has split the Russian armies and driven headquarters into confusion — Prince Andrei observes from the Drissa camp that the Russian command has no coherent plan to counter Bonaparte's advance, and the various theorists and advisors around Alexander represent competing visions of how to face him.

177.modern-en: News arrives at Drissa of a new French movement that might endanger the army, and the informal council convenes to debate Pfuel's fortified camp theory — Napoleon's advance is the pressure forcing these arguments, even though he himself is not present in the chapter.

178.modern-en: The council at Drissa debates strategies against Napoleon's advance — Paulucci furiously denounces the Drissa camp as madness, and the various generals' arguments reveal that no one has a clear answer to what Bonaparte is about to do.

186.modern-en: Pierre, in the grip of his Masonic numerology, calculates that the letters of 'l'russe Besuhof' add to 666 — the number of the Beast — and convinces himself he is destined to assassinate Napoleon and thereby end the Antichrist's reign, a private delusion that captures how Napoleon has become a kind of apocalyptic figure in Russian imagination.

191.modern-en: Tolstoy argues that Napoleon began the war not through grand strategic decision but through a series of personal weaknesses and vanities — he couldn't resist Dresden's flattery, couldn't control his anger with Kurakin and Balashev, and each small surrender of will led inevitably to the next, making the invasion the product of character rather than genius.

195.modern-en: Napoleon's armies have swept past Smolensk and are drawing nearer to Moscow — the burning of Smolensk marks an epoch for Prince Andrei, who feels a new personal fury against the enemy replacing his earlier abstract disillusionment.

196.modern-en: In Petersburg salons, Napoleon remains the great dividing question — Helene's pro-French circle regards him as the 'great man' and hopes for peace, while Anna Pavlovna's circle speaks of him with moral horror and rallies around patriotic sentiment, each circle reading the same dispatches in opposite directions.

197.modern-en: Napoleon on the march toward Moscow interrogates the captured serf Lavrushka, who plays the role of a simple Cossack while secretly observing everything — Napoleon asks eagerly about Kutuzov's appointment, and Lavrushka gives him a satirical performance that Napoleon takes at face value, revealing the emperor's susceptibility to what he wants to hear.

203.modern-en: Napoleon hovers in the background of Rostov's approach to Bogucharovo — Ilyin jokingly points to Lavrushka as 'Napoleon himself,' and the guerrilla ease with which Russian officers joke about the invader reflects how his presence has become both real threat and dark comedy in the Russian rear.

207.modern-en: Moscow society discusses Napoleon's approach with a strange festive lightness — Rostopchin's broadsheets mock the French as too small for Russian peasant women to worry about, yet the city's evacuation is already underway, and the gap between public bravado and private fear grows wider.

208.modern-en: Pierre reads Rostopchin's latest broadsheets and understands for the first time with certainty that the French will enter Moscow — the revelation crystallizes his vague Masonic obsession with Napoleon into a concrete resolve to remain in the city and attempt something decisive.

209.modern-en: Tolstoy frames the Battle of Borodino with a philosophical argument that neither Napoleon nor Kutuzov acted rationally — both emperors and commanders chose a battle that mathematically could only weaken them, driven by forces larger than any individual will.

213.modern-en: Pierre views the battlefield preparations at Borodino, and from the fleches observers spot a small group of horsemen on the Shevardino Redoubt — officers speculate that Napoleon or Murat is among them, and Pierre strains to identify which distant figure might be the emperor.

216.modern-en: Napoleon at Valuevo on the eve of Borodino receives a portrait of his son as a gift from de Beausset, which he displays publicly to give his troops an emotional spectacle — he calls it an excellent work of art, presents Fabvier with cold irony about the Spanish campaign, and prepares for battle with an elaborate performance of serene confidence.

217.modern-en: Napoleon surveys the Russian positions and dictates his battle plan — Tolstoy presents the famous deployment orders in full and then systematically dismantles them, arguing they contain nothing exceptional and that the forthcoming actions will have nothing to do with Napoleon's paper instructions.

218.modern-en: Tolstoy demolishes the historians' claim that Napoleon's cold at Borodino changed the outcome — the broader argument is that Napoleon's will, genius or otherwise, played no meaningful role; the battle was the product of mass forces, not individual command.

219.modern-en: Napoleon on the eve of Borodino tells de Beausset that 'the chess pieces are set up — the game begins tomorrow,' then sleeps badly, goes out at three in the morning with his worsened cold to check the fires, and confesses to Rapp that fortune is 'frankly a courtesan' and that the army has shrunk terribly since Smolensk.

223.modern-en: During the Battle of Borodino, Napoleon stands on the Shevardino knoll peering through his field glass but is unable to see through the smoke what is actually happening — the battle proceeds entirely beyond his ability to direct it, his orders irrelevant to the chaos below.

224.modern-en: As Murat and then Belliard send urgent requests for reinforcements, Napoleon refuses or delays — he says it is 'not yet noon' and that he cannot see his 'chessboard clearly,' then sends Claparede's division while remaining fundamentally passive, unable to grasp what the scale of casualties actually means.

228.modern-en: After Borodino, Napoleon sits exhausted and sick on his camp stool, his face sallow and heavy — the sight of the dead has briefly broken through his 'artificial illusion of life,' and for a moment he wants only rest and freedom rather than Moscow or glory, before mechanically ordering more cannon fire because it seems expected of him.

229.modern-en: The chapter following Borodino reflects on both sides' exhaustion and the mysterious force that kept men fighting beyond the point of reason — Napoleon's will is shown to have been entirely powerless over events, the battle having consumed a quarter of his army with no decisive result.

230.modern-en: Tolstoy opens his philosophical digression on historical causation with an image of Achilles and the tortoise — the impossibility of understanding historical motion through discrete events applies directly to the narrative of Napoleon's campaign, which cannot be reduced to the will of one man.

232.modern-en: At Fili, with Napoleon's army approaching Moscow, Kutuzov sits amid his generals' arguments about whether to defend the city — the French emperor's imminent arrival is the crisis that forces the impossible decision to abandon Moscow without a final battle.

234.modern-en: The burning of Moscow is analyzed as a natural, inevitable Russian response to occupation — Napoleon's entry into the city will be met not by organized resistance but by the organic instinct of a people who would rather burn their city than see it serve the enemy.

248.modern-en: Napoleon stands on Poklonny Hill at ten in the morning of September 2 and surveys Moscow spread below him in the autumn sunlight — he waits for the traditional delegation of boyars with the city's keys, experiences a strange mix of envious curiosity and aesthetic wonder at the 'strange and beautiful' city, but no delegation comes.

249.modern-en: Moscow, now abandoned by most of its population, is compared to a queenless hive — Napoleon has taken the city in form but finds an empty shell, its life withdrawn, its purposes dissolved, the very thing he sought reduced to ash and silence before he arrived.

256.modern-en: Pierre, hiding in occupied Moscow in peasant clothes with his pistol, is entirely absorbed in his private obsession with killing Napoleon — his plan has by now taken on a lunatic logic entirely disconnected from any real possibility of action.

258.modern-en: Pierre shelters a wounded French captain, Ramballe, and does not yet carry out his plan to kill Napoleon — their conversation is genial and oddly civilized, the personal humanity of a French officer cutting across Pierre's grandiose fantasy of assassination.

262.modern-en: Pierre sets out through burning Moscow to find and kill Napoleon but is immediately distracted by the fires and the chaos of the city — his assassination plan dissolves into the reality of the occupied, burning streets before he ever comes close to the emperor.

265.modern-en: In Petersburg, Kutuzov's first report from the battlefield of Borodino is received as news of a victory — Napoleon's name goes unspoken in the thanksgiving service, but the courtiers' conversation is full of him, and the false reading of events will soon be corrected by the news of Moscow's fall.

280.modern-en: Tolstoy opens his analysis of the flank march with a philosophical meditation on historical causation — Napoleon's decision-making is used as the prime example of why attributing historical events to individual will is as primitive as believing the earth is fixed; the French army's fate was determined by forces neither Napoleon nor anyone else controlled.

281.modern-en: Napoleon, wounded at Borodino, sends the envoy Lauriston to Kutuzov with peace proposals — 'the beast wounded at Borodino' is Tolstoy's image, and Napoleon's letter is presented as the words of a man grasping at something he no longer controls, written 'with his usual certainty that whatever entered his head was right.'

282.modern-en: Napoleon in Moscow writes letters to Alexander through captured Russians, dispatches Yakovlev and Tutolmin to Petersburg, issues proclamations and constitutions, and generally performs the motions of governing a conquered capital — all while the real situation outside the Kremlin walls is dissolving beyond his reach.

287.modern-en: Tolstoy catalogs Napoleon's missed opportunities in Moscow — he had enough supplies for six months, could have wintered in the city, marched on Petersburg, or retreated south, yet chose the most foolish available option, lingering while his troops looted, then retreating along the already devastated Smolensk road.

288.modern-en: Napoleon in Moscow micromanages administrative details — he orders fortifications, writes diplomatic letters, establishes a municipal government, issues proclamations to the citizens — performing all the gestures of an emperor in full command while the city burns around him and not a single order produces any real effect.

289.modern-en: Every one of Napoleon's measures in Moscow comes to nothing — the military plan is never executed, the diplomatic overtures receive no reply from Alexander, the legal orders don't stop the burning, and the administrative constitution is used only by those who loot under its cover.

291.modern-en: Pierre, a prisoner of the French, has reached a profound inner peace — and one sign of that peace is that Napoleon no longer seems real to him, the whole Masonic fantasy of killing the emperor now appearing 'meaningless and even ridiculous.'

294.modern-en: Napoleon sends another peace letter to Kutuzov, falsely dated from Moscow though he is already retreating — Kutuzov replies as he did to Lauriston: there can be no question of peace.

296.modern-en: Napoleon's wounded army, still in Moscow, sends Lauriston to Kutuzov with peace proposals — Kutuzov interprets the approach as proof that the beast is mortally wounded and holds back, resisting pressure from the staff to attack prematurely.

297.modern-en: Napoleon retreats from Moscow and the collapse of his army's discipline accelerates — Tolstoy argues that whatever road Napoleon chose, the army was already dissolving from within, carrying the chemical elements of its own destruction since Borodino and the looting of Moscow.

299.modern-en: Tolstoy uses the paradox of Borodino — a French 'victory' that led to the destruction of the French army — to argue that historical rules about military success and national power break down entirely in 1812, and that no meaningful causal account can place Napoleon's will at the center of what happened.

315.modern-en: Napoleon's retreating army, like a blindman's buff player clutching its bell, lurches back along the devastated Smolensk road — the once-magnificent Grande Armée has become a mob, and even Napoleon himself flees at the front, his presence no longer shaping but simply joining the general panic.

316.modern-en: Tolstoy dismantles every historian's claim that Napoleon's retreat showed military genius — the retreat from Malo-Yaroslavets, the heroics at Krasnoe, and finally his abandonment of the army are shown to be plain cowardice dressed up in retrospective mythology.

317.modern-en: The chapter raises the question of why the Russian army, with superior numbers, failed to capture Napoleon and the French remnant at Krasnoe and the Berezina — the answer lies not in Russian failure but in the fact that the destruction of the French was already complete without any further action.

321.modern-en: Napoleon's army is fleeing so rapidly that the pursuing Russians cannot keep up — the French emperor is somewhere at the front of the column, but his presence has no more strategic meaning; he is simply one of the many thousands running westward.

322.modern-en: Tolstoy contrasts the historical treatment of Napoleon and Kutuzov — Napoleon, 'the most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere showed human dignity, even in exile,' is treated as 'grand' by historians, while Kutuzov, who actually understood what was happening, is dismissed as vague and pathetic.

334.modern-en: Napoleon is far in the past by this chapter — Pierre, recovering in Moscow, tells Princess Mary and Natasha about his experiences during the occupation, his plan to kill the emperor now seeming a distant curiosity rather than a serious purpose.

338.modern-en: The Epilogue opens with Napoleon reduced to a footnote of history — among the 'historical figures' who 'spun in place' after the great flood of the Napoleonic wars subsided, he is listed alongside Alexander and Madame de Stael as one of those condemned or praised by historians for 'reaction.'

339.modern-en: Tolstoy uses Napoleon as the central example in his argument against the concept of historical genius — the ram fattened for slaughter who is mistaken for a genius by the rest of the flock is his image for how Napoleon's apparent exceptionalism was really just position and circumstance.

340.modern-en: Tolstoy traces Napoleon's rise as a product of historical necessity rather than genius — a man without convictions, traditions, or even French blood, raised by coincidences through the chaos of the Revolution to the position history required, his 'self-confident narrow-mindedness' perfectly fitted to lead the westward-eastward movement.

341.modern-en: Napoleon's return from Elba and final collapse at Waterloo is presented as the last required act of a historical role — the 'stage manager' shows him to the audience afterward as proof that it was never the man but the historical force moving through him, and his years on St. Helena are a 'pitiful comedy' of a man trying to justify himself when justification is no longer needed.

354.modern-en: Tolstoy's Second Epilogue uses Napoleon as the prime example of the inadequacy of modern history's explanatory framework — attributing the invasion of Russia to Napoleon's will is as incoherent as the ancient historians' appeal to divine intervention, just translated into the secular language of 'genius.'

355.modern-en: Napoleon appears as the paradigm case for the contradictions of universal history — when multiple historians describe the same event each attributing it to Napoleon's will, their accounts immediately contradict each other, exposing the conceptual bankruptcy of treating one man's will as the cause of mass movement.

357.modern-en: Tolstoy uses Napoleon's command to invade Russia as his central example in analyzing the nature of historical power — Napoleon never issued a single order to invade Russia as such, only a series of small consecutive commands, each contingent on the last, none of which individually caused the war.

358.modern-en: Napoleon's rule is used to illustrate the theoretical impossibility of the 'transfer of collective will' theory — the theory cannot explain how one man commands millions, and Napoleon's example shows that power is not the cause of events but a label we attach to whatever person happens to be at the front of the herd.

359.modern-en: Napoleon's invasion of Russia serves as Tolstoy's concluding example in the Second Epilogue — he never commanded the invasion as a single act but issued millions of consecutive small orders, and the fact that he spent more time planning an invasion of England that never happened than Russia which did shows that historical outcomes are independent of any individual's intentions.

epithet.en: Russian commander-in-chief, wise old general

4.modern-en: Prince Andrei mentions at Anna Pavlovna's salon that he is going to war as aide-de-camp to General Kutuzov — the first reference to Kutuzov in the novel, establishing him as the commander who has taken Andrei into his service.

29.modern-en: At Braunau in October 1805, the regiment Kutuzov commands prepares nervously for his inspection — officers have kept the men up all night polishing and mending, though the one problem no one can solve, the soldiers' ruined boots, remains conspicuously on display.

30.modern-en: Kutuzov arrives by carriage to review the regiment, steps down heavily and calmly as though the two thousand soldiers holding their breath simply don't exist, then walks the ranks pausing occasionally to speak with veterans of the Turkish campaign and, crucially, pointing out the boots — acknowledging the real problem rather than the parade-ground show.

31.modern-en: Kutuzov receives the Austrian general after the review and conducts a brilliantly polite diplomatic exchange, declining to join the Archduke's advance on grounds of circumstance rather than ability — his smile suggests he doesn't care whether he is believed, but he cannot be caught in a direct lie.

37.modern-en: Leading the Russian army of thirty-five thousand in a desperate retreat along the Danube, Kutuzov crosses to the left bank, attacks Mortier's division at Dürrenstein and shatters it — the first Russian success of the campaign and a genuine morale victory, though the strategic situation remains dire.

38.modern-en: Kutuzov's victory at Dürrenstein is the good news Prince Andrei brings to Brünn — it earns praise and decorations from the Austrian court, though the larger picture remains precarious and Bilibin's ironic commentary on the campaign frames what Kutuzov has actually managed to salvage.

40.modern-en: Emperor Francis receives Prince Andrei carrying Kutuzov's dispatch, asking perfunctory questions about the battle — Kutuzov's health and his movements become the emperor's only real interest, and the Austrian court gratefully bestows decorations and honors on the report of the Dürrenstein action.

41.modern-en: Prince Andrei rides back through the chaos of the retreating Russian army to find Kutuzov — the disorganized mass of men, wagons, and equipment he encounters stands in bitter contrast to Kutuzov's attempt to preserve the army as a fighting force.

42.modern-en: Receiving intelligence that the French have crossed the Vienna bridge, Kutuzov faces an apparently impossible strategic situation — he chooses to retreat to Olmütz and uses the inspired stratagem of sending Bagration's four thousand to Hollabrünn to deceive Murat and buy time for the main body to escape.

43.modern-en: Kutuzov's order has sent Bagration to Hollabrünn to delay the French — Prince Andrei arrives there as Bagration's trusted representative, giving orders about the retreat as 'very important,' and the chapter is shaped entirely by Kutuzov's strategic thinking even in his absence.

49.modern-en: Kutuzov is not present in this chapter but his army's battered condition after the retreat and rearguard actions shapes everything — Tushin's exhausted battery reflects the cost of the retreat Kutuzov has managed.

56.modern-en: Before the grand review at Olmütz, the Guards march in perfect order past Kutuzov's battle-tested troops on the right flank — the contrast between the fresh-from-Russia Guards and Kutuzov's exhausted veterans is visible in their different bearing.

57.modern-en: At the great Olmütz review of both emperors, Kutuzov's battle-experienced army is prominently placed on the right flank, forming a visible contrast with the newly arrived Guards — both emperors and the Archdukes inspect the combined force before the fateful Austerlitz campaign.

58.modern-en: At headquarters in Olmütz, Boris finds Kutuzov's adjutants and Prince Andrei in their shared hall — the commander in chief's establishment is a scene of controlled busyness, and Boris's awe at the whole headquarters world captures the prestige Kutuzov's position commands.

60.modern-en: On the eve of Austerlitz the activity spreads from the Emperor's headquarters down to Kutuzov's staff and the column commanders — the plan born at Alexander's court is now cascading through the army, and Kutuzov, who opposed it, can do little more than watch the machinery engage.

61.modern-en: At the war council before Austerlitz, Kutuzov sits in an armchair apparently asleep, his uniform unbuttoned, while the energetic Weyrother presents his elaborate battle plan — Kutuzov's strategic skepticism is expressed entirely through his physical absence from the discussion, and he dozes off during the reading of the dispositions.

64.modern-en: Kutuzov rides at the head of Miloradovich's column at Pratzen — Prince Andrei behind him is full of expectation for a heroic moment, and Kutuzov moves with calm authority even as the fog thins and the situation begins to clarify.

65.modern-en: The French appear suddenly just five hundred yards from where Kutuzov stands, and the Russian troops break into panicked retreat — Kutuzov receives a graze wound on the cheek but stays at his post while his aide Nesvitsky begs him to ride away, and his one displayed response is to pull out a handkerchief to stanch the blood.

67.modern-en: In the chaos after Austerlitz, Rostov searches desperately for the Emperor and Kutuzov — a wounded officer says Kutuzov was killed by a cannonball but another corrects him, and nobody knows where the commander in chief actually is amid the rout.

70.modern-en: Kutuzov's name surfaces briefly in Moscow society — at the English Club, people joke that Kutuzov had clearly failed to learn from Suvorov the trick of crowing like a rooster at Austrian war councils, and the older members sternly silence the wit.

71.modern-en: At the English Club dinner celebrating Bagration, Shinshin's joke that Kutuzov had failed to learn Suvorov's trick of crowing at Austrian councils is suppressed by the senior members — Kutuzov's reputation is defended even in social settings.

75.modern-en: Kutuzov writes personally to old Prince Bolkonski with news of Prince Andrei's fall at Austerlitz — the letter is carefully worded, expressing hope that the prince is still alive since no body was found among those listed, and conveying genuine respect for the Bolkonski family's sacrifice.

175.modern-en: After Natasha's broken engagement, Prince Andrei encounters Kutuzov in Petersburg — the old general, who has always been well-disposed toward him, suggests Andrei accompany him to the army in Moldavia, offering both a position and an escape from his private misery, which Andrei accepts.

196.modern-en: In the Petersburg salons, Kutuzov becomes a dividing figure — Anna Pavlovna's circle quotes him approvingly while Helene's pro-French circle dismisses the Russian army's efforts, and the political atmosphere of the salons mirrors the larger struggle of which Kutuzov is now the symbol.

205.modern-en: Kutuzov has just received command of the armies and is reviewing troops near Tsarevo-Zaimishche when Prince Andrei reports — the new commander in chief's carriage stands at the priest's house, and from the field come shouts of 'Hurrah!' as the men hail their new leader.

206.modern-en: Kutuzov meets Prince Andrei warmly and with evident genuine feeling — he expresses sorrow over old Prince Bolkonski's death, insists on keeping Andrei at his side, and when the young man declines and asks to stay with his regiment, Kutuzov lets him go with a shrewd and kindly smile, saying, 'It's not here that men are needed.'

209.modern-en: Kutuzov accepted the Battle of Borodino despite knowing it made no mathematical sense — Tolstoy argues he was not guided by reason but by some force larger than individual will, just as Napoleon was, and both men were ultimately instruments rather than directors of events.

210.modern-en: At Mozhaysk on the eve of Borodino, Kutuzov's movements are tracked indirectly — the stream of wounded coming down toward Pierre, and the general atmosphere of preparation for battle, reflect the system of command through which Kutuzov operates.

211.modern-en: Before Borodino, Pierre surveys the field and glimpses the Russian dispositions — Kutuzov's headquarters and the command structure it represents are the invisible framework behind the troops Pierre sees spread across the plain.

212.modern-en: Kutuzov is seen seated in the shade of a house near the village before Borodino, surrounded by an immense retinue — he has just arrived to review the troops, and Boris shows Pierre around camp while angling to present Kutuzov's dispositions as strategically brilliant.

220.modern-en: On the morning of Borodino, Pierre sees Kutuzov's gray head and white cap visible on the knoll as the firing begins — the commander in chief is looking through his field glass down the road, surrounded by his staff, already receiving and processing the morning's first reports.

225.modern-en: During the Battle of Borodino, Kutuzov sits on his bench outwardly passive but inwardly tracking the one thing that matters — the spirit of the army — and his occasional laconic orders reflect his deep conviction that a battle is won by morale, not by command.

231.modern-en: After Borodino, Kutuzov alone among the commanders grasped that it had been a victory — he reported this to the Emperor, prepared for a further engagement, and, Tolstoy argues, understood intuitively what no calculation could have shown: that the French army was mortally wounded.

232.modern-en: Before the Council of Fili, Kutuzov sits alone on a bench on Poklonny Hill listening to the generals debate — he cannot bring himself to accept that Moscow must be abandoned, but when Ermolov reports that the city cannot be defended, Kutuzov checks his pulse and says he is not well, unable yet to face the decision.

233.modern-en: Kutuzov presides over the Council of Fili from a dark corner of the peasant hut, hidden behind the stove — he barely speaks but his presence dominates, and after hearing all opinions he gives the order to retreat through Moscow, accepting the decision history required.

239.modern-en: The news of Kutuzov's decision to abandon Moscow is circulating through the city's officials — Rostopchin receives a note from Kutuzov in the middle of the night ordering police escorts for the retreating army, and the abruptness and simplicity of the note infuriates and humiliates him.

248.modern-en: Kutuzov's order to retreat through Moscow to the Ryazan road is executed through the night — Kutuzov himself takes a detour through side streets to avoid the press of troops at the Dorogomilov bridge, slipping out of Moscow as the army passes through.

253.modern-en: Kutuzov receives Rostopchin at the camp near Moscow but pays no attention to his offer to help defend the city — he is focused entirely on the army and its needs, and Rostopchin's humiliation at being treated as irrelevant captures Kutuzov's single-minded concentration.

254.modern-en: Kutuzov's brief note to Rostopchin ordering the army's passage through Moscow arrives in the middle of the night — its businesslike terseness, treating Moscow's governor as a logistical instrument, leaves Rostopchin stunned and furious.

265.modern-en: Kutuzov's dispatch from Borodino arrives in Petersburg on the Emperor's birthday — he reports it as a victory, and Petersburg erupts in thanksgiving, with even Prince Vasili claiming he always knew Kutuzov was the only man who could defeat Napoleon.

266.modern-en: Kutuzov's message is delivered to Alexander through the French courier Michaud — the emperor learns that Moscow has been abandoned and burned, and Michaud conveys Kutuzov's reasoning that the only choice had been between losing the army and Moscow together or Moscow alone.

281.modern-en: Tolstoy presents Kutuzov's true merit after Moscow — not the flank march (which the army would have done on its own) but his solitary insistence that Borodino had been a victory, and his unflinching determination to hold the troops back from pointless engagements while the dying French army destroyed itself.

282.modern-en: Kutuzov's brief, politic response to the campaign plan sent from Petersburg — 'plans made at a distance are always difficult to execute' — captures his operating style: not direct confrontation but patient deflection while pursuing his own understanding of what the situation requires.

283.modern-en: Kutuzov signs the orders for the Tarutino attack but then watches the whole operation unravel through incompetence and lost messages — the chapter shows how little his formal authority translates into actual control over an army that can't even get the orders delivered to the right general.

284.modern-en: Kutuzov drives to the assembly point for the Tarutino attack and finds troops eating breakfast instead of already in position — he erupts in fury at the officers responsible, venting his genuine anger and humiliation before composing himself and salvaging what he can of the operation.

286.modern-en: During the Tarutino action Kutuzov accompanies a column but deliberately holds back, declining to order advances and stopping whenever Miloradovich wants to press forward — he knows the battle was poorly planned and refuses to deepen the chaos, and the remark to Ermolov about maneuvers only looking good on paper closes the affair.

287.modern-en: While Napoleon wastes his month in Moscow, Kutuzov holds his army at Tarutino in deliberate strategic patience — the chapter presents Kutuzov's restraint as the unconscious wisdom of a man who does not know exactly why he waits but knows that waiting is correct.

294.modern-en: Kutuzov receives Napoleon's peace letter dated falsely from Moscow and replies as he did to Lauriston: there can be no peace discussion — his refusal is categorical and requires no elaboration.

295.modern-en: In the middle of the night at Litashevka, a courier from Dokhturov brings urgent intelligence that Napoleon is at Forminsk — the message passes through Konovnitsyn, who immediately realizes it must reach Kutuzov, and the sleeping old man must be woken.

296.modern-en: Lying awake at night at Tarutino, Kutuzov thinks through his strategy — his maxim 'patience and time are my warriors' expresses his deep conviction that the French army is already mortally wounded and that the greatest danger would be premature attack or pointless engagement.

297.modern-en: From the moment news of Napoleon's retreat from Moscow reaches him, Kutuzov directs all his energy toward following the retreating enemy at a steady distance rather than racing to cut it off — he understands that the French army is already dissolving and that chasing it harder would only exhaust the Russians.

298.modern-en: As the French flee toward Smolensk along the old road, Kutuzov's pursuit tracks them steadily — the chapter's analysis of momentum and motion frames the pursuit as something beyond individual command, though Kutuzov's policy of steady pressure rather than desperate interception is the correct one.

317.modern-en: Tolstoy addresses the question of why Kutuzov did not capture Napoleon at Krasnoe and the Berezina — his answer is that Kutuzov did not aim at capture but at destruction, which had already occurred, and that his restraint reflected his understanding that the French army was already annihilating itself.

321.modern-en: After Vyazma, Kutuzov can no longer hold his troops back from pursuing the retreating French — but he still directs their efforts to follow steadily rather than outrun themselves, even as the Russian army's own losses from forced marches mount alarmingly.

322.modern-en: Tolstoy delivers his great tribute to Kutuzov — not as a man of conventional genius or strategic brilliance, but as the one commander who understood from beginning to end of the 1812 campaign what was actually happening, never wavering in his understanding that Russia's task was patience rather than glory.

323.modern-en: At Krasnoe, Kutuzov watches seven thousand French prisoners shuffle past his horse — he stares long and pityingly at two soldiers tearing at raw flesh with their hands, then rides on in distressed silence, expressing compassion rather than triumph.

327.modern-en: Kutuzov's strategy is vindicated at the Berezina — not the dramatic last act of a planned trap but the natural conclusion of the course he had steered: follow the dying army steadily and let it destroy itself, which it does, regardless of any plan from Petersburg.

328.modern-en: At Vilna, the Emperor honors Kutuzov with the Order of St. George First Class but is visibly displeased — the old field marshal's refusal to support the coming European campaign, his insistence that Russia has done enough, earns him the contempt of court even as the forms of honor are preserved.

epithet.en: Tsar of Russia

1.modern-en: Emperor Alexander is mentioned at Anna Pavlovna's soirée as the ideal of virtue and greatness, with Andrei skeptically dismissing the flattery surrounding his name.

4.modern-en: Alexander is discussed approvingly among the Petersburg elite, who view him as a liberal-minded reformer bringing Russia into a new era.

7.modern-en: Alexander's progressive reputation is invoked in conversation as the Russian court debates the direction of the country under his reign.

10.modern-en: Boris seeks a transfer and advancement through imperial favor, successfully leveraging connections to the Emperor's circle to secure a better posting.

21.modern-en: Alexander's policies and character are debated at Andrei's dinner, with Andrei expressing growing disillusionment about the gap between the Emperor's ideals and reality.

30.modern-en: At Austerlitz, Alexander is present on the battlefield, his inexperience and idealism contrasted with the practical wisdom Kutuzov tries to counsel him; the Emperor's confidence in the coming battle proves disastrously misplaced.

32.modern-en: After Austerlitz, Alexander is devastated by the defeat—Pierre hears reports of the Emperor weeping alone by a pond, shattered by the catastrophe he helped cause by overriding Kutuzov.

39.modern-en: Alexander's military failure at Austerlitz is discussed among the Moscow society, his reputation shaken though his subjects still express loyalty and hope for future victories.

40.modern-en: Alexander meets Napoleon at Tilsit; the two emperors confer on a raft in the Niemen River, and Rostov watches from the bank, struggling to reconcile his devotion to Alexander with the spectacle of his hero fraternizing with the enemy.

42.modern-en: Rostov sees Alexander during the Tilsit negotiations and is deeply moved by the Emperor's presence, finding it impossible to believe his tsar could conclude an unjust peace despite all evidence.

43.modern-en: Alexander and Napoleon conclude the Treaty of Tilsit; Rostov, tormented by questions of honor and justice, ultimately suppresses his doubts and reaffirms his unquestioning loyalty to the Emperor.

51.modern-en: Alexander's Tilsit alliance with Napoleon is discussed critically in Moscow society, seen as a humiliation; Andrei's disillusionment with the tsar deepens.

58.modern-en: Alexander and Napoleon are discussed in the context of the Franco-Russian alliance following Tilsit; Russian society is divided between those who accept the new political reality and those who see it as a betrayal.

59.modern-en: Alexander's domestic reforms under Speransky's influence are the subject of conversation; the Emperor is portrayed as genuinely committed to modernizing Russia's administration.

60.modern-en: Napoleon and Alexander exchange diplomatic courtesies in the spirit of the Tilsit alliance; the relationship between the two emperors is superficially cordial but internally strained.

62.modern-en: Alexander's reformist agenda, guided by Speransky, is discussed; Andrei becomes involved with the reform commission and is initially enthusiastic about the Emperor's progressive program.

64.modern-en: Alexander's administration and the Speransky reforms are debated in Petersburg society; some see the Emperor as a genuine reformer while others are skeptical of lasting change.

66.modern-en: Alexander is praised and analyzed in court circles; his character—charming, idealistic, but easily influenced—is a subject of quiet discussion among those who know him.

72.modern-en: The Emperor's court continues to be shaped by the Speransky reform movement, and Alexander's reputation as a reforming tsar is at its height, though personal rivalries complicate the project.

100.modern-en: Alexander dismisses Speransky from his position, abruptly ending the reform era; the decision shocks Petersburg society and reveals the Emperor's susceptibility to court intrigue over principled governance.

102.modern-en: The fall of Speransky is discussed widely; Alexander's reversal on reform is seen by some as weakness and by others as a necessary course correction, leaving his reputation for liberalism in tatters.

104.modern-en: Rostov encounters both Emperor Alexander and Napoleon at Tilsit in his memories and current experience; his reverence for Alexander remains unshaken despite the political compromises the tsar has made.

105.modern-en: Alexander reviews his troops and is greeted with genuine adoration; Rostov in particular is overwhelmed by emotion at the sight of his emperor, his doubts swept away by the power of the imperial presence.

106.modern-en: Alexander's personal charisma is on display during military reviews; the soldiers and officers respond to him with fervent loyalty, and even skeptics are temporarily won over by his manner.

110.modern-en: The Speransky era of reform is discussed in retrospect; Alexander's vision for modernizing Russia's government is seen as genuine but ultimately thwarted by the conservative forces he could not resist.

120.modern-en: Alexander attends the great ball in Petersburg, his presence electrifying the room; Natasha is awed when the Emperor notices her and smiles, an encounter that forms one of the evening's memorable moments.

121.modern-en: At the ball, Alexander dances and moves through the crowd with practiced imperial grace; his notice of Natasha Rostova is brief but significant, cementing the evening as a triumph for her.

122.modern-en: Alexander continues to move through the ball, the center of attention; his presence elevates the occasion for everyone there, and his easy charm is universally admired.

123.modern-en: Alexander is present at court events and is discussed in the salons; his political decisions continue to be analyzed and debated by the Petersburg elite.

124.modern-en: The Emperor's court policies and personal inclinations are the subject of discussion; Alexander's character—idealistic yet indecisive—is a recurring theme in Petersburg society.

148.modern-en: As war with Napoleon looms, Alexander's court is consumed with planning and diplomacy; the Emperor personally oversees preparations and attempts to manage the political situation.

170.modern-en: Alexander is discussed in the context of the diplomatic mission; Balashëv is dispatched by the Emperor to Napoleon with a letter seeking to avoid war or negotiate terms.

171.modern-en: Balashëv carries Alexander's letter to Napoleon, navigating through French-occupied territory; the mission represents Alexander's last diplomatic attempt before full-scale war begins.

172.modern-en: Balashëv is finally received by Napoleon, who uses the audience to lecture, mock, and assert his dominance; Alexander's message is essentially ignored as Napoleon makes clear he will not stop the war.

173.modern-en: Napoleon continues his audience with Balashëv, dismissing Alexander's overtures and demonstrating contempt for Russian diplomatic efforts; the mission fails entirely.

174.modern-en: Balashëv returns to Alexander empty-handed, reporting Napoleon's dismissive response; the failure of the mission confirms that war is inevitable and diplomacy is exhausted.

185.modern-en: As the French invasion begins, Alexander issues a ringing manifesto calling the Russian people to defend the fatherland; the document inflames patriotic feeling across the country.

186.modern-en: Alexander's manifesto galvanizes Moscow society; the Emperor's call to arms is read and discussed everywhere, and the patriotic response begins to take shape.

187.modern-en: Alexander arrives in Moscow and is received with extraordinary popular enthusiasm; the streets are thronged with crowds shouting their devotion, and the Emperor is visibly moved by the reception.

188.modern-en: Alexander meets with Moscow's nobility and gentry, appealing for support and sacrifices for the war effort; the response is enthusiastic, with pledges of money and men.

189.modern-en: At a gathering of Moscow nobles, Alexander addresses the assembly personally, inspiring pledges of military service and financial donations; the mood is one of intense patriotic fervor.

190.modern-en: Alexander receives the combined pledge of the Moscow nobility and merchants; the meeting is a powerful demonstration of elite loyalty, though the practical organization of the response remains chaotic.

191.modern-en: As Napoleon approaches, Alexander refuses all overtures for negotiation; his position hardens into total resistance, rejecting any compromise that would end the war on Napoleon's terms.

196.modern-en: Alexander's war policy is discussed; the Emperor's refusal to negotiate is both admired as principled and criticized as inflexible by different factions in the Russian court.

207.modern-en: Alexander receives news from the front as Borodino approaches; his court at Petersburg is anxious, and the Emperor weighs the military situation with his advisors.

208.modern-en: Alexander's strategic decisions regarding the campaign are debated; his earlier reluctance to appoint Kutuzov as commander-in-chief is recalled as tension mounts before the great battle.

209.modern-en: The Emperor is kept informed of military developments; Alexander's relationship with Kutuzov—uneasy and marked by mutual distrust—shapes the command structure at a critical moment.

216.modern-en: On the eve of Borodino, Alexander is discussed in the army's conversations; his overall direction of the war effort is both praised and questioned by officers who wish for clearer leadership.

218.modern-en: Alexander's presence in the broader war narrative is felt as Borodino is fought; his authority and his generals' actions unfold against the backdrop of the Emperor's stated war aims.

219.modern-en: As the battle of Borodino unfolds, Alexander's strategic decisions from Petersburg continue to shape how the army is deployed; commanders on the field must navigate between his directives and battlefield reality.

224.modern-en: Alexander learns of the results of Borodino; the bloody and inconclusive outcome leaves the Emperor's court in a state of shock and anxiety about what comes next.

248.modern-en: News of the fall of Moscow reaches Alexander; the Emperor is devastated but resolves never to make peace with Napoleon, even with the old capital in French hands.

258.modern-en: Alexander's refusal to negotiate with Napoleon, even as Moscow burns, is reported and analyzed; his determination is seen as both courageous and potentially catastrophic.

264.modern-en: Kutuzov's dispatch announcing the victory at Borodino arrives at Alexander's court on the Emperor's birthday, creating a brief moment of celebration before the darker news arrives.

265.modern-en: The arrival of Kutuzov's Borodino dispatch on Alexander's birthday briefly raises spirits at court, but the full picture of Russian losses and the retreat to Moscow soon dispels any euphoria.

266.modern-en: Alexander receives Colonel Michaud's report on the fall of Moscow; the Emperor is visibly shaken but responds with steely resolve, declaring he will grow a beard and eat potatoes in Siberia before surrendering.

281.modern-en: Alexander continues to reject all peace overtures from Napoleon; his resolve hardens as the occupation of Moscow drags on and Napoleon's position weakens.

282.modern-en: Alexander sends a letter to Kutuzov reprimanding him for perceived passivity; the communication reflects the Emperor's impatience with Kutuzov's strategy of waiting and attrition.

288.modern-en: Napoleon writes a letter to Alexander seeking peace negotiations; Alexander does not reply, confirming his absolute refusal to engage with the French emperor on any terms.

289.modern-en: Napoleon's various diplomatic and administrative measures in Moscow all fail because Alexander refuses to acknowledge them; the French envoys to Alexander are ignored, and their messages go unanswered.

297.modern-en: As the French retreat begins, Alexander's strategic decisions guide the pursuit; his advisors debate how aggressively to follow the retreating army.

312.modern-en: Napoleon is glimpsed by Pierre during the retreat—a marshal in a carriage passes the prisoners—but Alexander's broader authority shapes the political context of Russia's advancing armies.

316.modern-en: The philosophical meaning of Napoleon's retreat is analyzed; Alexander's role in refusing to negotiate and sustaining Russian resistance is identified as the decisive factor in the campaign's outcome.

322.modern-en: Alexander is dissatisfied with Kutuzov's conduct of the final stages of the campaign; despite Kutuzov's strategic genius, the Emperor views him as failing to deliver a decisive blow against the retreating French.

327.modern-en: As the Berezina crossing marks the final collapse of the Grande Armée, Alexander's military strategy—refusing to let diplomacy slow the campaign—is vindicated by events.

328.modern-en: Alexander honors Kutuzov with the Order of St. George, First Class, but his personal displeasure with the field marshal is apparent; the Emperor is already looking beyond the Russian campaign toward a wider European war.

338.modern-en: Seven years later, Alexander is listed among the historical figures of the post-war era who are accused of promoting 'reaction'; the novel's philosophical discussion places him in the context of European political history.

339.modern-en: Alexander's role as a historical actor is examined philosophically; the novel argues that attributing Europe's fate to his will or genius misunderstands the real forces driving history.

340.modern-en: The forces that shaped the Napoleonic era—and Alexander's place within them—are analyzed; the novel argues that both Napoleon and Alexander were instruments of larger historical currents rather than their authors.

341.modern-en: The Epilogue traces the aftermath of the war and Alexander's place in the new European order; the novel suggests that 'the reaction' attributed to Alexander and others was itself a product of forces beyond any individual's control.

350.modern-en: Alexander is not directly present in this domestic scene among the Rostovs and Bolkonskys, but the political era he has shaped forms the background of the characters' settled post-war lives.

351.modern-en: Young Nicholas Bolkonsky listens avidly to Pierre's account of his political activities; the new Russia that Alexander has helped create provides the context for the next generation's dreams.

354.modern-en: The Second Epilogue's philosophical argument uses Alexander as a case study in the limits of 'great man' history; the novel challenges the idea that his will drove events rather than expressing deeper historical forces.

355.modern-en: Napoleon and Alexander are explicitly named as examples of the 'historical figures' whose will supposedly determines events; Tolstoy argues that attributing the era's history to them is a fundamental misunderstanding of causation.

57.modern-en: Alexander reviews the combined Austrian and Russian forces before Austerlitz alongside the Austrian Emperor; the pageant of military power impresses everyone, but Kutuzov's grim mood hints at the disaster to come.

67.modern-en: After the catastrophe of Austerlitz, a soldier reports to Rostov that he saw the Emperor in a carriage, white-faced, being driven at speed from the battlefield—a humiliating flight that shatters the heroic image of the day.

68.modern-en: Napoleon surveys the Austerlitz battlefield and comes upon the wounded Prince Andrei; Alexander's defeat is implicit in every detail of Napoleon's triumphant inspection of the Russian dead and dying.

70.modern-en: Back in Moscow after the campaign, Rostov finds that his passion for the Emperor has 'cooled somewhat,' though he still speaks of Alexander with reverential loyalty and hints at a special bond that others cannot understand.

71.modern-en: At the English Club, Moscow society discusses the war's progress; Alexander's reputation is debated, with mixed feelings about the Tilsit settlement and the new Franco-Russian alliance.

90.modern-en: After Pierre's duel with Dolokhov, society notes that duels are technically forbidden under Alexander's orders, yet neither Pierre nor his seconds face consequences—a sign of how the Emperor's decrees are selectively applied.

93.modern-en: Bilibin's sardonic letter to Andrei describes the Russian army's sorry state after Austerlitz; Alexander's political maneuvering and diplomatic failures in the wake of the defeat are mocked with affectionate irony.

103.modern-en: Rostov arrives at Tilsit carrying Denisov's letter for the Emperor; Boris is also present, carefully observing Alexander and Napoleon's historic meeting on the raft as a career opportunity, timing the encounter to the minute.

111.modern-en: Andrei arrives in Petersburg and is drawn into the Speransky reform circle; Alexander is the visionary behind this modernizing movement, and the excitement in reformist circles reflects the Emperor's genuine engagement with the project.

168.modern-en: The novel's philosophical analysis of the 1812 war begins; Alexander's firmness and diplomatic stance are cited by historians as among the causes of the war, though Tolstoy dismisses such explanations as superficial.

169.modern-en: Napoleon crosses the Niemen and invades Russia; Alexander is his ultimate opponent, and Napoleon's letter to 'mon frere' expressing false friendship underscores how completely diplomacy has broken down between the two emperors.

176.modern-en: Andrei arrives at the Drissa camp where Alexander is headquartered; the Emperor is surrounded by competing advisors offering contradictory strategic plans, and the atmosphere of confusion and indecision is striking.

177.modern-en: Alexander summons Andrei to meet him personally for his views on the campaign; the Emperor is observed dismounting, looking fatigued and displeased after inspecting the poorly conceived Drissa fortifications.

178.modern-en: Alexander enters Bennigsen's headquarters and greets Andrei warmly; the council gathered there—full of quarreling advisors—reflects the disorder and confusion surrounding the Emperor's military planning at this crisis moment.

195.modern-en: The retreat from Smolensk continues through scorching heat; Andrei commands his regiment along the dusty highway, and Alexander's authority and strategic decisions shape the desperate circumstances of the army's withdrawal.

197.modern-en: Napoleon approaches Moscow, described by Tolstoy as 'the sacred city of Alexander's people'; the philosophical analysis frames the campaign as driven by forces no individual—not Napoleon, not Alexander—could control or predict.

epithet.en: Russian general at Schon Grabern and Austerlitz
epithet.da: Russisk general ved Schon Grabern og Austerlitz

41.modern-en: Bagration is not yet on scene in this chapter — Andrei rides to find the army after his Vienna mission; the chapter establishes the chaotic retreat Bagration's detachment is part of.

42.modern-en: Kutuzov sends Bagration's detachment of six thousand men on a desperate flank march to hold the road at Schöngraben while the main army retreats to Znaim — Bagration is tasked with a near-suicidal rearguard mission against a much larger French force.

43.modern-en: Bagration receives Andrei at his Grünth headquarters before the Battle of Schöngraben with quiet respect; he tells Andrei there will probably be an engagement and gives him full freedom to observe or join the rearguard — Bagration himself is calm and unhurried while his detachment braces for the French attack.

45.modern-en: As the battle begins, Andrei gallops back from the battery to report to Bagration; Bagration is riding toward the front in his Cossack cloak with the characteristic serene composure that will become his hallmark — calmly directing without visible agitation.

46.modern-en: Bagration rides to the right flank through smoke and chaos, past streams of wounded men; he moves to the firing line and by his calm, unhurried presence steadies the soldiers more than any order could — they fight harder simply because he is there.

47.modern-en: The left flank is outflanked and collapses partly because Bagration's order to retreat was never delivered — Zherkov's cowardice means the courier never reached the commanders there; Bagration himself holds the right flank.

48.modern-en: The infantry panic on the left flank echoes through the battle; Bagration holds his portion of the line through sheer force of will and presence while the broader action falls into confusion.

49.modern-en: The battle of Schöngraben ends with the army pulling back; Bagration's detachment has accomplished its mission — holding off the French long enough for Kutuzov's main army to reach safety — but the cost has been heavy.

59.modern-en: Bagration commands the advance at Wischau; Rostov watches from the reserve as the engagement proceeds successfully and Bagration's detachment takes French prisoners — a small but cheering victory on the eve of Austerlitz.

61.modern-en: Bagration declines to attend the council of war before Austerlitz, sending his orderly with the excuse that he cannot come — an implicit protest against the complex Weyrother battle plan he distrusts; his absence speaks louder than words.

62.modern-en: Bagration commands the right flank at Austerlitz; on skirmish duty ahead of his position, Rostov watches the distant glow of French campfires and dreams of the Emperor.

66.modern-en: On the morning of Austerlitz, Bagration delays attacking on the right flank, buying time by proposing to send a message to Kutuzov — a shrewd tactical pause while the disastrous battle unfolds on other parts of the line; he sends Rostov on the mission.

70.modern-en: Bagration is not directly present; this chapter follows Rostov's return to Moscow where his heroic service under Bagration is part of his social currency.

71.modern-en: At the English Club dinner, Bagration is celebrated as the hero of Schöngraben; a toast is drunk to his health and a cantata composed in his honor — he sits at the table surrounded by admirers, the most celebrated commander of the 1805 campaign.

176.modern-en: Bagration is not present in this scene at army headquarters; Prince Andrei observes the chaos at Drissa and the conflicting opinions of generals.

178.modern-en: Not present; the war council scene at Drissa where multiple generals argue over strategy.

191.modern-en: The chapter is a philosophical reflection on causation in history — Bagration is not directly present but is named among the actors of 1812 whose personal aims served larger historical forces they could not foresee.

221.modern-en: Not directly present in this Borodino scene following Pierre's wanderings on the battlefield.

225.modern-en: At Borodino's critical moment, news reaches Kutuzov that Prince Bagration has been wounded; Kutuzov groans and shakes his head — the wound is severe, and the loss of Bagration's steadiness on the left flank is felt immediately.

epithet.en: Humble artillery officer, hero of Schon Grabern
epithet.da: Ydmyg artilleriofficer, helt fra Schon Grabern

43.modern-en: Captain Tushin is first encountered shoeless in the sutler's tent at Grunth, philosophizing with fellow officers about death and the soul — the staff officer reprimands him for leaving his post, but Prince Andrew is immediately struck by the little artillery officer's distinctive quality: something completely unsoldierly but deeply appealing.

44.modern-en: From his battery position with the best view of the field, Tushin philosophizes with fellow officers about what lies beyond death — his voice is pleasant, calm, and genuinely thoughtful; when the first French shell lands near the hut he rushes out still with his pipe clenched between his teeth, and then returns immediately to his guns.

45.modern-en: As Bagration rides to inspect the position before battle, Tushin is found already lobbing incendiary shells at the village of Schöngraben on his own initiative — nobody ordered it, but he decided it would be useful; he greets the general with a clumsy, priest-like gesture and goes on directing his battery with cheerful absorption.

48.modern-en: During the battle of Schöngraben, Tushin's four undefended guns keep firing throughout the entire engagement — their aggressiveness convinces the French that the Russian main force is concentrated there; Tushin himself enters a fantastical dream-world, naming his guns, picturing the enemy as ant-like figures, immune to fear, until the staff officer and then Prince Andrew arrive to order him to withdraw.

49.modern-en: Tushin withdraws his two surviving guns through the night, carrying wounded soldiers including Rostov on the gun carriages — at Bagration's headquarters he is brought up before the generals and stands speechless with trembling jaw, unable to explain why he lost the guns without getting another officer in trouble; Prince Andrew's unexpected speech in his defense saves him from censure.

102.modern-en: Tushin reappears in the military hospital, now missing an arm — he greets Rostov warmly, remembering the ride he gave him at Schöngraben, and serves as the voice of gentle, practical reason in the ward: he advises Denisov to sign the petition for pardon rather than fight the system, and listens with patient, disapproving headshakes while Denisov reads his defiant letter aloud.

epithet.en: Peasant soldier, embodies Russian folk wisdom

275.modern-en: In the ruins of the prison shed after the executions, Platon Karataev is the small, round, warm figure who first reaches out to Pierre — he unwraps potatoes from a rag, shares them with quiet simplicity, asks gentle questions about Pierre's life, tells a long story about his own misfortune that became a blessing, and falls asleep praying; in his presence, Pierre feels the shattered world beginning to reconstitute on new foundations.

276.modern-en: The narrative describes Karataev directly: a round, supple, fifty-year-old former peasant soldier, always busy, always cheerful, incapable of thinking about yesterday or tomorrow, telling proverbs and folk stories whose meaning he could not repeat but which carried profound wisdom — for Pierre he becomes an embodiment of something eternal, simple, and true.

290.modern-en: During the weeks of captivity, Karataev sews a shirt for a French soldier and handles the transaction with such natural, unselfconscious generosity that even the Frenchman is moved and returns the leftover cloth — Karataev receives this small act of humanity with quiet joy, reflecting simply that even among these people there are souls.

291.modern-en: The narrative describes what Pierre has gained from captivity and especially from Karataev: not through intellect but through life itself he has found the peace of mind and inner harmony he had sought everywhere else in vain — in philanthropy, Freemasonry, wine, heroic sacrifice, and romantic love — and all of it flows from the simple, round, unconscious truth that Karataev embodies.

310.modern-en: On the retreat from Moscow, Karataev falls ill again with fever and grows weaker each day — Pierre, who has loved him without acknowledging it, begins keeping his distance as Karataev deteriorates, unable to face the coming loss; the march has by now stripped all the prisoners to their essentials, and Karataev's decline is one of the facts Pierre tries not to look at.

311.modern-en: The night before his death, Karataev tells Pierre the story of the merchant who was falsely convicted and suffered innocently in Siberia — the true killer eventually confesses, but the merchant dies just before the pardon arrives; Karataev tells it with radiant, joyful emotion, the story's meaning residing not in any logical moral but in the mysterious beauty of suffering accepted and forgiven.

312.modern-en: As the column moves on, Karataev sits against a birch tree, too weak to walk — Pierre sees him looking with kind, tear-filled eyes, clearly wanting to say something, but Pierre looks away and walks on; a shot sounds from behind, the dog begins to howl, and the soldiers around Pierre avoid looking back; Karataev is dead.

313.modern-en: Chapter 313 focuses on Pierre's liberation and the aftermath of the partisans' rescue — Karataev's dog, which has been following the column, reappears beside a Russian prisoner at the campfire; when Pierre almost speaks his name, the accumulated memory of Karataev, his death, and the meaning of everything he represented floods back, and Pierre is on the verge of understanding something he cannot quite hold.

334.modern-en: In the epilogue, Natasha asks Pierre whether Platon Karataev would have approved of his current life and political ambitions — Pierre thinks seriously and concludes that Karataev would not have understood the public work but would have approved of the family life; Karataev has become for Pierre a permanent moral touchstone, the embodiment of the simplest and most complete way of being.

epithet.en: Vera's pragmatic German husband

14.modern-en: Berg is mentioned only obliquely — Natasha teases Vera about 'her Berg,' establishing him as Vera's suitor and implying the relationship is already a family joke before he ever appears in the narrative.

18.modern-en: At the Rostov dinner, Berg delivers a lengthy, self-absorbed monologue comparing the financial advantages of the Guards over the infantry — pay, allowances, social prospects — while the other guests mock him behind his back; he does not notice, ends by going into the dining room with Vera on his arm, satisfied with himself.

56.modern-en: At Olmutz, Berg is found in a spotlessly clean uniform playing chess with Boris — when Rostov visits, Berg handles the incident of the Grand Duke's fury with textbook rule-following certainty, and Boris finds his reliability convenient; Berg is already a model of self-interested correctness.

117.modern-en: Berg proposes to Vera in Petersburg with precise methodical preparation, negotiating the dowry down to a specific sum ('or at least twenty thousand in cash') and explaining to acquaintances his systematic approach to career advancement and social positioning; he gets engaged on his own terms.

126.modern-en: Berg invites Pierre to his new apartment for 'a small gathering,' describing every detail — the furniture, the expected guests including a general — with the same self-satisfied precision he applies to his career; the invitation is less about friendship than about maintaining appearances.

127.modern-en: Berg's first evening party at his new apartment is a perfect imitation of every other party he has observed — the right furniture, the right guests, the samovar, the card table — and he is radiantly pleased that it is exactly like all the others; when the general starts an important-sounding discussion, Berg pulls Pierre into it to supply the final required element.

194.modern-en: In the chaos of burning Smolensk, Berg appears on horseback as assistant chief of staff and shouts at Prince Andrew for standing by while houses burn — then immediately backtracks with obsequious apologies when he recognizes who he is addressing; he has no useful function in the crisis, only the authority to reprimand, and Prince Andrew ignores him and rides away.

245.modern-en: Berg arrives at the Rostov house in Moscow during the evacuation, makes patriotic speeches about Russian heroism, and then asks his father-in-law for a cart — not for the wounded, but to carry away a chiffonier and dressing table he wants to buy for Vera; the count explodes with disgust, and it is Berg's craven request that triggers Natasha's furious intervention on behalf of the wounded soldiers.

epithet.en: Boris's wealthy wife

4.modern-en: Chapter 4 does not feature Julie Karagina — it focuses on Prince Andrew's arrival at Anna Pavlovna's salon and Anna Mikhaylovna Drubetskaya lobbying Prince Vasili about Boris; Julie is not present.

10.modern-en: Marya Lvovna Karagina and her daughter Julie arrive at the Rostov name-day reception — they are announced formally and received by the countess, who is tired of guests but sees them anyway; Julie's presence at the family gathering sets her up as a fixture in the Rostov social world.

12.modern-en: During the name-day celebration, Julie talks with young Nicholas Rostov — she addresses him tenderly and draws him into private conversation, flirting with the involuntary charm of a society girl, while Sonya watches in jealous anguish; Julie's attention to Nicholas is light and social, not serious, but it wounds Sonya deeply.

18.modern-en: At the Rostov dinner, Julie goes into the dining room with Nicholas as his partner, continuing the easy social flirtation of the name-day — she is part of the assembled company but takes no significant individual action; her presence anchors her role as a recurring family acquaintance in these early chapters.

20.modern-en: Julie plays a piece on the harp when the guests gather around the clavichord — after performing, she joins the young women who urge Natasha and Nicholas to sing; she is a pleasant, capable participant in the musical evening, representing the comfortable social world the Rostovs inhabit.

25.modern-en: Princess Mary receives a long, gossipy letter from Julie, full of sentimental confessions: Julie writes that Nicholas Rostov's departure for the army has been 'a great sorrow' to her, that she considers their bond 'sweet friendship' if not love, and that all Moscow is discussing the Bezukhov inheritance — she also mentions the rumor that Anatole Kuragin may be proposed as a husband for Princess Mary; the letter reveals Julie as a romantic, socially connected young woman who uses sentiment as social currency.

131.modern-en: Princess Mary writes to Julie (now in Petersburg and in mourning for a brother killed in Turkey) a long letter of spiritual comfort, defending her view of death as God's providence, expressing concern for Prince Andrew, and firmly denying rumors of his engagement to young Natasha Rostova; Julie is the recipient who occasions Princess Mary's deepest private reflections.

140.modern-en: Julie Karagina is identified by Countess Rostova as the only viable wealthy match for Nicholas — the countess has written to Julie's mother in Moscow proposing a marriage and received a favorable reply; Julie has recently become a wealthy heiress through her last brother's death, and the entire Rostov financial recovery is staked on whether Nicholas will agree to court her.

147.modern-en: When Princess Mary moves to Moscow for the winter, she meets Julie in person for the first time in years and is disappointed — Julie, now one of Moscow's wealthiest heiresses, has transformed into a society hostess affecting fashionable melancholy, surrounded by young men and consumed by parties; the warm epistolary friendship proves hollow in person, and Princess Mary finds she has no one left to confide in.

149.modern-en: Pierre tells Princess Mary that Boris Drubetskoy is courting both Julie and Princess Mary simultaneously, playing the role of melancholy suitor at Julie's house — Julie has adopted the current fashion of theatrical sadness and Boris performs alongside her; Pierre's amused account reveals Julie's social performance as transparent to outside observers.

150.modern-en: Boris formally courts and proposes to Julie — after a month of shared melancholy sketches and mournful harp music, threatened by Anatole Kuragin's arrival in her drawing room, he finally declares himself; Julie accepts triumphantly, the Penza estates and Nizhegorod forests secured on both sides, and the engagement is arranged with satisfied efficiency by two people who have calculated rather than loved.

153.modern-en: At the opera, Natasha spots Julie and Boris in their box as an engaged couple — Julie sits beside her mother wearing pearls and a happy expression, with Boris leaning over her ear; Natasha observes them without envy, dismissed by her own preoccupations, and the glimpse confirms Julie's social success after a marriage of convenience.

156.modern-en: Julie is mentioned as one of the rich heiresses Anatole Kuragin was sent to Moscow to pursue — Prince Vasili pointed his son toward both Princess Mary and Julie Karagina, though Anatole's arrival ultimately accelerates Boris's proposal rather than producing any courtship of his own; Julie functions here as part of the social landscape through which Anatole moves.

192.modern-en: Now Julie Drubetskaya (Boris's wife), she writes patriotic letters to Princess Mary from Moscow as Napoleon's army approaches — her letter is full of performative fervor ('we in Moscow are filled with enthusiasm for our adored Emperor') and personal news about bandage-making parties; Princess Mary reads the letter as one of many outside signals about the war that she cannot quite grasp.
