207.modern-en: Julie hosts a farewell gathering in Moscow as the city empties before Napoleon's advance — she presides over a parlor game in which French must not be spoken and fines are paid for slipping into Gallicisms, while gossiping about the Rostovs' financial troubles and Natasha's recovery; she departs for Nizhny the next day, remarking breezily that she is not Joan of Arc.

214.modern-en: Julie Drubetskaya is mentioned by Pierre in passing — he tells Prince Andrew, who asks about his family, that Julie told him the Bolkonskys had arrived in Moscow and then gone to their estate; Julie's brief mention connects the two storylines on the eve of Borodino.

epithet.en: French companion to Princess Marya

25.modern-en: Princess Mary's letter to Julie mentions Mademoiselle Bourienne only in the postscript — 'my dear friend Mademoiselle Bourienne sends you kisses' — establishing her as the warm, socially integrated companion at Bald Hills without any individual action in this chapter.

26.modern-en: Mademoiselle Bourienne bursts out of the sitting room when Prince Andrew and his wife arrive at Bald Hills, 'beside herself with excitement' — she greets the little princess warmly, is embraced, and weeps alongside Princess Mary when the sisters-in-law are reunited; her presence is cheerful, socially fluent, and eager to please.

27.modern-en: At dinner at Bald Hills with the old prince, Prince Andrew, and Mikhail Ivanovich, Mademoiselle Bourienne joins in conversation when talk of Napoleon and France arises — the prince addresses her in French as 'another admirer of that gunpowder-monkey emperor,' and she protests that she is not a Bonapartist; she fulfills her role as the lively social companion who navigates the household's tensions with practiced ease.

28.modern-en: Prince Andrew encounters Mademoiselle Bourienne for the third time that day in a corridor — she appears with her 'ecstatic, seemingly artless smile' and pretends she thought he was in his room; he looks at her with cold contempt and she slips away without a word; later she is present at the farewell gathering when the little princess faints, rubbing her temples after Prince Andrew leaves.

52.modern-en: During Anatole Kuragin's visit to Bald Hills, Mademoiselle Bourienne stands beside the frightened Princess Mary before dinner with 'a bright expression that said, I know nothing, I'm the same as always' — she smooths the social awkwardness, tells the prince the little princess is unwell as 'natural in her condition,' and chats about the conservatories and flowers to lighten the atmosphere.

53.modern-en: When Anatole arrives in the drawing room, Mademoiselle Bourienne is animated and especially pretty — she joins in the artificial reminiscences about Petersburg parties, and Anatole, noticing her, immediately decides life at Bald Hills might not be boring after all; during Princess Mary's clavichord playing, Anatole's eyes are fixed on Mademoiselle Bourienne's foot, which he nudges with his own under the piano, while Bourienne returns looks of fearful excitement and hope.

54.modern-en: After the evening gathering, Mademoiselle Bourienne paces the conservatory waiting for Anatole — the next morning they meet there in secret and are caught embracing by Princess Mary, who has just refused the proposal; Mademoiselle Bourienne runs away when discovered, and later Princess Mary finds her weeping and comforts her, saying she loves her more than ever; the chapter establishes Bourienne as a woman ruled by romantic fantasy who has genuinely let herself fall into temptation.

131.modern-en: In Princess Mary's letter to Julie, Mademoiselle Bourienne is mentioned as someone Princess Mary has kept at a distance but writes greetings from — meanwhile the old prince has begun using Bourienne to wound Princess Mary, turning to her in the daughter's presence to mock religious subjects and ask her opinions in front of the daughter he is tormenting.

132.modern-en: After the old prince hears of Prince Andrew's engagement to Natasha, he erupts in rage and sarcastically threatens to marry Bourienne himself — 'She'll make a splendid princess!' — and from this point begins overtly courting Bourienne's company to hurt Princess Mary, showing her exaggerated affection and using her as a weapon in the household power struggle.

147.modern-en: In Moscow, Princess Mary finds that Mademoiselle Bourienne has become unpleasant to her and she now avoids her — the old prince publicly humiliates Princess Mary by kissing and embracing Bourienne in her presence; when Mary shouts at her to get out, the prince declares Bourienne 'the first person in this house' and orders Mary to beg her pardon.

148.modern-en: On the old prince's name day, after Dr. Metivier is thrown out as a 'spy,' the prince mentions the incident at the dinner table — Mademoiselle Bourienne had been the one who originally advised him to consult Metivier and introduced the doctor to the household; after the outburst the prince retreats to his room and sends for Bourienne.

152.modern-en: When the Rostovs visit Bald Hills to introduce Natasha to Prince Andrew's family, Mademoiselle Bourienne greets them with 'special politeness' and shows them to Princess Mary's room — she then stays in the room chattering about Moscow theaters despite Princess Mary's visible wish to speak privately with Natasha; her presence prevents any real conversation between the two women, and when the old prince bursts in, Bourienne is the first to recover and change the subject.

166.modern-en: After Anatole's failed elopement attempt, Mademoiselle Bourienne has stolen Natasha's letter breaking off the engagement with Prince Andrew and given it to the old prince — this is revealed when Prince Andrew returns to Moscow; Bourienne's act of betrayal poisons Prince Andrew's remaining time at home and confirms her alignment with the old prince against both Princess Mary and any prospect of the family accepting Natasha.

175.modern-en: When Prince Andrew returns to Bald Hills before leaving for war, he finds the household split into two hostile camps — Mademoiselle Bourienne and the architect belong to the old prince's camp, while Princess Mary, Dessalles, and little Nicholas form the other; Prince Andrew tells his father bluntly that 'the worthless woman who is not fit to be my sister's companion' is to blame for the household tensions, triggering the old prince's fury and their final estrangement.

192.modern-en: After Prince Andrew's departure, the old prince falls ill and — significantly — excludes Mademoiselle Bourienne from his room along with Princess Mary, attended only by Tikhon; after recovering, he breaks off his ostentatious relationship with Bourienne and resumes cold formality toward his daughter, with 'instead of Mademoiselle Bourienne — a servant boy read to him.'

200.modern-en: After the old prince's death, Mademoiselle Bourienne comes to Princess Mary in the garden in mourning dress, weeps with her, and then reveals that she has obtained a French general's proclamation promising protection to those who stay — she urges Princess Mary to remain at Bogucharovo under French protection rather than flee; Princess Mary is horrified, rejects the plan as a betrayal of her family name, and orders that Bourienne not be admitted to her room.

269.modern-en: At Voronezh, Mademoiselle Bourienne is present when Nicholas Rostov visits Princess Mary — she observes Princess Mary's transformed face and demeanor with 'bewildered surprise,' thinking 'either black is particularly becoming to her, or she really has greatly improved'; as a 'consummate flirt herself' she recognizes that Princess Mary has maneuvered better in this moment than she could have herself.

277.modern-en: During the difficult journey from Voronezh to Yaroslavl to reach the dying Prince Andrew, Mademoiselle Bourienne travels with the party — the travelers are astonished at Princess Mary's energy and strength of spirit; when they arrive and are met by Princess Mary's courier, Mademoiselle Bourienne asks 'How is the prince?' on behalf of the too-frightened Princess Mary.

343.modern-en: In the epilogue winter in Moscow, when Nicholas Rostov visits Princess Mary to fulfill a social obligation, she sends for Mademoiselle Bourienne and goes with her to the drawing room as chaperone — Bourienne helps keep the conversation going; at the end, as the crucial emotional moment unfolds between Nicholas and Princess Mary, Bourienne leaves the room on a pretext to fetch a cushion, giving them privacy for their breakthrough conversation.

epithet.en: Partisan guerrilla fighter

26.modern-en: Tikhon the old valet is the first to greet Prince Andrew on his return to Bald Hills — he whispers that the prince is sleeping and quickly shuts the door, maintaining the household's rigid routine even for the young prince's arrival; Prince Andrew remarks 'you've gotten older, Tikhon' as he passes.

52.modern-en: As Prince Vasili's visit approaches and the old prince is in a foul mood, Tikhon warns the architect not to go to the prince — he draws attention to the sound of the prince's footsteps: 'Flat on his heels — we know what that means'; Tikhon functions as the household's barometer and protector against the old prince's rages.

54.modern-en: Late at night, after the failed Anatole courtship, Tikhon helps the old prince undress and get into bed — he hears the prince muttering his thoughts aloud about Princess Mary and Mademoiselle Bourienne; when the prince shouts at him asking if the guests have gone to bed, Tikhon confirms they have, and the old prince settles into his bitter, solitary reflections.

76.modern-en: During the night of the little princess's labor, the old prince sends Tikhon repeatedly to ask the midwife for news — Tikhon carries the message 'the prince asked me to inquire' and returns with the reply 'labor has begun'; later Tikhon enters the study, sees the prince lying on the sofa with a troubled face, silently kisses him on the shoulder, and leaves without a word — a gesture of wordless devotion.

193.modern-en: As the old prince deteriorates in his final summer, Tikhon helps him try to find a comfortable place to sleep — the prince cannot bear his usual couch and tries various rooms, ordering Tikhon and a footman to move the bed; when the prince wakes in the night with anxiety about Prince Andrew's letter and the French advance, he calls out 'Tikhon!' and then dismisses him: 'No, no, I don't need anything!'

198.modern-en: During the old prince's final days at Bogucharovo after his stroke, Tikhon attends him constantly — Princess Mary hears 'the steps of Tikhon and the doctor as they turned him over' through the night; in the dying man's last lucid moments, the prince asks Tikhon to wipe away his tears after weeping over Russia's ruin; Tikhon alone deciphers the old man's failing speech throughout his decline.

200.modern-en: After the old prince's death, Tikhon — 'with his sunken, gaunt face bearing the stamp of inconsolable grief' — replies only 'Yes, Princess' to all Princess Mary's questions 'and could barely hold back his sobs as he looked at her'; Tikhon's grief is as total as his long service, and in these moments he expresses more of the household's sorrow than anyone.

202.modern-en: Princess Mary, lying awake after her father's death, recalls the last night at Bald Hills when she listened at the conservatory door and heard her father talking to Tikhon — speaking of the Crimea and the Empress, clearly wanting company; when Tikhon reminded him the late princess Lise was dead, the old prince shouted 'Fool!' — Princess Mary reproaches herself for not entering instead of leaving her father with Tikhon who couldn't understand him.

301.modern-en: Tikhon Shcherbaty (a different character from the old valet — a peasant from Pokrovsk near the Gzhat River) is introduced as the most indispensable man in Denisov's partisan band — he began by fetching water and skinning horses but quickly revealed an extraordinary talent for guerrilla warfare; Denisov sends him to Shamshevo overnight to capture a French 'tongue' for interrogation.

303.modern-en: Tikhon Shcherbaty reappears running through a marsh under French fire after his mission to capture a prisoner goes wrong in daylight — the Cossacks watch from the hill as he plunges into a stream and scrambles out dripping; Denisov is amused but annoyed: 'What a brute! What's he been doing all this time?'; Tolstoy then describes Tikhon's extraordinary character: a gap-toothed peasant who fights with an axe like a wolf uses its teeth, bravest and most useful man in the band.

304.modern-en: Tikhon returns to Denisov and gives his comic account of the failed prisoner-capture — he had grabbed one Frenchman, decided he was 'no good,' let him go to fetch a better one, then was chased by four soldiers and barely escaped; when pressed about what happened to the first prisoner, Tikhon grins his gap-toothed grin, implying he killed the man rather than release him; Denisov threatens lashes but Tikhon offers cheerfully to bring three prisoners after dark.

305.modern-en: Tikhon Shcherbaty is mentioned as Petya's deciding reason to stay with Denisov's band — among Denisov, the esaul, and Tikhon, 'Tikhon was a hero too,' and leaving them at a moment of difficulty seems to Petya unthinkable; Tikhon belongs to the campfire world of the guerrilla detachment that Petya has decided to join for the night's attack, though Tikhon himself does not appear directly in this chapter.

epithet.en: Russian diplomat sent to Napoleon

170.modern-en: Balashëv is dispatched by Emperor Alexander as a diplomatic envoy to Napoleon, carrying a letter seeking to avoid or limit the war before it fully begins.

171.modern-en: Balashëv travels through French-occupied territory toward Napoleon's headquarters, observing the French army's confident advance and being passed from one French officer to another before reaching his destination.

172.modern-en: Balashëv is finally received by Napoleon, who uses the audience to harangue him, mock Russia's military prospects, and demonstrate his utter contempt for Alexander's peace overture; Balashëv listens with dignified restraint.

173.modern-en: Napoleon continues his lengthy audience with Balashëv, lecturing him on military strategy and political reality; Balashëv manages a single dignified reply when Napoleon dismisses Moscow's importance, but the mission is clearly a failure.

174.modern-en: Balashëv dines with Napoleon and is treated with calculated condescension before being dismissed; he returns to Alexander with a full account of Napoleon's refusal to negotiate, confirming that war is now inevitable.

epithet.en: Witty diplomat, friend of Prince Andrei
epithet.da: Vittig diplomat, ven af Fyrst Andrej

38.modern-en: Bilibin welcomes Andrei to his luxurious diplomatic quarters in Brünn after the victory at Schöngraben; he regales his guest with witty, mordantly cynical accounts of Austrian incompetence and the absurd situation of the allied army — his gift for ironic analysis in perfect French immediately charms Andrei.

39.modern-en: Bilibin introduces Andrei to his circle of young diplomats — 'ours' — and helps prepare him for his audience with Emperor Francis; his wry commentary on court life and the gap between the war's reality and its diplomatic performance is on full display.

40.modern-en: After Andrei's brief, disappointing audience with the Austrian Emperor, Bilibin's diplomatic circle commiserates with Andrei and continues their witty dissection of the campaign; Bilibin provides the social and intellectual context that makes Andrei's mission feel both important and faintly ridiculous.

58.modern-en: Boris goes to Bilibin's quarters when seeking an introduction to Andrei; he finds a circle of well-dressed young diplomats there but Andrei is out, and the experience of watching these elegant insiders only sharpens Boris's determination to break into their world.

60.modern-en: Bilibin is not the focus of this chapter; the scene follows the Emperor at Wischau and the diplomatic maneuvers around the proposed meeting with Napoleon.

92.modern-en: Bilibin's long, witty letter to Andrei from army headquarters arrives at Bald Hills, describing the disasters of the Prussian campaign with devastating irony — the Prussians' rapid capitulation, the Russian generals' confusion, the whole farce of coalition warfare laid bare in brilliant, self-mocking French prose.

93.modern-en: The content of Bilibin's letter to Andrei continues — he describes the Russian army's blundering responses to Napoleon's offensive, the diplomatic absurdities, the moral of the Prussian debacle — his letter is one of the few voices of honest clarity amid the official cheerfulness.

236.modern-en: Bilibin is not directly present; this chapter follows Hélène's scandalous attempts to arrange a second marriage while still technically Pierre's wife — Bilibin's world of Petersburg society is the backdrop.

264.modern-en: Bilibin is not directly present; the chapter depicts the artificial calm of Petersburg's salon life during the Borodino crisis — exactly the world Bilibin navigates as a diplomat, though he himself does not appear.
